items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which operation produces the arithmetic mean of four comparable readings?
A. Their sum divided by four
B. Their sum multiplied by four
C. Largest minus smallest
D. The last reading divided by four

2. What does the prefix kilo mean?
A. 100
B. 0.001
C. 1000000
D. 1000

3. Which length is a radius?
A. Around the circle
B. Between arbitrary polygon vertices
C. Centre to circumference
D. Across a circle through its centre

4. Which expression gives triangular area?
A. base × height
B. ½ × base × perpendicular height
C. base + height
D. base × sloping side

5. Which is the SI unit of mass?
A. kg
B. N
C. W
D. Pa

6. Which bearing points east?
A. 000°
B. 180°
C. 270°
D. 090°

7. Which expression is the reciprocal of a nonzero period T?
A. 2T
B. T/2
C. 1/T
D. T²

8. Three repeated times are 9.0 s, 9.2 s and 9.1 s. What is their mean?
A. 3.03 s
B. 9.1 s
C. 27.3 s
D. 0.2 s

9. What is 72 ms in seconds?
A. 0.072 s
B. 72 s
C. 0.72 s
D. 72000 s

10. A square has side 0.50 m. What is its area?
A. 1.0 m²
B. 2.0 m²
C. 0.50 m²
D. 0.25 m²

11. What percentage is 9 J out of 30 J?
A. 0.30%
B. 300%
C. 30%
D. 3.33%

12. What is 6.284 rounded to three significant figures?
A. 6.29
B. 6.28
C. 6.284
D. 6.3
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: The total is shared across the number of readings. B: This scales the total instead of averaging it. C: This gives the range. D: This discards the other readings.

2. Key D. A: This is not the kilo factor. B: This is the milli factor. C: This is the mega factor. D: Kilo multiplies the unit by 10³.

3. Key C. A: That is circumference length. B: That describes neither a circle radius nor its fixed endpoints. C: A radius starts at the centre. D: That is a diameter.

4. Key B. A: This misses the factor one half. B: The triangular region is half the matching parallelogram. C: Adding lengths does not give area. D: The height must be perpendicular and a half is needed.

5. Key A. A: The kilogram measures mass. B: A newton measures force. C: A watt measures power. D: A pascal measures pressure.

6. Key D. A: This points north. B: This points south. C: This points west. D: Bearings are clockwise from north.

7. Key C. A: Doubling is not taking a reciprocal. B: Halving is not taking a reciprocal. C: The reciprocal reverses the ratio. D: Squaring is not taking a reciprocal.

8. Key B. A: This divides a single representative reading by three. B: The sum 27.3 s divided by three is 9.1 s. C: This is the sum, before division. D: This is the range.

9. Key A. A: Milliseconds are divided by 1000. B: The prefix has been ignored. C: This uses the wrong factor. D: This changes in the wrong direction.

10. Key D. A: This adds two sides instead of multiplying. B: This is numerically the perimeter, with the wrong unit. C: This leaves the side value unchanged. D: The product is 0.50 × 0.50.

11. Key C. A: This omits multiplication by 100. B: This introduces an extra factor of ten. C: The ratio is 0.30, or thirty per hundred. D: This reverses the ratio and misuses percent.

12. Key B. A: This rounds upward despite the next digit being less than five. B: The next digit is 4, so the retained hundredths digit stays unchanged. C: This keeps four significant figures. D: This gives two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

(b) s⁻¹

(c) They should estimate the same physical time. Changing the motion would mix different quantities rather than simply reduce random variation.

(d) The total is 37.5 s; 37.5/3 gives a mean of 12.5 s.

(e) 1850/1000 gives 1.85 s.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for timing repeated pendulum oscillations.

| Oscillation count | Elapsed time / s |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 8 |
| 10 | 16 |
| 15 | 24 |
| 20 | 32 |
| 25 | 40 |
| 30 | 48 |

(a) Draw the graph with Elapsed time / s on the vertical axis and Oscillation count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Put oscillation count horizontally and elapsed time vertically. Plot the six points and a straight fitted line through their trend; these idealised values give a zero intercept.

Gradient: 40 ÷ 25 = 1.6 s per oscillation. The gradient estimates the period because it is elapsed time divided by the number of complete oscillations.

Plan: 1. Suspend a small bob from a fixed-length string and mark a consistent reference point for counting. 2. Release it from the same small angle without pushing, keeping the length unchanged. 3. Time a chosen number of complete oscillations using a stopwatch, counting a return to the same position and direction as one cycle. 4. Repeat the timing at that count and calculate a mean, investigating any anomalous reading. 5. Repeat for several oscillation counts while retaining the same pendulum and release conditions.
Control and accuracy: Keep string length and release angle fixed. Count consistently at the same reference; keep the swinging bob clear of people.
Table: Record oscillation count, each elapsed time / s and the mean elapsed time / s in separate labelled columns.
Graph and conclusion: Plot mean elapsed time against oscillation count. A straight trend with a near-zero intercept supports a constant time per cycle; obtain that time from the gradient.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-1.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: add, subtract, multiply and divide rounding the answer correctly
blocks.text:
Addition and subtraction combine measured amounts or find their difference. Multiplication and division combine a measurement with a scale factor or form a ratio.

Choose the operation from the physical question before touching the calculator. A change in temperature is a subtraction, whereas energy supplied at fixed power is found by multiplication. Keep units beside the values so that a sum of unlike quantities is not mistaken for a physical result. Retain extra digits during a calculation and round the final answer. If several steps are required, write them in order; rounding an early intermediate can change the last reported digit.

blocks.heading: Add and subtract with justified rounding
blocks.text:
A measured change is the final value minus the initial value. A sum or difference of measurements should not imply finer decimal-place precision than its least precise input.

A water temperature changes from 18.6 °C to 37.2 °C, giving a rise of 18.6 °C. Subtract the initial reading from the final reading, rather than adding the two temperatures. If the final temperature is lower, the signed change is negative. When adding 6.25 cm to 1.8 cm, the calculator gives 8.05 cm, but a sensible recorded sum is 8.1 cm because one measurement was given to only one decimal place. Do not discard useful digits until the final result.

blocks.heading: Multiply and divide with justified rounding
blocks.text:
Products and quotients relate physical quantities through multiplication or division. For measurements multiplied or divided, final precision is usually limited by the input with the fewest significant figures.

If a model moves 5.4 m in 2.0 s, distance divided by time gives 2.7 m/s. The quotient carries units because metres are divided by seconds. Multiplying instead would produce m s, which is a different kind of quantity. In a longer calculation retain the unrounded quotient until it is used in the next step. A value such as 2.666666 on a display does not mean the original measurements were that precise; a two-significant-figure final answer is 2.7.

blocks.heading: use averages, decimals, fractions, percentages, ratios and reciprocals
blocks.text:
A mean summarises repeated values, while a ratio compares two quantities. Fractions, decimals and percentages can represent the same proportion; a reciprocal reverses a nonzero ratio.

Use a mean when several readings estimate the same quantity under the same conditions. Do not replace the physics of a whole journey by simply averaging speeds when their durations differ. A fraction describes a part relative to a whole, and multiplying that fraction by 100 expresses it as a percentage. A ratio can also carry a unit, such as metres per second. Before using a reciprocal, identify which quantity belongs in the numerator; reversing a ratio changes its meaning and its unit.

blocks.heading: Calculate a mean
blocks.text:
The arithmetic mean is the total of the values divided by their number. Repeated readings should describe the same quantity under comparable conditions before their mean is used.

Three timings of an unchanged motion are 8.2 s, 8.4 s and 8.3 s. Their sum is 24.9 s; dividing by three gives 8.3 s. Include a unit in the result. Check for an anomalous reading before calculating, and investigate it rather than silently deleting an inconvenient number. A mean can reduce the influence of random variation, but does not automatically remove a zero error that shifts every reading together. Keep a record of the original readings so that the calculation can be followed.

blocks.heading: Use decimal and fractional representations
blocks.text:
A decimal can be expressed as a fraction by using its place value. The numerator and denominator of a fraction can be scaled together without changing its value.

The decimal 0.35 means thirty-five hundredths, so it equals 35/100 and simplifies to 7/20. To turn a fraction back into a decimal, divide its numerator by its denominator. For example, 3/8 equals 0.375. Distinguish a fraction of a measured amount from the amount itself: three eighths of 16 m is 6 m, not 0.375 m. Write the fraction first, then apply it to the stated total. Equivalent representations should give the same result when used consistently.

blocks.heading: Use percentages
blocks.text:
A percentage is a proportion expressed per hundred. Percentage = part divided by whole, multiplied by 100.

If a device converts 18 J of an input of 60 J to the desired output, the useful fraction is 18/60. Multiplying by 100 gives 30%. Identify the relevant whole before calculating: using the output as the denominator would answer a different question. A percentage does not carry the unit of the original quantities when like units cancel. Convert unlike energy units before forming the fraction. Conversely, to find 30% of an amount, multiply the amount by 0.30.

blocks.heading: Use ratios
blocks.text:
A ratio compares quantities by division or by an equivalent colon notation. Quantities expressed in the same units can form a dimensionless ratio.

A comparison of 12 cm with 8 cm can be written 12:8 and simplified to 3:2. Both lengths must use compatible units: comparing 0.12 m with 8 cm requires conversion first. The ratio does not state the total size of the objects; 30 cm and 20 cm have the same 3:2 ratio. When dividing a total in a ratio, add the ratio parts first. A total length of 25 cm shared in a 3:2 ratio has five parts, each 5 cm long.

blocks.heading: Use reciprocals
blocks.text:
The reciprocal of a nonzero number is one divided by that number. Taking a reciprocal also reverses the units of a physical ratio.

The reciprocal of 0.20 is 5.0 because 1 divided by 0.20 equals 5.0. If the original quantity is a time of 0.20 s, its reciprocal has units s⁻¹. This is useful when frequency is obtained from a period. The reciprocal of a fraction is found by reversing its numerator and denominator. Zero has no finite reciprocal, so a zero denominator signals that the chosen calculation is not defined. State which physical quantity the reciprocal represents; a numerical reversal alone does not explain its meaning.

blocks.heading: use direct and inverse proportion
blocks.text:
In direct proportion, doubling one quantity doubles the other when relevant conditions are fixed. In inverse proportion, their product is constant, so doubling one quantity halves the other.

For direct proportion, y/x stays constant and a graph of y against x is a straight line through the origin. A straight line with a nonzero intercept is not direct proportion between those plotted quantities. For inverse proportion, xy stays constant and the y-versus-x graph is curved. Compare numerical ratios or products to distinguish the cases. Keep the stated conditions: pressure varies inversely with area only if the force stays fixed. A changing second condition can invalidate a simple scaling prediction.

blocks.heading: use positive and negative, whole number indices and exponents in calculations
blocks.text:
A positive integer index means repeated multiplication of the base. A negative integer index represents the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power.

For example, 10³ is 1000, while 10⁻³ is 0.001. A square applies to an entire quantity: (2 m)² is 4 m², so both the number and the unit are squared. Keep brackets around a negative value before squaring it: (−3)² is positive nine, whereas −3² conventionally means the negative of nine. When multiplying powers of the same base, add their indices; when dividing, subtract them. Indices help express small prefixes and derived units clearly.

blocks.heading: make approximate evaluations of numerical expressions
blocks.text:
An estimate uses rounded values to judge a numerical result before or after exact calculation. An estimate should retain the scale and unit of the original physical problem.

A quotient of 398 by 19.8 should be near 400 divided by 20, or 20. If the calculator result is around 2000, inspect the decimal places and the entered denominator. Estimation is especially helpful with powers of ten and small unit prefixes. It does not replace the final calculation when precise data are available. State that a value is approximate, rather than presenting rounded input as an exact measurement. A rough upper or lower bound can also reveal an impossible answer.

blocks.heading: use usual mathematical instruments (ruler, compasses, protractor, set square)
blocks.text:
A ruler measures lengths, a protractor measures angles, compasses transfer distances or draw circles, and a set square establishes straight perpendicular directions. Choosing an instrument depends on the geometric feature that needs to be measured or constructed.

The tools can be combined in one construction. A ruler can draw a ray, a protractor can measure its angle, and a set square can construct the normal at a surface. Compasses can keep a radius unchanged while a circle or arc is drawn. Read the instrument before using it: identify the zero, direction of numbering and smallest division. Using a more elaborate tool does not automatically make a result accurate if it is aligned incorrectly.

blocks.heading: Use a ruler
blocks.text:
A ruler measures the separation of two positions along its graduated scale. The measured length is the final scale reading minus the initial reading.

Align the ruler with the length to be measured and view the graduation directly above it. The physical end of a ruler may be worn or separated from its zero mark. An intact internal mark can be used as a start, provided its reading is subtracted. For an object extending from 1.2 cm to 7.6 cm, the length is 6.4 cm. Do not automatically treat the end reading as the length when the start is not zero.

blocks.heading: Use compasses
blocks.text:
Compasses draw a circle or arc at a fixed distance from their pivot point. The distance between the point and pencil is the radius of the construction.

Set the separation against a ruler before drawing a circle of a given radius. Place the point at the chosen centre, then rotate the pencil while keeping the opening unchanged. A circle of radius 3 cm has a diameter of 6 cm; setting the compasses to 6 cm instead would make the circle too large. Compasses can also transfer an existing separation without reading it numerically. Hold the point carefully so that it does not slip or damage the working surface.

blocks.heading: Use a protractor
blocks.text:
A protractor measures the angle between two directions. Its centre must be placed at the vertex and its zero line aligned with one ray.

Choose the row of numbers that begins at the aligned ray. Many protractors carry clockwise and anticlockwise scales; using the wrong scale changes an acute angle into its supplementary obtuse angle. For example, an intended 40° construction may be misread as 140°. Extend a short ray with a ruler so that it reaches the scale clearly. In optics, identify the normal before measuring incidence or refraction: an angle to the surface is generally a different angle.

blocks.heading: Use a set square
blocks.text:
A set square provides a right-angle edge for constructing or checking perpendicular directions. A perpendicular normal makes a 90° angle with the surface at the point of interest.

Place one straight edge along the surface or baseline. Draw along the adjoining right-angle edge through the required point. This is useful when a ray diagram needs a normal, or when a ruler must be viewed squarely to a scale. The normal is a geometrical reference line; it is not a light ray or a force by itself. If the baseline is tilted, the normal tilts with it rather than remaining automatically vertical on the page.

blocks.heading: explain the meaning of angle, curve, circle, radius, diameter, square, parallelogram, rectangle, diagonal
blocks.text:
Geometric terms describe the features used in measurement and physical diagrams. An angle describes a turn, while lengths such as radius, diameter and diagonal describe particular separations.

Name the relevant feature before choosing a formula. A radius runs from the centre of a circle to its boundary, whereas a diameter passes across the circle through the centre. A diagonal joins non-adjacent vertices of a polygon. These are not interchangeable lengths even when they appear on the same drawing. Shapes also determine area formulas: multiplying two perpendicular side lengths works for a rectangle, but a triangle uses half the corresponding base-height product.

blocks.heading: Define an angle
blocks.text:
An angle is the amount of turn between two directions meeting at a vertex. A full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°.

When an angle is drawn, label its vertex and the two rays that define it. The size does not depend on how long those rays are drawn. A very short ray and a long ray can make the same angle. In physical diagrams an angle should be measured from the reference specified in the question, such as a normal or a horizontal line.

blocks.heading: Describe a curve
blocks.text:
A curve is a line whose direction changes along its length. A graph can contain a smooth curve rather than a straight fitted line.

Distinguish the shape of the line from errors caused by thick plotting marks. A smooth curve should follow the trend of the readings without joining every neighbouring pair by straight segments. Its steepness can change from one location to another. An arc of a circle is one example of a curve, but not every curve is circular.

blocks.heading: Describe a circle
blocks.text:
A circle is a plane curve whose points are the same distance from one centre. That fixed centre-to-curve distance is its radius.

The centre may lie inside the drawn region without being a marked point on the curve. Use a labelled centre when identifying a radius or diameter. If a string traces points that are not the same distance from the centre, it has not constructed a circle. The region enclosed by the circumference has area πr².

blocks.heading: Define radius
blocks.text:
A radius is a straight distance from the centre of a circle to its circumference. Radii of the same circle have equal lengths.

Draw a radius from the labelled centre to any point on the circle, rather than from one boundary point to another. A circle can have many drawn radii but one radius value. If its diameter is given, divide that value by two before using an equation containing r.

blocks.heading: Define diameter
blocks.text:
A diameter is a straight line segment across a circle through its centre. Its length is twice the radius.

A line joining two points on a circle is a chord, but it is a diameter only when it passes through the centre. This distinction matters when a wide object is measured with calipers. An off-centre chord is shorter than the diameter, so alignment can affect the reading.

blocks.heading: Describe a square
blocks.text:
A square is a four-sided plane shape with equal side lengths and right angles. Its area is the square of its side length.

Check both conditions when recognising the shape. Equal sides without right angles describe a different quadrilateral, while right angles without equal side lengths may describe a non-square rectangle. For a square surface the two perpendicular dimensions have the same value, which is why its area can be written a².

blocks.heading: Describe a parallelogram
blocks.text:
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with opposite sides parallel. Its perpendicular height is not generally the length of a sloping side.

The separation between its parallel base lines is the relevant height in an area construction. A diagonal runs across the shape and is another distinct length. In a vector diagram a parallelogram helps combine two directions: the resultant runs from their shared starting point to the opposite corner.

blocks.heading: Describe a rectangle
blocks.text:
A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. Opposite sides are equal and parallel.

Length and width are measured along perpendicular directions. Its area is their product, so a thin strip and a wider strip can have equal areas even though their side lengths differ. A square is the special rectangular case in which all sides have equal lengths. Avoid identifying the diagonal as the width.

blocks.heading: Define a diagonal
blocks.text:
A diagonal joins two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon. In a rectangle its length can be found using the two perpendicular sides and Pythagoras’ theorem.

A diagonal crosses the inside of a convex polygon instead of following one of its edges. Mark the endpoints to distinguish it from a height drawn to the middle of an edge. In a rectangle with sides 3 cm and 4 cm, the diagonal is 5 cm. Its length is not the sum of the side lengths.

blocks.heading: recall and use formulae for the area of a square, rectangle, triangle and circle
blocks.text:
An area describes how much surface is enclosed by a boundary. The correct area equation depends on the shape and on perpendicular dimensions.

For a square use a²; for a rectangle use length times width. A triangle is half a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height, so its area is ½bh. For a circle use πr². Do not use a sloping triangle side as its height unless it is perpendicular to the chosen base. Give an area unit such as m² or cm². Changing the length unit changes the numerical area by a squared scale factor.

blocks.heading: Calculate square area
blocks.text:
A square of side a has area a². Both dimensions must be expressed in the same length unit.

For a square tile with side 0.30 m, the area is 0.090 m². Squaring the unit is part of the calculation. A side described in centimetres can first be converted to metres, or the resulting area can be converted afterwards using the squared conversion. Doubling the side length makes the area four times larger, because two dimensions change.

blocks.heading: Calculate rectangle area
blocks.text:
A rectangle has area equal to length multiplied by perpendicular width. An area calculation requires two lengths, not a boundary length added to another.

For a rectangular panel 0.80 m long and 0.25 m wide, the product is 0.20 m². Adding the dimensions gives a length, not a surface area. If the widths of two panels differ, compare the products rather than their lengths alone. A width labelled in centimetres must be put into a compatible unit before multiplying by a length in metres.

blocks.heading: Calculate triangle area
blocks.text:
A triangle has area equal to half its base multiplied by its perpendicular height. The height meets the chosen base line at a right angle.

A sloping edge is not automatically the height. Draw or identify the perpendicular separation to the base, even when its foot lies outside an obtuse triangle. For a triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm, the area is 30 cm². Omitting the half would calculate the surrounding parallelogram or rectangle instead of the triangular region.

blocks.heading: Calculate circle area
blocks.text:
A circle of radius r has area πr². The radius is half the diameter and its square carries an area unit.

For a circular opening of diameter 8 mm, first identify its radius as 4 mm. Then its area is 16π mm², approximately 50.3 mm². A diameter mistaken for a radius gives an area four times too large. Keep π or additional calculator digits until the final rounding. Annular regions require subtraction of the inner circular area from the outer area, using radii consistently.

blocks.heading: recall and use formulae for the volume of a cuboid and a cylinder
blocks.text:
A volume measures the three-dimensional space occupied by a region. A cuboid uses three perpendicular dimensions, while a cylinder uses circular cross-sectional area multiplied by length.

A volume unit is cubic, such as m³, cm³ or mm³. A cuboid has volume lwh. A cylinder has volume πr²h, where h is measured perpendicular to its circular face. Distinguish the wall material of a hollow object from its internal capacity: they are not necessarily the same volume. Check whether a stated diameter belongs to an outer wall or an inner opening before choosing the radius.

blocks.heading: Calculate cuboid volume
blocks.text:
A cuboid has volume equal to length times width times height. All three dimensions must use compatible length units.

A box 20 cm long, 10 cm wide and 5 cm high has an internal volume of 1000 cm³ if those are its internal dimensions. Its outer dimensions would include the wall thickness and give a larger value. Write the three lengths with their units before multiplying. If every length is doubled, the volume is multiplied by eight because three factors each double. A volume is not found by adding lengths or by using just a face area.

blocks.heading: Calculate cylinder volume
blocks.text:
A cylinder has volume πr²h. The value h is the perpendicular distance between its circular end faces.

Find the circular area first, then multiply by the height. A cylinder of radius 2 cm and height 10 cm has volume 40π cm³, approximately 126 cm³. If its diameter rather than radius is supplied, halve the diameter before squaring it. Keep the same length unit in r and h. A tilted sketch does not change which length is perpendicular to the circular base; labels and geometry determine the dimensions.

blocks.heading: use the refractive index n = sin i /sin r
blocks.text:
Refractive index for the stated boundary can be calculated as sin i divided by sin r. The incidence and refraction angles are measured from the normal, with the calculator in degree mode when the angles use degrees.

The sine operation must be applied to each angle; dividing the angles themselves does not give the index. For incidence 30° and refraction 20°, the ratio is approximately 1.46. To find a missing angle, first isolate its sine and then use the inverse-sine function. A sine value greater than one signals that the assumed refracted ray or the entered quantities need reconsideration. The optical meaning of refraction is developed later; here the focus is using the mathematical ratio correctly.

blocks.heading: solve equations of the form x = y + z and x = yz for any one term when the other two are known
blocks.text:
An equation remains balanced when the same valid operation is applied to both sides. Rearrangement isolates the unknown before numerical substitution.

From x = y + z, subtract z to obtain y = x − z. From x = yz, divide by the nonzero factor z to obtain y = x/z. Do not merely move a symbol and guess its new sign or position. Check a rearrangement by inserting simple known values. In physical equations the units provide an additional guide: if distance equals speed times time, time is distance divided by speed, giving seconds. Brackets preserve grouped terms when more than one operation is involved.

blocks.heading: recall and use Pythagoras’ theorem for a right angled triangle
blocks.text:
For a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the perpendicular sides. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.

Identify the right angle before using a² + b² = c². The result does not apply directly to an arbitrary non-right-angled triangle. With perpendicular sides 5 m and 12 m, the sum of their squares is 169 m² and the hypotenuse is 13 m. Remember the final square root. If one perpendicular side is missing, subtract the square of the known side from the hypotenuse squared. This method also gives the magnitude of a resultant built from perpendicular components.

blocks.heading: recognise and use points of the compass (N, S, E, W), bearings taken and the rules for bearing taking
blocks.text:
A bearing specifies a direction by an angle measured clockwise from north. Bearings are conventionally recorded using three digits, such as 090° for east.

Draw a north reference at the starting point before measuring. East has bearing 090°, south 180° and west 270°. A northeast direction halfway between north and east is 045°. A reverse bearing differs by 180°; add 180° to a bearing below 180°, or subtract it from a larger bearing. For example, the reverse of 070° is 250°. A compass diagram keeps direction information separate from the magnitude of a displacement or velocity.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which operation produces the arithmetic mean of four comparable readings?
A. Their sum divided by four
B. Their sum multiplied by four
C. Largest minus smallest
D. The last reading divided by four

2. What does the prefix kilo mean?
A. 100
B. 0.001
C. 1000000
D. 1000

3. Which length is a radius?
A. Around the circle
B. Between arbitrary polygon vertices
C. Centre to circumference
D. Across a circle through its centre

4. Which expression gives triangular area?
A. base × height
B. ½ × base × perpendicular height
C. base + height
D. base × sloping side

5. Which is the SI unit of mass?
A. kg
B. N
C. W
D. Pa

6. Which bearing points east?
A. 000°
B. 180°
C. 270°
D. 090°

7. Which expression is the reciprocal of a nonzero period T?
A. 2T
B. T/2
C. 1/T
D. T²

8. Three repeated times are 9.0 s, 9.2 s and 9.1 s. What is their mean?
A. 3.03 s
B. 9.1 s
C. 27.3 s
D. 0.2 s

9. What is 72 ms in seconds?
A. 0.072 s
B. 72 s
C. 0.72 s
D. 72000 s

10. A square has side 0.50 m. What is its area?
A. 1.0 m²
B. 2.0 m²
C. 0.50 m²
D. 0.25 m²

11. What percentage is 9 J out of 30 J?
A. 0.30%
B. 300%
C. 30%
D. 3.33%

12. What is 6.284 rounded to three significant figures?
A. 6.29
B. 6.28
C. 6.284
D. 6.3

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: The total is shared across the number of readings. B: This scales the total instead of averaging it. C: This gives the range. D: This discards the other readings.

2. Key D. A: This is not the kilo factor. B: This is the milli factor. C: This is the mega factor. D: Kilo multiplies the unit by 10³.

3. Key C. A: That is circumference length. B: That describes neither a circle radius nor its fixed endpoints. C: A radius starts at the centre. D: That is a diameter.

4. Key B. A: This misses the factor one half. B: The triangular region is half the matching parallelogram. C: Adding lengths does not give area. D: The height must be perpendicular and a half is needed.

5. Key A. A: The kilogram measures mass. B: A newton measures force. C: A watt measures power. D: A pascal measures pressure.

6. Key D. A: This points north. B: This points south. C: This points west. D: Bearings are clockwise from north.

7. Key C. A: Doubling is not taking a reciprocal. B: Halving is not taking a reciprocal. C: The reciprocal reverses the ratio. D: Squaring is not taking a reciprocal.

8. Key B. A: This divides a single representative reading by three. B: The sum 27.3 s divided by three is 9.1 s. C: This is the sum, before division. D: This is the range.

9. Key A. A: Milliseconds are divided by 1000. B: The prefix has been ignored. C: This uses the wrong factor. D: This changes in the wrong direction.

10. Key D. A: This adds two sides instead of multiplying. B: This is numerically the perimeter, with the wrong unit. C: This leaves the side value unchanged. D: The product is 0.50 × 0.50.

11. Key C. A: This omits multiplication by 100. B: This introduces an extra factor of ten. C: The ratio is 0.30, or thirty per hundred. D: This reverses the ratio and misuses percent.

12. Key B. A: This rounds upward despite the next digit being less than five. B: The next digit is 4, so the retained hundredths digit stays unchanged. C: This keeps four significant figures. D: This gives two significant figures.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for timing repeated pendulum oscillations.

| Oscillation count | Elapsed time / s |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 8 |
| 10 | 16 |
| 15 | 24 |
| 20 | 32 |
| 25 | 40 |
| 30 | 48 |

(a) Draw the graph with Elapsed time / s on the vertical axis and Oscillation count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Put oscillation count horizontally and elapsed time vertically. Plot the six points and a straight fitted line through their trend; these idealised values give a zero intercept.

Gradient: 40 ÷ 25 = 1.6 s per oscillation. The gradient estimates the period because it is elapsed time divided by the number of complete oscillations.

Plan: 1. Suspend a small bob from a fixed-length string and mark a consistent reference point for counting. 2. Release it from the same small angle without pushing, keeping the length unchanged. 3. Time a chosen number of complete oscillations using a stopwatch, counting a return to the same position and direction as one cycle. 4. Repeat the timing at that count and calculate a mean, investigating any anomalous reading. 5. Repeat for several oscillation counts while retaining the same pendulum and release conditions.
Control and accuracy: Keep string length and release angle fixed. Count consistently at the same reference; keep the swinging bob clear of people.
Table: Record oscillation count, each elapsed time / s and the mean elapsed time / s in separate labelled columns.
Graph and conclusion: Plot mean elapsed time against oscillation count. A straight trend with a near-zero intercept supports a constant time per cycle; obtain that time from the gradient.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: explain and use the relationship between length, surface area and volume and their units on metric scales
blocks.text:
Length, area and volume scale with one, two and three powers of a length conversion respectively. A conversion factor must be squared for area and cubed for volume.

Because one metre is 100 centimetres, one square metre contains 10,000 square centimetres and one cubic metre contains 1,000,000 cubic centimetres. Picture the number of small squares covering a face before extending the idea to small cubes filling a box. Dividing 500 cm² by 100 would be wrong; divide by 10,000 to obtain 0.050 m². When a numerical result appears unexpectedly large, check whether the problem involved a squared or cubed unit rather than a length.

blocks.heading: identify the correct SI unit and derived units (see annexe C)
blocks.text:
An SI unit states the standard physical quantity represented by a number. Derived units combine base units, such as metres per second for speed.

Use metres for length, kilograms for mass, seconds for time, amperes for current and kelvin for absolute temperature. Common derived units include newtons for force, joules for energy, watts for power and pascals for pressure. A correct number without its unit is incomplete because it does not identify the physical size. Distinguish a quantity from its unit: mass is the quantity and kilogram the unit. Unit symbols are not shortened versions of every word, so learn the accepted forms such as kg, s, N and Pa.

blocks.heading: explain and use multiple prefixes (mega, kilo) and sub-multiple prefixes (centi, milli, micro, nano) of units
blocks.text:
A prefix multiplies a unit by a specified power of ten without changing the kind of quantity measured. The prefix symbol is part of the unit and its case matters, for example M and m have different meanings.

A prefixed unit can make a very large or small value easier to read. A kilometre is longer than a metre, so the same distance uses fewer kilometres than metres. A millimetre is shorter, so more millimetres are needed. Before substitution into an equation, choose a consistent set of units and apply the prefix factor explicitly. Do not assume that matching initial letters mean matching factors. Mega, milli and micro describe very different scales.

blocks.heading: Use mega and kilo prefixes
blocks.text:
Kilo represents 10³ and mega represents 10⁶. A value in kilounits or megaunits is multiplied by the appropriate factor to obtain the unprefixed unit.

A generator rated at 2.4 kW has power 2400 W. An energy of 1.8 MJ equals 1,800,000 J. Keep the physical quantity unchanged while converting its unit: energy in MJ does not become power in W. Capital M is the mega prefix; lower-case m represents milli. To convert in the opposite direction, divide by the same factor. For example, 7500 W is 7.5 kW. Include the unit on both sides of a conversion.

blocks.heading: Use centi and milli prefixes
blocks.text:
Centi represents 10⁻² and milli represents 10⁻³. For area or volume units the entire prefixed length factor must be raised to the appropriate power.

A length of 8 mm is 0.008 m, while 8 cm is 0.08 m. These conversions concern one dimension. A cross-sectional area of 8 mm² is 8 × 10⁻⁶ m² because each of its two dimensions contributes a factor of one thousandth. Write the unit powers before entering values into a calculator. A millisecond is likewise one thousandth of a second, but it is a time conversion rather than a squared length conversion.

blocks.heading: Use micro and nano prefixes
blocks.text:
Micro represents 10⁻⁶ and nano represents 10⁻⁹. A micrometre is one thousand nanometres.

These small units are useful for wavelengths and fine dimensions. A wavelength of 650 nm equals 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m. Moving between micro and nano requires the ratio of their factors, not simply moving a decimal point by one place. The symbol μ is used for micro, while n is used for nano. Read the unit carefully before using a wavelength in an equation whose other quantities are in SI units. A wavelength in nanometres is still a length, not a frequency.

blocks.heading: use standard notation
blocks.text:
Standard notation writes a nonzero number as a coefficient from 1 up to but not including 10 multiplied by an integer power of ten. A negative power is used for a positive number smaller than one.

The value 0.00072 becomes 7.2 × 10⁻⁴. Moving the decimal four places right makes the coefficient larger, so the power of ten compensates by dividing by ten four times. A value of 720,000 becomes 7.2 × 10⁵. Keep the unit attached; standard notation changes the representation, not the quantity. For calculations involving powers, write the coefficient and the power separately so that order-of-magnitude mistakes are easier to spot.

blocks.heading: round a value correctly to an appropriate number of significant figures when required
blocks.text:
Significant figures count the meaningful digits used to report a value. Leading zeros locate the decimal point, whereas zeros after a significant digit can carry precision information.

In 0.00480, the significant digits are 4, 8 and the final zero, giving three significant figures. To round 3.746 to three significant figures, retain 3.74 and inspect the following 6; the result becomes 3.75. Do not confuse three significant figures with three decimal places. Preserve intermediate calculator digits until the final result, because rounding at several successive stages can shift the final value. If a requested precision is given explicitly, follow it consistently across a results table.

blocks.heading: use acceptable methods of stating units, e.g. metres per second or m per s can be written as m/s or m s -1
blocks.text:
A compound unit can be written using a solidus or a negative exponent. Metres per second can be written m/s or m s⁻¹.

The negative index applies to the unit, not to the sign of the physical quantity. A positive speed of 4 m s⁻¹ is four metres travelled per second, not a negative speed. Acceleration can be written m s⁻² because velocity changes by metres per second during each second. Use spacing to separate unit factors and brackets when needed to avoid an ambiguous chain of divisions. A unit expression should make clear which factors belong in a numerator and which in a denominator.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the prefix factor represented by milli. [1]

(b) State the unit notation for seconds to the power minus one. [1]

(c) Explain why repeated timings should refer to the same unchanged motion before a mean is used. [2]

(d) Calculate the mean of timings 12.4 s, 12.6 s and 12.5 s. [2]

(e) Calculate the time in seconds represented by 1850 ms. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Milli represents 10⁻³.

(b) s⁻¹

(c) They should estimate the same physical time. Changing the motion would mix different quantities rather than simply reduce random variation.

(d) The total is 37.5 s; 37.5/3 gives a mean of 12.5 s.

(e) 1850/1000 gives 1.85 s.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for controlled low-voltage water heating.

| Heating time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 22 |
| 30 | 24.4 |
| 60 | 26.8 |
| 90 | 29.2 |
| 120 | 31.6 |
| 150 | 34 |

(a) Draw the graph with Temperature / °C on the vertical axis and Heating time / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Put heating time horizontally and temperature vertically. The idealised points follow a straight increasing line with a 22 °C temperature intercept.

Gradient: 12 ÷ 150 = 0.08 °C/s. The slope is the temperature rise per second over the stated heating interval; it is not the mean temperature.

Plan: 1. Place a fixed measured mass of water in a stable container with a suitable low-voltage heater and thermometer. 2. Record the initial water temperature and start the stopwatch as the heater is switched on. 3. Read the water temperature at regular time intervals, keeping the thermometer positioned in the water rather than against the vessel wall. 4. Repeat the sequence under matched starting conditions to judge the consistency of the readings. 5. Compare readings over a suitable heating duration while keeping the heater setting, water mass and container unchanged.
Control and accuracy: Keep heater power and water mass fixed; stir gently for a representative water temperature and handle hot apparatus safely.
Table: Use columns for heating time / s and temperature / °C; add separate repeat-temperature columns if repeats are taken.
Graph and conclusion: Plot temperature against time. Use the fitted trend and its gradient to describe the observed heating rate; do not substitute a theoretical prediction for the measured pattern.

Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: make observations accurately; use appropriate techniques; handle apparatus/ material competently and have due regard to safety
blocks.text:
A useful experiment combines suitable apparatus, accurate observations and a controlled safe procedure. The numerical reading is affected by how the apparatus is selected, arranged and used.

Before collecting results, identify the physical quantity to be measured and the range of values expected. Select an instrument whose scale and sensitivity can distinguish the changes of interest. Check its zero and the way the reading is viewed. A thermometer touching a hot vessel wall can describe the wall rather than the bulk liquid; a tilted ruler can describe a longer diagonal distance. Record what was actually observed instead of changing readings to fit a predicted result. Practical safety should be built into the method, not added as a vague final sentence.

blocks.heading: Make accurate observations
blocks.text:
An observation should describe the measured quantity as faithfully as the instrument permits. Correct alignment, a checked zero and a clearly identified scale reduce avoidable reading errors.

For a liquid-in-glass thermometer, view the top of the liquid column straight on and wait for the reading to settle. For a measuring cylinder, place it upright on a level surface and read the appropriate meniscus at eye level. The instruction depends on the instrument: a thermometer column is not read by looking for the bottom of a water meniscus. Distinguish a genuine measured change from a change caused by moving the eye or the instrument. Use the scale divisions to decide what precision can reasonably be recorded.

blocks.heading: Select and handle apparatus appropriately
blocks.text:
Appropriate apparatus matches the physical quantity, its expected range and the required resolution. Its arrangement must let the instrument respond to the intended quantity.

A ruler may be suitable for a long strip, while a micrometer is better for a very small thickness. A stopwatch measures a time interval rather than a length. In electrical work, an ammeter belongs in the current path and a voltmeter compares two circuit points. Do not assume that a digital display removes all possible errors; an incorrect range, connection or zero can still produce misleading values. In a plan, name the instrument alongside the quantity and describe how it is connected or positioned.

blocks.heading: Apply practical safety precautions
blocks.text:
A safety precaution addresses a specific hazard in the proposed experiment. The precaution must reduce that hazard while still permitting the required measurement.

Hot water can burn skin, suspended loads can fall, and an unstable stand can tip. For a heating experiment, place the container securely and handle hot apparatus with suitable protection. Use a low-voltage supply for school circuit investigations and follow the teacher’s equipment instructions. A statement such as be careful does not explain which action prevents injury. Choose a precaution appropriate to the actual setup rather than listing unrelated equipment. Safe working does not by itself guarantee accurate results; the two requirements should both be considered.

blocks.heading: distinguish between dependent, independent, and control variables
blocks.text:
The independent variable is deliberately changed, the dependent variable is measured, and relevant controls are kept fixed. These roles are defined by the investigation aim rather than by the name of a physical quantity.

In a test of how the amount of water affects cooling, water volume is changed and temperature change during a stated interval is measured. Initial temperature and the type of container may need to be controlled. In another experiment, water volume could instead be the measured response. Identify the roles in a sentence that connects the aim to the procedure. Changing several influential quantities together makes it difficult to decide which produced the observed effect. Controls should therefore be chosen for a physical reason, not merely because they appear in an apparatus list.

blocks.heading: Identify the independent variable
blocks.text:
The independent variable is the quantity deliberately changed in the investigation. It is distinguished from a measured response by the role assigned in the method.

If the aim is to test how heating duration affects water temperature, choose several durations and take a temperature reading at each. Heating duration is then independent even though time can also be measured with a stopwatch. The fact that an instrument measures a quantity does not by itself decide its variable role. Use the aim and the planned intervention. A suitable range of settings should be wide enough to reveal a trend without creating unsafe conditions or changing the experiment into a different physical situation.

blocks.heading: Identify the dependent variable
blocks.text:
The dependent variable is the quantity measured as the response to the deliberate change. Its measurement method should be stated clearly enough for another person to obtain comparable readings.

In a spring-loading test, the load may be deliberately changed while extension is measured. The response is extension, not simply the loaded length: subtract the initial length from each loaded length. The same basic investigation could record a different quantity if the aim were changed, so identify what the result must reveal. State the instrument, reference points and unit. A table should reserve a separate column for a calculated response when it is obtained from more than one raw reading.

blocks.heading: Select a relevant control variable
blocks.text:
A control variable is an influential quantity held fixed for a fair comparison. Naming a control should be accompanied by a practicable way of maintaining it.

When comparing two container surfaces during cooling, use equal water volumes and similar starting temperatures, with the container shape and material matched as far as possible. Merely saying keep everything the same is too vague. Some factors, such as room temperature, can be monitored even when not perfectly controlled. Explain how a change in the suggested control could affect the response. Holding the independent variable fixed throughout would defeat the aim, so do not accidentally label the quantity being tested as a control.

blocks.heading: predict the hypothesis or aim of the investigation in relation to dependent, independent and control variables
blocks.text:
An investigation aim states the relationship that the measurements are intended to test. A hypothesis predicts a possible outcome and must remain open to comparison with the results.

An aim can ask how heating duration affects water temperature at fixed heater power and fixed water mass. A hypothesis might predict a rising temperature, but that prediction is not a conclusion already established by the experiment. Write the dependent quantity and the independent quantity into the aim so that the required table is clear. Specify important fixed conditions. A method should lead to evidence that could support, qualify or contradict the prediction, rather than simply repeating the expected relationship as though it were a measured result.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: locate, select and organise information from a variety of sources
blocks.text:
Experimental planning may require relevant information from several sources. The selected information should be organised by the quantities and conditions needed for the investigation.

An apparatus diagram may identify connections, a label may give an instrument range, and a results table may provide measured values. Read each source for its particular role. Copy a number with its unit and any condition that limits its use. A voltage rating is not a current reading, and a table value from a different temperature may not describe the present experiment. Keep calculated values separate from measured ones. When several sources disagree, inspect the definitions and conditions before assuming that one should simply replace the other.

blocks.heading: record results of experimental investigations in a logical manner (tables or graphs) and explain the importance of units and recording results of experimental investigations
blocks.text:
A results record should preserve readings in a logical order with identified quantities and units. Tables organise numerical relationships, while graphs make patterns easier to examine.

Arrange rows by the independent variable rather than by an accidental order of loose notes. Keep each set of repeated readings alongside the setting that produced it. If a mean or an extension is calculated, show it in a separate labelled column rather than overwriting raw data. A graph can then be constructed from the appropriate columns. Record readings during the experiment so that units, unusual events and apparent anomalies are not reconstructed from memory later. A neat table is useful only if its entries remain traceable to the actual measurements.

blocks.heading: present each column of a table by heading it with the physical quantity and the appropriate unit, e.g. time/s (units should be in the heading of the column and not in the measurements in the column)
blocks.text:
A table heading identifies the physical quantity and the unit used for that column. Numerical entries can then be written without repeating the unit in every cell.

A heading such as Temperature / °C means that each numerical entry is a temperature expressed in degrees Celsius. A heading of Time / s distinguishes an elapsed time from a temperature even if the two columns contain similar numbers. State the quantity, not a unit by itself. If the unit changes, the numerical values must be converted consistently rather than leaving the old numbers under a new label. Keep raw quantities and their derived combinations in distinct columns so that their units can be checked separately.

blocks.heading: use column headings of the table to be directly transferred to the axes of a constructed graph
blocks.text:
Graph axis labels should carry the same physical quantity and unit as the table column being plotted. The usual experimental arrangement puts the independent variable horizontally and the dependent response vertically.

For a table of heating time and temperature, transfer Heating time / s to the horizontal axis and Temperature / °C to the vertical axis. Do not transfer numerical table entries into the axis labels. Select scales that include the range of readings and allow values between major divisions to be located. If the graph instruction specifies a different orientation, follow that orientation and use the resulting axis ratio when interpreting its gradient. The title describes the dependent quantity against the independent quantity.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for position readings from a slowly moving model vehicle.

| Time / s | Position / cm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 5 |
| 2 | 11 |
| 4 | 17 |
| 6 | 23 |
| 8 | 29 |
| 10 | 35 |

(a) Draw the graph with Position / cm on the vertical axis and Time / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Time is horizontal and position vertical. The six idealised points follow a straight line starting at 5 cm, not at the origin.

Gradient: 30 ÷ 10 = 3 cm/s. The gradient is the model vehicle’s rate of position change. A nonzero starting position does not prevent a constant speed, but position is not directly proportional to the stated elapsed time.

Plan: 1. Mark a straight, level track and choose a fixed origin for reading the model vehicle position. 2. Use a steady low-speed drive and start timing at a clearly defined event. 3. Record position at regular time intervals with the measuring scale aligned along the track. 4. Repeat the run with matched starting position and drive setting to assess variation. 5. Use the repeated positions at each time to obtain a representative trend while preserving any anomalous readings for investigation.
Control and accuracy: Keep the track arrangement, drive setting and starting position matched; reduce parallax by reading the scale consistently.
Table: Record Time / s and Position / cm, with separate repeat columns and a calculated mean where repeats are used.
Graph and conclusion: Plot position against time and examine the fitted line. Use its gradient to describe the rate and its intercept to distinguish constant speed from direct proportionality of position to the chosen time.

blocks.heading: explain that precise measurements are all close to one another and that accurate measurements have an average close to the true value
blocks.text:
Accuracy is closeness of a measurement to the accepted true value. Precision is how closely repeated measurements agree.

A balance could repeatedly give 21.4 g for an object whose accepted mass is 20.0 g. Its readings might be precise but inaccurate because they share a bias. A more scattered group centred near 20.0 g describes another situation: individual readings vary but their mean may be closer to the accepted value. These ideas are not interchangeable. Repeating and averaging may reduce the influence of random scatter; it does not identify or remove a persistent balance offset. Compare both the spread and the reference value when judging the quality of a dataset.

blocks.heading: explain that any measurement may involve error, which is the difference between the measurement and the true value
blocks.text:
A measurement error is the difference between a measured value and the true value. An individual error is often not known exactly because the true value itself is not available.

If a reference object is known to be 10.0 cm long but a measurement gives 10.3 cm, the signed measurement error is +0.3 cm. That is a known comparison with a reference. In an ordinary experiment, an uncertainty estimate is used instead of pretending to know the exact error. Do not interpret the word error as evidence of carelessness alone. Instrument limitations, fluctuations and the measurement method can introduce deviations even when the procedure is performed carefully.

blocks.heading: explain uncertainty as the interval on either side of a measured value within which the true value is expected to lie
blocks.text:
Uncertainty is a stated interval around a measured value within which the true value is expected. It communicates a plausible range rather than an exact correction to add or subtract.

A length recorded as 24.0 ± 0.2 cm suggests values from 23.8 cm to 24.2 cm within the stated estimate. It does not say that the true length is definitely 24.2 cm. The estimate depends on resolution, repeatability and the method; the smallest scale division is not a universal complete account of uncertainty. Compare a proposed difference with the relevant uncertainties before treating it as physically meaningful. Reporting many more digits than the uncertainty supports gives a misleading impression of precision.

blocks.heading: handle and process experimental observations and data, including dealing with anomalous or inconsistent results
blocks.text:
An anomalous reading is inconsistent with the surrounding pattern and should be investigated. A result should not be discarded merely because it disagrees with a preferred theory.

Suppose repeated timings are 7.3, 7.4, 11.8 and 7.2 s for an unchanged motion. The 11.8 s reading deserves investigation because it is far from the other repeats. Check whether a counting interruption, transcription mistake or changed condition occurred. Repeat the measurement if possible and keep a record of the original value and the reason for excluding it from a mean. A genuine unexpected physical effect can also create unusual data, so an unexplained disagreement is not permission to edit the evidence.

blocks.heading: evaluate presented results or experimental data by applying scientific knowledge and interpret and draw appropriate conclusions from practical observations and data in relation to the hypotheses
blocks.text:
A conclusion answers the investigation aim using the measured pattern or numerical evidence. It should distinguish an observed relationship from a theoretical prediction or a claim of exact proportionality.

If a quantity rises steadily while another is increased, first state that trend. Direct proportionality requires more: the ratio must remain constant within the quality of the measurements, or the fitted straight line should be consistent with the origin. A nonzero intercept can rule out direct proportionality between the plotted quantities even when the line is straight. Quote an appropriate comparison, such as similar increments or ratios, instead of simply saying the values prove the hypothesis. Consider anomalies, scatter and the range tested when stating how strong the evidence is.

blocks.heading: discuss trends in results and suggest sources of error (random and systematic errors)
blocks.text:
A data trend describes how the response changes as the other quantity changes. Random scatter and systematic bias affect the strength or position of that trend in different ways.

State whether the response increases, decreases, stays similar or changes at a varying rate, using the plotted range. Then identify limitations that could affect the conclusion. A noisy set may still show a clear overall trend, while a precise-looking line can be shifted by an instrument zero error. Avoid calling every difference random or every straight trend correct. A useful evaluation links a possible error to the particular reading it affects and explains its consequence for a ratio, intercept, gradient or comparison.

blocks.heading: Describe a data trend
blocks.text:
A trend describes the direction and pattern of change in a dataset. Increasing does not automatically mean directly proportional.

For values x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 5, 10, the response increases but its increments and ratios are not constant. A steeper part of a graph indicates a larger change in the vertical quantity per change in the horizontal quantity, provided the same axes are being compared. Use comparative language that names the quantities. Saying the line goes up gives less information than saying temperature rises more rapidly during the first interval than during the last. Restrict the conclusion to the measured range unless a justified model supports extrapolation.

blocks.heading: Identify a random error
blocks.text:
A random error produces unpredictable variation between repeated readings. Taking repeats and calculating a mean can reduce its effect on an estimate.

Human reaction-time variation in stopwatch measurements can make some durations a little high and others a little low. Repeating an unchanged event reveals some of that spread. Timing several cycles rather than one may also reduce the relative influence of the starting and stopping delay. A mean does not guarantee the exact true value, and it does not remove an offset shared by all measurements. Explain the physical source of the variation rather than using random error as a general label for any discrepancy.

blocks.heading: Identify a systematic error
blocks.text:
A systematic error introduces a consistent bias through the instrument or method. An unchanged zero offset is not removed by simply repeating and averaging the biased readings.

An ammeter that reads +0.03 A before current flows will over-read subsequent indications if the offset is not corrected. More repeats under the same biased condition can produce a very consistent but displaced mean. Inspect the zero, compare with a suitable reference or correct the known offset where justified. Some biases depend on scale or conditions rather than being a fixed addition, so identify the actual source. Do not change the sign of a correction without thinking about whether the instrument is reading too high or too low.

blocks.heading: suggest possible improvements to reduce errors
blocks.text:
An improvement should address a specified limitation of the measurement. Its purpose is to reduce that limitation’s effect, not merely to make the apparatus sound more sophisticated.

If reaction-time variation is important, time several oscillations and repeat the interval. If parallax affects a ruler reading, use a suitable alignment aid and view squarely. If thermal contact with a vessel wall biases a water-temperature reading, reposition the thermometer and ensure a representative liquid temperature. Link the change to its expected effect. Replace the instrument may be reasonable only if its range or resolution is the actual difficulty. A source of uncertainty can remain even after careful technique, so avoid blaming every variation on poor handling.

blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: record entries in tables with constancy in terms of decimal places for initial readings and significant figures for calculations
blocks.text:
A results column should use a consistent precision appropriate to the instrument or calculation. Raw readings are commonly recorded to consistent decimal places, while derived values are rounded to a justified number of significant figures.

If a ruler reading is recorded in centimetres to one decimal place, write 4.0 cm as 4.0 rather than changing to 4 in the same column. The zero communicates how the measurement was reported. A calculated column is different: values obtained from several measurements should not simply copy every calculator digit. Keep raw readings available and round derived results consistently at the end of the calculation. Precision does not improve merely because more decimal places are typed into a table. The instrument and the quality of the input data set the sensible limit.

blocks.heading: select suitable scales and axes for graphs
blocks.text:
Graph scales should place the data clearly across a useful part of the grid. Equal intervals along an axis must represent equal changes in the quantity.

Choose a simple sequence such as 0, 2, 4, 6 rather than squeezing most points into a corner. The scale need not begin at zero if the measured range is narrow, but show any offset clearly. A large usable scale makes a small difference easier to read. The horizontal and vertical scales can be different because the quantities and units are different. Before plotting, test the largest and smallest readings against both axis ranges. A line that appears steep under one scale may look shallow under another, so physical comparisons should use gradients with their units.

blocks.heading: plot the independent variable on the x-axis (horizontal axis) and plot the dependent variable on the y-axis (vertical axis)
blocks.text:
The deliberately changed independent quantity is usually plotted horizontally. The measured dependent response is usually plotted vertically unless a graph instruction states otherwise.

In a heating experiment, time may be the chosen independent setting and temperature the response. For that arrangement, time belongs on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis. Swapping the axes changes the gradient and its units; it is not a harmless redrawing when a gradient is later used to obtain a physical quantity. Identify the variable roles from the investigation aim, not from a rule that time must be horizontal in every possible graph. The plotted orientation must match the stated problem.

blocks.heading: Graph headings and orientation
blocks.text:
A graph heading identifies the dependent quantity plotted against the independent quantity. A useful heading describes the relationship shown rather than merely saying graph.

For water-heating results, a heading such as Water temperature against heating duration tells the reader how the axes are related. The heading does not replace axis labels: each axis still needs its own quantity and unit. If two datasets share a graph, distinguish the conditions that produced them, such as insulated and uninsulated containers. Do not use a title that asserts a conclusion unsupported by the readings. A clear heading helps someone interpret the graph even when it is separated from the original table.

blocks.heading: label each axis with the physical quantity and the appropriate unit, e.g. time/s
blocks.text:
An axis label identifies the physical quantity and its unit. A numerical scale without a quantity cannot by itself communicate a physical measurement.

Write Time / s rather than just s, because the quantity is elapsed time and the unit is seconds. Write Mass / g rather than merely mass if the numbers are in grams. Transfer these labels from the table without silently changing the units. A current recorded in milliamperes must either retain an mA label or be converted before an A label is used. A gradient then carries the vertical unit divided by the horizontal unit, so accurate labels are part of interpreting the result.

blocks.heading: draw the graph as the whole diagrammatic presentation. It may have one or several curves plotted on it, which should be labelled
blocks.text:
A graph includes axes, numerical scales, plotted data and the lines or curves representing the trend. Different datasets on the same axes should be distinguishable by labels or a clear key.

Two cooling curves can share time and temperature axes when they use the same units and comparable ranges. Label each curve by its container condition, rather than relying on colour alone. Where points overlap, use a second plotting symbol that remains visible. Draw the fitted line or curve separately from the data marks so that the observations can still be checked. A collection of unlabelled lines is not enough to compare the experiments or identify which condition produced the faster change.

blocks.heading: draw appropriate lines through relevant points being a straight line or smooth curve
blocks.text:
A fitted line or curve represents the overall data trend. Its form should be chosen from the observed pattern and the physical relationship, not by joining every neighbouring point.

If readings are scattered around an approximately straight trend, draw a straight line passing through their central pattern with a reasonable balance on either side. It need not pass through every point. If the trend bends smoothly, a suitable smooth curve is more informative than a zigzag. A theoretical expectation that a quantity is zero should not force a line through the origin when the actual readings show an offset. Investigate possible offsets or limitations and describe what the evidence supports.

blocks.heading: present points on the curve as crosses (x) or encircled dots (). If a further curve is included, vertical crosses (+) may be used to mark the points
blocks.text:
Small crosses or clear encircled dots show the intended coordinates of plotted readings. Thick blobs make the centre and accuracy of a plotted value difficult to judge.

Plot the coordinate where the horizontal and vertical scale values meet. A fine cross gives two intersecting strokes whose centre can be read clearly. The fitted line should not hide every observation. For a second dataset, use a distinguishable symbol and state its meaning in the key. Accuracy depends on the numerical scale as well as the neatness of the mark: a carefully drawn cross in the wrong square is still a wrong point. Read subdivisions before plotting values between large labelled intervals.

blocks.heading: Calculate straight-line gradient as change in vertical quantity divided by change in horizontal quantity; retain sign and axis-ratio units
blocks.text:
A straight-line gradient is the change in vertical quantity divided by the change in horizontal quantity. The sign and unit follow from the plotted coordinates and must be retained.

Choose widely separated points on the fitted line and mark the triangle used. Subtract vertical coordinates in the same order as the horizontal coordinates. If temperature decreases from 75 °C to 63 °C while time increases from 20 s to 80 s, the changes are −12 °C and 60 s, giving a gradient of −0.20 °C/s. The negative sign describes a fall as time increases. Do not call a slope a familiar constant without examining its axes: volume against mass gives volume per mass, which is reciprocal density.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which instrument is calibrated for a liquid volume?
A. Measuring cylinder
B. Stopwatch
C. Ammeter
D. Metre rule

2. Which caliper feature measures the inside width of an opening?
A. Outside jaws only
B. The zero-checking label
C. An external micrometer anvil
D. Internal jaws

3. Why is a micrometer ratchet useful?
A. It changes a diameter into a radius
B. It measures internal volume
C. It helps limit measuring force
D. It removes all zero error

4. What counts as one full pendulum oscillation?
A. Any visible movement
B. Return to the same position and direction
C. Any crossing of the centre
D. Travel from one extreme to the other

5. Which quantity is scalar?
A. Energy
B. Force
C. Velocity
D. Displacement

6. What additional information distinguishes a vector from a scalar magnitude?
A. Whether a unit exists
B. Whether it changes
C. Whether it is measured experimentally
D. Direction

7. In a tip-to-tail construction, where does the resultant begin?
A. At the midpoint of either component
B. At a new unrelated origin
C. At the first vector’s original tail
D. At the final tip, pointing back

8. A rod extends from 2.0 cm to 10.7 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
A. 5.35 cm
B. 8.7 cm
C. 10.7 cm
D. 12.7 cm

9. A 0.1 mm vernier gives 12 mm on the main scale and alignment at division 4. With no zero error, what is the reading?
A. 12.4 mm
B. 16 mm
C. 12.04 mm
D. 11.6 mm

10. A micrometer sleeve shows 4.5 mm and the thimble adds 0.18 mm. With no zero error, what is the result?
A. 4.18 mm
B. 4.32 mm
C. 18.45 mm
D. 4.68 mm

11. Twenty complete cycles take 32.0 s. What is the period?
A. 0.625 s
B. 32.0 s
C. 1.60 s
D. 640 s

12. Two perpendicular forces have magnitudes 5 N and 12 N. What is the resultant magnitude?
A. 169 N
B. 13 N
C. 17 N
D. 7 N
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Its graduations report volume. B: It measures time. C: It measures current. D: It directly measures length.

2. Key D. A: Those enclose an outer dimension. B: This is not a measuring contact. C: It cannot span the inside opening in the usual external arrangement. D: They contact the inner surfaces.

3. Key C. A: That is a separate geometrical calculation. B: A micrometer is not a volume vessel. C: This reduces excessive squeezing of the sample. D: A ratchet does not set every scale zero.

4. Key B. A: The interval must be defined. B: Both position and direction identify a completed cycle. C: The opposite-direction crossing occurs after half a cycle. D: This is half a cycle.

5. Key A. A: It has magnitude without a direction. B: Force is a vector. C: Velocity includes direction. D: Displacement includes direction.

6. Key D. A: Scalars can have units too. B: Either kind can change. C: Both kinds can be measured. D: Direction is part of the vector specification.

7. Key C. A: The overall endpoints determine the sum. B: The construction must retain the combined displacement. C: It connects the overall start to the final tip. D: That gives the reversed resultant.

8. Key B. A: Halving one endpoint has no measurement basis. B: Subtract the starting position. C: This assumes a zero start. D: This adds the endpoint positions.

9. Key A. A: Add four times 0.1 mm to 12 mm. B: This treats divisions as millimetres. C: This assumes a 0.01 mm resolution. D: There is no stated correction requiring subtraction.

10. Key D. A: This misses the half-millimetre sleeve value. B: This subtracts instead of adding. C: This misreads the scales as decimal strings. D: Add the two scale contributions.

11. Key C. A: This reverses the quotient. B: This is the time of the whole sequence. C: Divide the elapsed time by twenty. D: This multiplies instead of dividing.

12. Key B. A: This omits the square root and has the wrong dimensional interpretation. B: Pythagoras gives the right-triangle resultant. C: This would add collinear same-direction magnitudes. D: This subtracts magnitudes without the stated directions.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.
