Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State whether mass is a scalar or a vector. [1]

(b) State what is meant by one complete oscillation. [1]

(c) Explain why timing 25 oscillations can give a better period estimate than timing one. [2]

(d) Calculate the period if 25 oscillations take 37.5 s. [2]

(e) Calculate the resultant magnitude of perpendicular displacements 9 m east and 12 m north. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Mass is a scalar.

(b) A return to the same position and direction in the repeated motion.

(c) Starting and stopping delays contribute a smaller fraction of the longer timed interval; dividing by 25 estimates one period.

(d) The period is 37.5/25 = 1.50 s.

(e) The magnitude is √(9² + 12²) = 15 m.

(b) One mark for a complete cycle rather than a half-cycle.
(c) One mark for the longer interval reducing relative reaction-time influence; one for division by the correct cycle count.
(d) One mark for dividing by 25; one for 1.50 s.
(e) One mark for the squared-component relation; one for 15 m.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for timing a pendulum with repeated complete oscillations.

| Oscillation count | Elapsed time / s |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 7 |
| 10 | 14 |
| 15 | 21 |
| 20 | 28 |
| 25 | 35 |
| 30 | 42 |

(a) Draw the graph with Elapsed time / s on the vertical axis and Oscillation count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot oscillation count horizontally and elapsed time vertically. The idealised straight trend passes through the origin.

Gradient: 35 ÷ 25 = 1.4 s per oscillation. The gradient gives the period of this fixed-length pendulum because it expresses elapsed time per complete cycle.

Plan: 1. Suspend a bob from a securely supported string and measure its length from pivot to bob centre. 2. Choose a small fixed release angle and define a reference crossing and direction for counting cycles. 3. Time a chosen number of complete oscillations with a stopwatch. 4. Repeat that count and calculate a mean elapsed time, investigating an anomalous timing. 5. Repeat for several counts with the same length and release conditions.
Control and accuracy: Keep pivot-to-centre length and small release angle fixed; avoid pushing the bob and keep its swing clear of people.
Table: Record cycle count and each elapsed time / s, with a mean-time column after repeats.
Graph and conclusion: Plot mean elapsed time against cycle count. Use the gradient to estimate a period and the scatter to judge consistency; this is a period measurement, not a test of length dependence.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-4.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: define a scalar as a quantity which has a magnitude, but no direction (e.g. mass)
blocks.text:
A scalar is a quantity described by magnitude without direction. Mass, distance, speed, energy and time are scalar quantities.

A mass of 2 kg does not need a compass direction to specify it. A scalar can still have a unit, uncertainty or a value that changes with time. Calling it scalar does not mean it is constant. When comparing distance with displacement, remember that distance describes the path length and remains a scalar even when the path bends. Magnitude gives the amount; it does not by itself say that a quantity is a vector.

blocks.heading: define a vector as a quantity which has both magnitude and direction (e.g. velocity)
blocks.text:
A vector is a quantity requiring magnitude and direction. Force, displacement, velocity and acceleration are vector quantities.

A force of 5 N east differs from a force of 5 N west even though their magnitudes match. An arrow can represent the vector: a chosen scale gives its magnitude and the arrowhead shows direction. Reversing the arrow reverses the vector, rather than making its magnitude a different size. In one-dimensional calculations, a sign convention can encode direction, but the positive direction must first be stated.

blocks.heading: explain the difference between scalars and vectors and give common examples
blocks.text:
The scalar/vector distinction concerns whether direction is part of the quantity. Speed is scalar whereas velocity includes direction; distance is scalar whereas displacement includes the start-to-finish direction.

Two vehicles can have equal speeds while travelling in opposite directions, so their velocities differ. Similarly, an object that returns to its start can travel a nonzero distance but have zero net displacement. A vector addition therefore cannot generally be replaced by adding magnitudes. Specify examples with enough information to reveal the distinction. A unit such as m/s can be shared by speed and velocity without removing the need to state velocity direction.

blocks.heading: add two vectors at right angles by calculation to determine a resultant in magnitude and direction
blocks.text:
Perpendicular vector components form a right-angled triangle with their resultant. Pythagoras gives the resultant magnitude and a trigonometric ratio gives its direction.

For components 8 N east and 6 N north, the resultant magnitude is 10 N. Its direction is approximately 36.9° north of east because tan θ is northward component divided by eastward component. Identify the reference direction in the answer: the complementary angle would be measured from north. Adding 8 and 6 to obtain 14 N would ignore the perpendicular directions. Keep the units and the arrow direction when drawing the corresponding triangle.

blocks.heading: add two vectors that are not at right angles by a graphical method to determine a resultant in magnitude and direction
blocks.text:
Vectors at an arbitrary angle can be added with a scale drawing using a tip-to-tail triangle or a parallelogram. The resultant runs from the starting tail to the final tip, not along the remaining side in the reverse direction.

Choose and state a length scale, such as 1 cm for 1 N. Draw the first vector at its direction, then move the second vector parallel to itself so that its tail meets the first tip. Its size and direction are unchanged by this translation. Join the original start to the final tip with an arrow and measure the resultant’s scaled length and direction. In a parallelogram construction, both component tails share an origin and the resultant is the diagonal to the opposite corner.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: use and describe the use of a metre rule, a ruler and measuring tape to determine length, and measuring cylinders to determine volume
blocks.text:
A rule or tape measures length, while a graduated cylinder measures liquid volume. Instrument choice depends on the quantity, its size and the resolution needed.

A long flexible distance is more conveniently measured with a tape than with repeated short ruler placements. A small liquid volume needs a suitably graduated vessel rather than a length scale alone. Read the graduation unit before recording a value and check the zero or reference point. A cylinder can have a large capacity yet still be unsuitable for a small change if its divisions are too wide. Name both instrument and technique in a measurement plan.

blocks.heading: Measure length with a ruler, metre rule or tape
blocks.text:
A measured length is the difference between the scale positions of its ends. The scale should be aligned with the intended length and viewed without avoidable parallax.

An object beginning at 3.0 cm and ending at 11.6 cm is 8.6 cm long. Its length is not 11.6 cm unless its first end is at zero. Use a tape for longer distances and keep it appropriately straight without stretching it. For a curved perimeter, a flexible thread can transfer the path length to a straight rule, with additional uncertainty from following and transferring the curve.

blocks.heading: Measure liquid volume with a measuring cylinder
blocks.text:
A measuring cylinder reports liquid volume from the level of its surface. For water in a clean cylinder, the bottom of the curved meniscus is read at eye level.

Place the cylinder vertically on a level surface and allow the liquid to settle. Read the appropriate scale division with the eye level with the meniscus, rather than viewing from above. Record a value consistent with the scale resolution. For displacement measurements, subtract the original water volume from the volume after the object is immersed. Avoid trapped bubbles and ensure the object is fully submerged when that method is intended.

blocks.heading: use and describe the use of mechanical methods for the measurement of a small distance (ruler, caliper (vernier or dial) and micrometer screw gauge)
blocks.text:
A small dimension may require greater resolution than an ordinary ruler provides. Vernier calipers and a micrometer use mechanical scales to resolve smaller changes, but their measuring faces suit different tasks.

Caliper outside jaws measure external widths, inside jaws can measure an opening and a depth probe can measure a recess. A conventional external micrometer encloses an object between an anvil and spindle; it is not a suitable instrument for an inside diameter. Check range and zero before measurement. Resolution describes the scale increment, not a guarantee that each measurement is accurate. Poor alignment or excessive measuring force can defeat the apparent precision.

blocks.heading: Measure a small distance with a ruler
blocks.text:
Repeated layers can magnify a thickness too small for a single ruler reading. Dividing the total thickness by the number of similar layers estimates the thickness of one layer.

A stack of 80 similar sheets measuring 8.0 mm gives an average sheet thickness of 0.10 mm. Check that the sheets are similar and pressed together consistently without large gaps or excessive compression. Measuring a stack reduces the fractional influence of the ruler reading uncertainty compared with measuring one thin sheet. The result is an average, so it does not establish that every sheet has precisely the same thickness.

blocks.heading: Use vernier or dial calipers
blocks.text:
A vernier reading combines the main-scale position with the aligned vernier division. The vernier resolution and zero correction must be known for the particular instrument.

For an instrument with 0.1 mm vernier resolution, a main-scale reading of 18 mm and an aligned sixth division gives 18.6 mm before a zero correction. Do not assume the same resolution for every vernier. Close the appropriate jaws gently and check that the measured surfaces are properly contacted. Read inside and outside dimensions using the correct jaw faces. Record a known zero error and apply the correction with the sign that removes its bias.

blocks.heading: Use a micrometer screw gauge
blocks.text:
A micrometer reading combines the sleeve reading with the thimble contribution. For a 0.5 mm screw pitch divided into 50 thimble divisions, each division represents 0.01 mm.

If the sleeve shows 5.5 mm and the thimble contributes 0.23 mm, the reading is 5.73 mm before correction. Look for a visible half-millimetre sleeve mark; overlooking it produces a substantial error. Use the ratchet or suitable light measuring force rather than tightening hard against the object. Check the zero with the faces closed cleanly. A very thin or compressible sample can change thickness under measuring pressure, so technique remains important.

blocks.heading: use and describe the use of clocks and devices for measuring an interval of time (wrist watch and stop watch)
blocks.text:
A time interval is the elapsed duration between a defined start and finish. A clock provides time readings, while a stopwatch can directly display elapsed time.

When two clock readings are used, subtract the starting time from the finishing time, accounting for a change of minute or hour. A stopwatch still needs a clearly defined event for starting and stopping. Choose a device with a resolution appropriate to the duration; the display’s last digit does not eliminate reaction-time uncertainty. For repeated motion, specify what counts as one complete cycle before timing it.

blocks.heading: Measure a clock time interval
blocks.text:
An elapsed interval from a clock is found by subtracting the starting reading from the finishing reading. Time notation must be handled as minutes and seconds rather than as a decimal fraction.

From 10:14:45 to 10:15:20 the interval is 35 s. The minute boundary does not mean that only the final seconds should be subtracted. Converting both readings to a common seconds count can make the subtraction clearer. A wristwatch may be sufficient for a long duration but unsuitable for a very short event. Define the start and end events so that the time being measured is reproducible.

blocks.heading: Measure elapsed time with a stopwatch
blocks.text:
A stopwatch measures elapsed time between its start and stop actions. Human reaction-time variation can be important when the physical event is short.

Check that the stopwatch is reset or note its starting indication before a run. Use an observable event such as a bob crossing a reference line in a specified direction. When several repeats are possible, record each rather than replacing them by a remembered average. Timing a longer repeated sequence can reduce the relative effect of starting and stopping delays. Repeats assess variation but do not automatically remove a consistent delay in the chosen technique.

blocks.heading: evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of the above devices
blocks.text:
Instrument choice involves trade-offs in resolution, range and the physical access needed. A smaller scale increment is useful only when the instrument can correctly measure the intended surfaces or interval.

A measuring tape covers a long distance conveniently but may sag. A micrometer gives fine external readings but has a limited opening and cannot replace internal caliper jaws. A stopwatch provides fine displayed increments, yet reaction timing may dominate a short event. Explain an advantage or limitation in relation to the actual measurement. A tool is not best simply because it displays more digits; suitability depends on the experiment.

blocks.heading: measure and describe how to measure a short interval of time including the period of a pendulum
blocks.text:
A period is the time for one complete repeated cycle. Timing several cycles and dividing by their count estimates the period while reducing the relative influence of start/stop delays.

For a pendulum, a complete oscillation returns to the same position and direction. A crossing in the opposite direction after half a cycle should not be counted as a full cycle. If 15 oscillations take 24.0 s, the estimated period is 1.60 s. Repeat the measurement under the same conditions to judge variation. Keep the length and release conditions fixed when the aim is to estimate one period rather than investigate how it changes.

blocks.heading: describe a simple experiment to establish that the only variable that affects the period of a pendulum is the length
blocks.text:
For a simple pendulum under small-angle school conditions at one location, its period depends on its length rather than its bob mass. A controlled test changes one candidate factor while keeping the others appropriately fixed.

To test length, measure from the pivot to the bob’s centre, choose several lengths and obtain a mean period at each. Keep bob mass and a small release angle matched. To test mass separately, change mass while retaining length and release angle. A large amplitude or changed gravitational field would invalidate the simple statement that length is the sole relevant factor. Within the stated conditions, compare periods using the measurement quality rather than declaring an effect from tiny inconsistent differences.

2. Which caliper feature measures the inside width of an opening?
A. Outside jaws only
B. The zero-checking label
C. An external micrometer anvil
D. Internal jaws

3. Why is a micrometer ratchet useful?
A. It changes a diameter into a radius
B. It measures internal volume
C. It helps limit measuring force
D. It removes all zero error

4. What counts as one full pendulum oscillation?
A. Any visible movement
B. Return to the same position and direction
C. Any crossing of the centre
D. Travel from one extreme to the other

5. Which quantity is scalar?
A. Energy
B. Force
C. Velocity
D. Displacement

6. What additional information distinguishes a vector from a scalar magnitude?
A. Whether a unit exists
B. Whether it changes
C. Whether it is measured experimentally
D. Direction

7. In a tip-to-tail construction, where does the resultant begin?
A. At the midpoint of either component
B. At a new unrelated origin
C. At the first vector’s original tail
D. At the final tip, pointing back

8. A rod extends from 2.0 cm to 10.7 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
A. 5.35 cm
B. 8.7 cm
C. 10.7 cm
D. 12.7 cm

9. A 0.1 mm vernier gives 12 mm on the main scale and alignment at division 4. With no zero error, what is the reading?
A. 12.4 mm
B. 16 mm
C. 12.04 mm
D. 11.6 mm

10. A micrometer sleeve shows 4.5 mm and the thimble adds 0.18 mm. With no zero error, what is the result?
A. 4.18 mm
B. 4.32 mm
C. 18.45 mm
D. 4.68 mm

11. Twenty complete cycles take 32.0 s. What is the period?
A. 0.625 s
B. 32.0 s
C. 1.60 s
D. 640 s

12. Two perpendicular forces have magnitudes 5 N and 12 N. What is the resultant magnitude?
A. 169 N
B. 13 N
C. 17 N
D. 7 N

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: Its graduations report volume. B: It measures time. C: It measures current. D: It directly measures length.

2. Key D. A: Those enclose an outer dimension. B: This is not a measuring contact. C: It cannot span the inside opening in the usual external arrangement. D: They contact the inner surfaces.

3. Key C. A: That is a separate geometrical calculation. B: A micrometer is not a volume vessel. C: This reduces excessive squeezing of the sample. D: A ratchet does not set every scale zero.

4. Key B. A: The interval must be defined. B: Both position and direction identify a completed cycle. C: The opposite-direction crossing occurs after half a cycle. D: This is half a cycle.

5. Key A. A: It has magnitude without a direction. B: Force is a vector. C: Velocity includes direction. D: Displacement includes direction.

6. Key D. A: Scalars can have units too. B: Either kind can change. C: Both kinds can be measured. D: Direction is part of the vector specification.

7. Key C. A: The overall endpoints determine the sum. B: The construction must retain the combined displacement. C: It connects the overall start to the final tip. D: That gives the reversed resultant.

8. Key B. A: Halving one endpoint has no measurement basis. B: Subtract the starting position. C: This assumes a zero start. D: This adds the endpoint positions.

9. Key A. A: Add four times 0.1 mm to 12 mm. B: This treats divisions as millimetres. C: This assumes a 0.01 mm resolution. D: There is no stated correction requiring subtraction.

10. Key D. A: This misses the half-millimetre sleeve value. B: This subtracts instead of adding. C: This misreads the scales as decimal strings. D: Add the two scale contributions.

11. Key C. A: This reverses the quotient. B: This is the time of the whole sequence. C: Divide the elapsed time by twenty. D: This multiplies instead of dividing.

12. Key B. A: This omits the square root and has the wrong dimensional interpretation. B: Pythagoras gives the right-triangle resultant. C: This would add collinear same-direction magnitudes. D: This subtracts magnitudes without the stated directions.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for timing a pendulum with repeated complete oscillations.

| Oscillation count | Elapsed time / s |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 7 |
| 10 | 14 |
| 15 | 21 |
| 20 | 28 |
| 25 | 35 |
| 30 | 42 |

(a) Draw the graph with Elapsed time / s on the vertical axis and Oscillation count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot oscillation count horizontally and elapsed time vertically. The idealised straight trend passes through the origin.

Gradient: 35 ÷ 25 = 1.4 s per oscillation. The gradient gives the period of this fixed-length pendulum because it expresses elapsed time per complete cycle.

Plan: 1. Suspend a bob from a securely supported string and measure its length from pivot to bob centre. 2. Choose a small fixed release angle and define a reference crossing and direction for counting cycles. 3. Time a chosen number of complete oscillations with a stopwatch. 4. Repeat that count and calculate a mean elapsed time, investigating an anomalous timing. 5. Repeat for several counts with the same length and release conditions.
Control and accuracy: Keep pivot-to-centre length and small release angle fixed; avoid pushing the bob and keep its swing clear of people.
Table: Record cycle count and each elapsed time / s, with a mean-time column after repeats.
Graph and conclusion: Plot mean elapsed time against cycle count. Use the gradient to estimate a period and the scatter to judge consistency; this is a period measurement, not a test of length dependence.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-4.png)

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which quantity is the full length of a travelled path?
A. Distance
B. Displacement
C. Velocity
D. Acceleration

2. With east positive, what does position −6 m indicate?
A. A speed of 6 m/s west
B. A negative path distance
C. That the object is slowing
D. Six metres west of the origin

3. Which expression gives average velocity?
A. Velocity change / time
B. Time / displacement
C. Net displacement / total time
D. Total distance / total time

4. What does a horizontal speed-time line above zero show?
A. A decreasing distance
B. Steady nonzero speed
C. Rest
D. Uniform acceleration away from rest

5. Which unit measures acceleration?
A. m/s²
B. m/s
C. m²/s
D. s/m

6. What does negative acceleration alone identify?
A. That speed must decrease
B. That the object is at a negative position
C. That no force acts
D. Its direction under the chosen sign convention

7. When are the standard equations v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² applicable?
A. Only when the object starts from rest
B. Only when all signs are positive
C. For the stated straight-line motion with constant acceleration
D. For any varying acceleration without modification

8. A learner walks 10 m east then 4 m west. What is the net displacement?
A. 0 m
B. 6 m east
C. 14 m east
D. 6 m west

9. An object travels 36 m in 6 s then 12 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?
A. 4 m/s
B. 8 m/s
C. 2 m/s
D. 6 m/s

10. Velocity changes from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. What is the average acceleration?
A. 3.33 m/s²
B. 18 m/s²
C. 14 m/s²
D. 2 m/s²

11. Speed is 5 m/s for 4 s. What distance is represented by that speed-time rectangle?
A. 9 m
B. 0 m
C. 20 m
D. 1.25 m

12. From rest, an object has constant acceleration 1.5 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement?
A. 3 m
B. 12 m
C. 6 m
D. 24 m
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Distance adds the path lengths. B: This measures the directed start-to-finish change. C: This is a rate, not a path length. D: This describes velocity change per time.

2. Key D. A: Position is not a velocity. B: Path length is a different quantity. C: A position coordinate does not determine acceleration. D: The negative coordinate locates the position west of the reference.

3. Key C. A: This is average acceleration. B: This reverses the physical ratio. C: Both direction and the complete interval matter. D: This is average speed.

4. Key B. A: Accumulated distance is not the vertical variable. B: The vertical value is a speed that is not changing. C: That would require zero speed. D: That needs a sloping speed-time line for unchanged direction.

5. Key A. A: Velocity changes by metres per second during each second. B: This is a speed or velocity unit. C: This is not the velocity-change/time dimension. D: This is reciprocal speed.

6. Key D. A: Negative velocity can grow in magnitude under negative acceleration. B: Position is independent information. C: A nonzero acceleration requires a resultant force in the simple constant-mass model. D: The effect on speed also depends on velocity direction.

7. Key C. A: They allow a nonzero u. B: Consistent signed components are permitted. C: The acceleration condition is built into them. D: That violates their condition.

8. Key B. A: The learner has not returned to the starting point. B: Subtract the opposing displacement components. C: This is the total path length with a direction incorrectly attached. D: This reverses the net direction.

9. Key A. A: The total is 48 m in 12 s. B: This adds stage speeds instead of averaging the full journey. C: This uses the second stage alone. D: This uses the first stage alone.

10. Key D. A: This divides final velocity by time and omits u. B: This multiplies the velocity change by time. C: This adds the velocities without a time ratio. D: The change is 6 m/s over 3 s.

11. Key C. A: This adds unlike quantities. B: Zero gradient means constant speed, not zero distance. C: Speed multiplied by duration gives the rectangular area. D: This divides speed by time instead of using area.

12. Key B. A: This does not account for the time-squared factor. B: Use one half times acceleration times time squared. C: This is the final speed value with the wrong dimension. D: This omits the factor one half.

blocks.heading: recognise and state that the concepts ‘position’ and ‘reference point’ (can be represented as x, y or z) are fundamental in the study of speed, velocity and acceleration
blocks.text:
Position describes where an object is relative to a chosen reference point. A coordinate and a positive direction make one-dimensional positions unambiguous.

A mark on a straight track can be chosen as x = 0, with east defined as positive. A trolley at x = 2 m is then two metres east of that mark. Choosing a different reference changes the coordinate assigned to the same physical place. It does not by itself move the trolley. State the reference and direction before comparing positions or using their changes to calculate velocity. In two or three dimensions, more than one coordinate is needed to locate an object.

blocks.heading: recognise that position, relative to a reference point, can be either positive or negative
blocks.text:
A position can be positive, zero or negative relative to a chosen origin. A negative position identifies one side of the origin; it does not by itself say how the object is moving.

With east positive, x = −4 m locates an object four metres west of the origin. It could be stationary, travelling east or travelling west at that instant. Position and velocity are different quantities. If the origin is moved, the coordinate changes even though the object may stay still. To find displacement, subtract initial position from final position using the same origin and sign convention for both readings.

blocks.heading: define distance as a measure of how far an object travels along a particular path (without considering direction)
blocks.text:
Distance is the length of the path travelled. It is a scalar and does not encode the direction between the starting and finishing positions.

Walking 7 m east and then 2 m west gives a travelled distance of 9 m. The return section adds to the path length even though it partly reverses the earlier movement. A route with several bends can have a long distance while the finishing position is close to the start. Keep total path length separate from a coordinate measured from an origin. Units of metres do not distinguish them by themselves; the physical definition does.

blocks.heading: define displacement as a vector which has a magnitude equal to the shortest distance between the initial and final points and a direction from the initial to the final point
blocks.text:
Displacement is the directed change in position from start to finish. Its magnitude is the straight-line separation of those positions, with a direction from initial to final position.

For motion on a straight east-positive line, a change from x = −2 m to x = +5 m gives displacement +7 m. An object that returns to its starting point has zero net displacement even if it has travelled a substantial distance. Draw a start-to-finish arrow to separate net displacement from the intermediate route. A negative component is a direction relative to the stated convention, not a negative path length.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which quantity is the full length of a travelled path?
A. Distance
B. Displacement
C. Velocity
D. Acceleration

2. With east positive, what does position −6 m indicate?
A. A speed of 6 m/s west
B. A negative path distance
C. That the object is slowing
D. Six metres west of the origin

3. Which expression gives average velocity?
A. Velocity change / time
B. Time / displacement
C. Net displacement / total time
D. Total distance / total time

4. What does a horizontal speed-time line above zero show?
A. A decreasing distance
B. Steady nonzero speed
C. Rest
D. Uniform acceleration away from rest

5. Which unit measures acceleration?
A. m/s²
B. m/s
C. m²/s
D. s/m

6. What does negative acceleration alone identify?
A. That speed must decrease
B. That the object is at a negative position
C. That no force acts
D. Its direction under the chosen sign convention

7. When are the standard equations v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² applicable?
A. Only when the object starts from rest
B. Only when all signs are positive
C. For the stated straight-line motion with constant acceleration
D. For any varying acceleration without modification

8. A learner walks 10 m east then 4 m west. What is the net displacement?
A. 0 m
B. 6 m east
C. 14 m east
D. 6 m west

9. An object travels 36 m in 6 s then 12 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?
A. 4 m/s
B. 8 m/s
C. 2 m/s
D. 6 m/s

10. Velocity changes from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. What is the average acceleration?
A. 3.33 m/s²
B. 18 m/s²
C. 14 m/s²
D. 2 m/s²

11. Speed is 5 m/s for 4 s. What distance is represented by that speed-time rectangle?
A. 9 m
B. 0 m
C. 20 m
D. 1.25 m

12. From rest, an object has constant acceleration 1.5 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement?
A. 3 m
B. 12 m
C. 6 m
D. 24 m

2. Key D. A: Position is not a velocity. B: Path length is a different quantity. C: A position coordinate does not determine acceleration. D: The negative coordinate locates the position west of the reference.

Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State whether displacement is scalar or vector. [1]

(b) State the SI unit of acceleration. [1]

(c) Explain why a horizontal distance-time line indicates rest whereas a horizontal speed-time line at 2 m/s does not. [2]

(d) Calculate the constant acceleration for a speed increase from 1 to 7 m/s in 3 s without changing direction. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Displacement is a vector.

(b) m/s²

(c) The first has no increase in path distance. The second directly states a constant nonzero speed, so the object continues moving.

(d) The acceleration is (7 − 1)/3 = 2 m/s² in the direction of motion.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: define speed as a rate of change of distance
blocks.text:
Speed is distance travelled per elapsed time. Instantaneous speed describes how rapidly distance is changing at a particular instant.

A vehicle speedometer indicates an instantaneous speed rather than necessarily the average over a whole journey. Average speed uses the total path length and the complete elapsed time being considered. A speed of 6 m/s means six metres of path are covered per second if that speed remains steady. Speed carries no direction, so two objects moving oppositely can have equal speeds. Use a velocity when the direction matters.

blocks.heading: define instantaneous velocity as a ‘rate of change of displacement’ or speed in a given direction
blocks.text:
Instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of displacement at an instant. It includes direction as well as the magnitude of motion.

With east positive, velocities +4 m/s and −4 m/s have the same speed but opposite directions. A velocity can change because the speed changes, the direction changes or both change. At this level a straight-line sign convention represents direction clearly. Do not infer direction from a speed-time graph alone unless the motion’s direction is supplied. The unit m/s is shared with speed, so the definition and sign convention must distinguish the two quantities.

blocks.heading: Define average velocity as total displacement divided by total elapsed time
blocks.text:
Average velocity is total displacement divided by total elapsed time. It can be zero for a return journey whose average speed is not zero.

If a learner travels 12 m away and then returns to the start in 8 s, the net displacement is zero and the average velocity is zero. The path distance is 24 m, so the average speed is 3 m/s. Stops count in the elapsed time if the requested average covers the full journey. A nonzero average velocity must be given with a direction or a signed component under a stated convention.

blocks.heading: explain what positive and negative values of velocity mean
blocks.text:
Positive and negative velocities identify opposite directions under the chosen sign convention. The sign of velocity is independent of whether the speed is increasing or decreasing.

A trolley moving west at a steady 2 m/s has velocity −2 m/s if east is positive. Its negative sign does not mean it is slowing. If it changes from −2 to −5 m/s, its speed grows from 2 to 5 m/s even though the signed velocity decreases. State the chosen positive direction before describing the change. On a position-time graph, a negative gradient indicates motion in the negative coordinate direction.

blocks.heading: Use average speed = total distance / total time, and speed = distance / time
blocks.text:
Average speed is total distance divided by total elapsed time. An average over unequal-duration stages cannot generally be found by an unweighted mean of their speeds.

A journey covers 24 m in 6 s and a further 12 m in 6 s. Total distance is 36 m and total time is 12 s, giving 3 m/s. If either stage included a stop, include that stopped interval when calculating a full-journey average. Identify the boundary of the journey before adding distances and times. A simple average of two stage speeds is valid for equal durations, but it should not replace the total-distance method when durations differ.

blocks.heading: plot readings for and interpret a distance-time graph
blocks.text:
The gradient of a distance-time graph represents speed. A horizontal section means that travelled distance is not increasing during that interval.

Plot accumulated path distance vertically and elapsed time horizontally. A straight rising segment indicates steady speed; a steeper segment on the same scales indicates a higher speed. A horizontal part indicates rest over the interval. If speed changes smoothly, the graph bends and a local gradient describes the instantaneous speed. A path-distance graph does not decrease when an object turns back: accumulated distance continues to grow. A signed position-time graph can decrease, because its vertical quantity is different.

blocks.heading: plot readings for and interpret a speed-time graph
blocks.text:
The gradient of a speed-time graph represents the rate of speed change during straight-line motion of unchanged direction. Area between the speed-time line and the time axis gives travelled distance.

A horizontal line at a positive speed represents steady motion, not rest. A line on the time axis represents zero speed. A straight sloping segment gives uniform speed change, while a curved segment gives a changing rate. Read the vertical quantity before interpreting the shape. For motion whose direction changes, use signed velocity information to determine acceleration direction; a speed graph alone omits that direction. Distance can be found by dividing the area into simple rectangles, triangles or trapezia.

blocks.heading: identify from the shape of a distance-time or speed-time graph when a body is - at rest - moving with constant speed - moving with changing speed
blocks.text:
Graph shape must be interpreted using the quantity on the vertical axis. Rest, steady motion and changing motion can look different on distance-time and speed-time graphs.

A horizontal distance-time line means that the accumulated distance does not grow, so the object is at rest. A horizontal speed-time line at 4 m/s describes an object continuing to travel at that speed. A straight rising distance-time line represents steady speed, while a straight rising speed-time line represents increasing speed. State the axis labels before describing any segment. If a line bends, examine how its gradient changes rather than attaching one memorised motion label to every curved line.

blocks.heading: distinguish between speed and velocity by means of similarities and differences
blocks.text:
Speed describes the rate of distance travelled without direction. Velocity describes the rate of displacement change and includes direction.

An object moving around a bend at steady speed can still have changing velocity because its direction changes. For straight-line examples, two objects at 5 m/s in opposite directions have equal speeds but different velocities. Whole-journey averages also differ when path distance is greater than the net displacement. A numerical answer expressed in m/s is incomplete as a velocity specification unless the direction is given or implied by a clear sign convention.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Whole-journey average speed uses total path distance and total elapsed time. An arithmetic mean of stage speeds requires equal durations to represent this average.

For 2 m/s during 6 s followed by 5 m/s during 2 s, the distances are 12 m and 10 m. The total is 22 m in 8 s, giving 2.75 m/s. The unweighted mean of the two speeds is 3.5 m/s and would give the shorter fast stage too much influence. Multiplying each stage speed by its duration first preserves how far the object actually travelled. Include any rest interval in a complete-journey time.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
A positive horizontal speed-time segment represents steady motion. A horizontal distance-time segment represents no additional path distance and therefore rest over the interval.

Consider graph A at a constant speed of 3 m/s and graph B at a constant accumulated distance of 12 m. During the next two seconds, A adds 6 m to its path, while B adds none. Both lines are horizontal, but they plot different vertical quantities. The error is treating the shape as a motion label without reading the axis. Use the quantity and its unit to decide whether the line directly states a speed or instead requires a gradient to obtain it.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity
blocks.text:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It has direction and a unit of metres per second per second, written m/s² or m s⁻².

If velocity changes by 6 m/s during 3 s, the average acceleration is 2 m/s² in the direction of that velocity change. For a constant acceleration the same change occurs during each equal time interval. Acceleration need not increase speed: it can oppose the current velocity and reduce the speed. A direction change can also be acceleration even when the speed stays the same. Straight-line examples require a stated positive direction to interpret the signs.

blocks.heading: explain what positive and negative values of acceleration mean
blocks.text:
The sign of an acceleration component gives its direction under the chosen coordinate convention. Whether speed increases depends on how the acceleration direction compares with the velocity direction.

For east-positive motion, changing from +7 to +3 m/s gives negative acceleration and a speed decrease. Changing from −3 to −7 m/s also gives negative acceleration, but the speed increases. The word negative therefore cannot be used as a universal synonym for slowing down. Compare initial velocity, final velocity and the chosen positive direction. If velocity and acceleration are oppositely directed, speed decreases while that direction relationship holds.

blocks.heading: identify linear motion for which the acceleration is constant and calculate the acceleration
blocks.text:
Constant acceleration gives equal velocity changes during equal time intervals. For uniform straight-line acceleration, a = (v − u)/t.

A model vehicle changing from 1 m/s to 5 m/s in 2 s has acceleration 2 m/s². The velocity-time plot is straight because its gradient stays constant. Identify both ends of the time interval; using the final velocity alone would be valid only if the initial velocity were zero. Include the sign in the velocity difference. The average acceleration formula still gives an interval average for nonuniform motion, but it does not establish that the acceleration was constant throughout.

blocks.heading: identify motion for which the acceleration is not constant
blocks.text:
Nonuniform acceleration means that the rate of velocity change varies during the motion. A curved velocity-time graph can show a changing gradient and therefore changing acceleration.

Velocities of 0, 1, 4 and 9 m/s at one-second intervals have successive increases of 1, 3 and 5 m/s. These changes are not equal, so one constant acceleration does not describe the sequence. A secant gradient between distant points gives an average over that interval, while the curve’s local slope describes the instantaneous change. When sketching such motion, choose a smooth changing gradient rather than a straight line simply because the velocity is increasing.

blocks.heading: calculate the area under a speed-time graph to determine the distance travelled for motion with constant acceleration
blocks.text:
Distance travelled is the area beneath a speed-time graph over the chosen interval. The graph’s area has units of speed multiplied by time, which reduces to a length.

For a speed rising uniformly from 2 to 6 m/s during 4 s, the trapezium area is one half of the sum of the parallel speed values multiplied by the time width. The distance is 16 m. The gradient of the same line is instead 1 m/s², which is an acceleration. Splitting the area into a rectangle and a triangle gives the same physical distance. With a signed velocity-time graph, signed area gives displacement; adding magnitudes of the appropriate areas is needed for total path distance.

blocks.heading: state that the acceleration of free fall for a body near the Earth’s surface is constant and has a value of approximately 10 m/s 2
blocks.text:
Near Earth’s surface, freely falling motion has a gravitational acceleration of approximately 10 m/s² when air resistance is negligible. The acceleration is directed downward and is not the same quantity as the object’s current speed.

A released object begins with an initial speed that may be zero but has a downward acceleration immediately. In the simple model its downward speed then increases by approximately 10 m/s during each second. A thrown object is still accelerated downward while rising, at its highest point and while falling. The sign assigned to this acceleration depends on the chosen positive direction. Air resistance can change the resultant acceleration, so the simple value should not be applied without considering the stated model.

blocks.heading: Use the constant-acceleration equations v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, a = (v − u)/t and s = (u + v)t/2
blocks.text:
Constant-acceleration equations connect u, v, a, t and displacement s for straight-line motion under fixed acceleration. Use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as and s = (u + v)t/2 only when their constant-acceleration condition applies.

Choose an equation containing the known quantities and the unknown required. To find final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration and time, use v = u + at. To find displacement without a time value, v² = u² + 2as may be appropriate. Use one sign convention for every vector component; displacement can be negative under that convention. An object may reverse direction during an interval, in which case displacement and total path distance differ. Do not replace a changing acceleration with a constant one merely to make an equation convenient.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Speed-time area gives distance, whereas speed-time gradient gives a rate of speed change. Their different units distinguish the two operations.

A straight line rising from 1 to 5 m/s over 2 s has area 6 m and gradient 2 m/s². The first result combines speed with time; the second divides a speed change by a time change. Calling the slope the distance is not a small numerical slip: it uses the wrong relationship between the plotted quantities. Identify the requested quantity before selecting the graphical operation.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What is the direction of a normal contact force?
A. Perpendicular to the contact surface
B. Along the surface
C. Geographically north
D. Along the object’s velocity

2. Which interaction is tension?
A. Earth attracting a stone
B. Air slowing a falling object
C. A table pressing perpendicular to a book
D. A taut string pulling a load

3. A cart moves with constant velocity. What is its resultant force in a constant-mass model?
A. Its mass multiplied by its speed
B. Necessarily its weight downward
C. Zero
D. Equal to its forward drive regardless of resistance

4. What is spring extension?
A. The load multiplied by total length
B. Loaded length minus unloaded length
C. Loaded length alone
D. The original length divided by the load

5. Where does the limit of proportionality occur?
A. Where the initial proportional graph trend ends
B. Where the spring necessarily breaks
C. At the first nonzero load for every spring
D. At zero extension only

6. What condition permits a system’s total momentum to be conserved?
A. Every body has zero velocity
B. Every body has equal mass
C. No internal interactions occur
D. No external resultant force

7. Which unit represents momentum?
A. N/m
B. J/s
C. kg m/s
D. kg m/s²

8. Forces of 17 N east and 5 N west act on one body. What is their resultant?
A. 0 N
B. 12 N east
C. 22 N east
D. 12 N west

9. A spring within its proportional range has k = 80 N/m and extension 0.025 m. What is the force?
A. 2.0 N
B. 3200 N
C. 80.025 N
D. 0.0003125 N

10. A 4 kg object has a 10 N resultant force. What is its acceleration?
A. 40 m/s²
B. 0.4 m/s²
C. 10 m/s²
D. 2.5 m/s²

11. A 0.30 kg trolley moves at 4 m/s east. What is its momentum?
A. 0.075 kg m/s east
B. 1.2 kg m/s west
C. 1.2 kg m/s east
D. 13.3 kg m/s east

12. An average resultant of 8 N acts east for 0.25 s. What momentum change does it cause?
A. 0 N s
B. 2 N s east
C. 32 N s east
D. 8.25 N s east
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: The normal direction is defined by the surface. B: That can describe friction instead. C: A surface normal is not a compass direction. D: Normal contact direction is not set by velocity.

2. Key D. A: That is gravitational force. B: That is drag. C: That is normal contact. D: The string transmits a pull along itself.

3. Key C. A: That gives momentum, not force. B: Other vertical forces can balance weight. C: Zero acceleration implies zero resultant. D: The other forces must be included.

4. Key B. A: This is not a length change. B: It is the increase in length. C: This includes the original length. D: This has a different meaning and unit.

5. Key A. A: The force/extension ratio ceases to be constant. B: Breaking is a different event. C: The initial proportional region can extend over many loads. D: The zero point does not define the end of the proportional range.

6. Key D. A: A moving system can conserve momentum. B: Equal masses are not required. C: Internal interactions can transfer momentum between bodies. D: This excludes a net external momentum transfer.

7. Key C. A: This can represent spring stiffness. B: This is power. C: Momentum is mass times velocity. D: This is a force unit.

8. Key B. A: The forces are unequal. B: The opposing components subtract. C: This adds opposing magnitudes. D: This reverses the stronger direction.

9. Key A. A: Use F = kx. B: This divides instead of multiplying. C: This adds quantities with different units. D: This reverses the ratio.

10. Key D. A: This multiplies force and mass. B: This reverses the quotient. C: This ignores the stated mass. D: Divide resultant force by mass.

11. Key C. A: This divides mass by velocity. B: This reverses the momentum direction. C: Multiply mass by velocity and retain direction. D: This divides velocity by mass.

12. Key B. A: A nonzero external resultant over time changes momentum. B: Multiply force by its duration. C: This divides by time. D: This adds incompatible quantities.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(b) The trend departs from its initial proportional straight line.

(d) k = F/x = 6/0.030 = 200 N/m.

(e) a = F/m = 15/2.5 = 6.0 m/s² west.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for loading a spring within its proportional range.

| Force / N | Extension / mm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.4 | 4.8 |
| 0.6 | 7.2 |
| 0.8 | 9.6 |
| 1 | 12 |

(a) Draw the graph with Extension / mm on the vertical axis and Force / N on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Use force horizontally and extension vertically. Plot the six idealised readings and a straight trend through the origin within the stated proportional range.

Gradient: 12 ÷ 1 = 12 mm/N. The plotted gradient is extension per force, so it is reciprocal stiffness in these units; k must instead be obtained as force per extension.

Plan: 1. Secure a spring vertically and place a ruler alongside it with a clear pointer or reference on the extending part. 2. Measure and record the unloaded length before applying any load. 3. Apply a known calibrated force gently and read the loaded length after oscillations settle. 4. Subtract the original length to obtain extension and repeat the reading where appropriate. 5. Repeat for several safe forces, keeping the spring within its proportional range.
Control and accuracy: Use the same spring and reference point, read the scale perpendicularly and protect against falling loads or overload.
Table: Record force / N, original length / mm, loaded length / mm and extension / mm, with repeated readings kept separately.
Graph and conclusion: Plot extension against force to test the proportional trend. Read its slope as extension per force; use the reciprocal with consistent unit conversion if stiffness is required.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-6.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: state that a force, measured in newtons, may produce a change in size, shape or velocity of a body and relate these ideas to Newton’s first and second laws of motion
blocks.text:
A force can deform a body or contribute to a change in its velocity. For constant mass, the resultant force determines acceleration through F = ma; zero resultant allows rest or constant velocity.

A force is an interaction between objects, measured in newtons. Newton’s first law states that an object keeps its velocity unless a resultant force changes it. A nonzero driving force can be balanced by resistance, so the presence of a force does not alone establish acceleration. Newton’s second law relates acceleration to the vector sum of the forces, not to one selected force when others also act. A force can also change size or shape when a body deforms.

blocks.heading: describe the ways in which a force may change the motion of a body
blocks.text:
A resultant force can change speed, direction or both. A change of velocity can occur even when the speed itself stays unchanged.

A ball speeding up along a straight line changes velocity through its magnitude. A ball slowing down has a velocity change opposing its motion. A moving object that turns also changes velocity because direction is part of a vector. In each case identify the resultant force rather than assuming that the direction of motion is the direction of the force. A force can act on a moving body without increasing its speed.

blocks.heading: identify in everyday life:  different forces (e.g. contact, electrical, magnetic, gravitational, weight, tension, friction and air resistance)  the agent applying the force  the object the force is applied to
blocks.text:
A force description should identify its type, the object exerting it and the object receiving it. Several different interactions can act on the same body at the same time.

A book on a table experiences gravitational attraction from Earth and a contact force from the table. These forces act on the book, but come from different agents. A rope can add a tension, and sliding can introduce friction. A force diagram should show the forces on the chosen body, not a mixture of forces on several unrelated objects. Labelling the interaction clarifies which forces must be combined when finding that body’s resultant.

blocks.heading: Identify contact and normal forces
blocks.text:
A normal contact force acts perpendicular to the contact surface. Its direction follows the surface orientation rather than a fixed upward direction.

For a book on a horizontal desk the support force is upward, but a wall’s normal force is horizontal. Other contact components, such as friction, can act along the surface. Identify the relevant contact before choosing an arrow direction. A support force need not equal weight if other forces or vertical acceleration affect the body.

blocks.heading: Identify an electrical force
blocks.text:
Electrical forces arise from interactions involving electric charge. They can attract or repel depending on the charge arrangement.

A charged rod can exert a force without touching another charged object. In simple charge comparisons, like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Attraction can also occur through induced charge redistribution, so attraction by itself does not establish that an initially neutral object carried the opposite net charge. Distinguish electrical interactions from the magnetic action of a magnet.

blocks.heading: Identify a magnetic force
blocks.text:
Magnetic forces act in interactions involving magnets, magnetic materials or suitable moving charges and currents. Two magnetic poles can attract or repel according to their orientation.

A bar magnet can pull an iron object without direct contact. Two magnets can repel, whereas attraction alone does not prove that a piece of iron is itself a permanent magnet. Magnetic force direction should be inferred from the actual pole or field arrangement. A magnet does not attract every material simply because it is a solid.

blocks.heading: Identify gravitational force and weight
blocks.text:
Weight is the gravitational force on a body. Near Earth, its direction is toward Earth’s centre rather than away from the supporting surface.

A suspended load still has weight even when a rope prevents it falling. Its mass is a property measured in kilograms, whereas weight is a force measured in newtons. A surface or rope may balance that weight, but balance does not remove the gravitational interaction. The mass–weight calculation is developed in topic 7.

blocks.heading: Identify tension
blocks.text:
Tension is the pulling force transmitted by a taut rope, string or cable. At the attachment it acts along the rope away from the object being pulled.

A simple rope can pull a load but does not push it along its length in the same way. Draw the tension direction from the actual rope segment attached to the chosen body. A slack rope may transmit no appreciable tension. Do not automatically set tension equal to weight when the load accelerates or when the rope is inclined.

blocks.heading: Identify friction and air resistance
blocks.text:
Friction opposes relative sliding or its tendency at a contact; air resistance opposes relative motion through air. These resistive forces are distinct from the weight of the object.

A sliding block can slow because of surface friction, while a falling object can experience upward air resistance. The size depends on the interaction and conditions. Friction is not necessarily backward relative to the overall motion of a vehicle: it can provide the forward force from a driven tyre. Specify the bodies or medium when identifying which relative motion is opposed.

blocks.heading: Identify the force agent and the object acted on
blocks.text:
The force agent is the body or field source exerting the interaction on the chosen object. Naming the receiving object prevents forces on different bodies from being mixed in one resultant.

For a magnet pulling a steel pin, the magnet is the agent and the pin receives the described force. For a hand pulling a rope, identify whether the question concerns the rope or an attached load before labelling its force. A complete statement such as the rope pulls the load upward communicates more than the word tension by itself.

blocks.heading: find the resultant of two or more forces acting along the same line
blocks.text:
Collinear forces can be combined using signed components along a chosen positive direction. Opposing directions use opposite signs, so the resultant may be smaller than either of the competing force totals.

With east positive, a pull of +18 N and resistance of −7 N give a resultant of +11 N. If the values become +7 N and −18 N, the resultant is −11 N, meaning west. Do not add magnitudes when arrows oppose. A zero resultant can occur with several nonzero forces acting. Combine forces on the same body when applying the result to its acceleration.

blocks.heading: plot and interpret extension-load graphs, describe the associated experimental procedure and use proportionality in simple calculations
blocks.text:
Spring extension is loaded length minus unloaded length. Within a proportional range, extension is directly proportional to the applied load.

Measure the unloaded spring length before adding loads. At each known load, record the new length and subtract the original length. Plot extension against force to see whether the trend is a straight line through the origin. If force is vertical and extension horizontal, the slope is stiffness k; reversing these axes gives reciprocal stiffness. Increase loads gently, avoid overloading and let the spring settle before reading. The loaded length itself is not the extension unless the original length were zero.

blocks.heading: state Hooke's law and recall and use the expression F = kx where F is the force applied, k is the spring constant and x is the extension of the spring
blocks.text:
Within its limit of proportionality, a spring obeys F = kx, where x is extension and k is stiffness. In SI units F is in newtons, x in metres and k in newtons per metre.

If 3 N extends a spring by 0.015 m within its proportional range, k is 200 N/m. Use extension rather than total length and convert millimetres to metres before obtaining k in N/m. A larger k means more force is required for the same extension. Do not assume the relation remains valid after the extension-load trend curves away from proportionality. The graph orientation determines whether the measured slope is k or its reciprocal.

blocks.heading: identify the 'limit of proportionality' for an extension-load graph
blocks.text:
The limit of proportionality marks where force and extension cease to follow a proportional straight-line relationship. Beyond that point, F/x is not represented by one unchanged proportional stiffness.

Look for departure from the initial straight trend in an extension-load graph. This limit is not automatically the same as the point at which the spring breaks or remains permanently stretched; those are different observations. If the data extend beyond the proportional region, do not use a single earlier k value to predict the entire response. In practical work use a suitable load range and stop before damage or unsafe loads occur.

blocks.heading: Relate resultant force, mass and acceleration using F = ma, including their directions
blocks.text:
For constant mass, resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. The acceleration direction is the direction of the resultant force, expressed using a consistent sign convention.

A 2 kg trolley with a resultant force of 6 N has acceleration 3 m/s². If 6 N is only the driving force and a resistance also acts, first calculate the resultant before using F = ma. Convert grams to kilograms when using newtons and m/s². A body can move steadily with a nonzero driving force if another force balances it. Its present velocity is not itself a measurement of acceleration.

blocks.heading: recall and use the formula momentum = mass × velocity
blocks.text:
Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. It is a vector, so its direction or signed component follows the velocity direction.

A 0.50 kg object moving west at 4 m/s has momentum 2 kg m/s west. With east chosen positive, the component is −2 kg m/s. A stationary object has zero momentum even though its mass is not zero. When several objects are considered, add signed momentum components rather than adding speed magnitudes indiscriminately. The unit kg m/s is equivalent to N s, linking momentum change with a force acting over time.

blocks.heading: recall and use the change in momentum = force × time of action
blocks.text:
A resultant force acting over a time interval changes momentum. For a constant or appropriate average resultant force, Δp = FΔt.

If a 10 N average resultant acts for 0.20 s, the momentum change is 2.0 N s in the force direction. The change is final momentum minus initial momentum. If an object stops, its final momentum is zero and the change opposes its initial motion. For the same required momentum change, increasing the stopping time reduces the average force. That is why cushioning can reduce a stopping force without changing the original momentum that must be removed.

blocks.heading: define the principle of conservation of momentum as when two or more objects interact, their total momentum remains constant, provided that no external resultant force is acting on them
blocks.text:
A system’s total momentum is conserved when no external resultant force acts on that system. Momentum can transfer between its interacting bodies while the system total stays unchanged under that external-force condition.

Choose the system boundary before applying the principle. Forces between two colliding trolleys are internal to the combined two-trolley system, but a push from a person outside it is external. Individual trolley momenta need not stay constant during their interaction. If the external resultant is negligible during a short collision, comparing the total immediately before and after is a useful model. Do not extend the conclusion to a system receiving a significant external impulse.

blocks.heading: apply the conservation of momentum in simple applications, including elastic and inelastic collisions between two bodies in one dimension (definitions of an elastic and inelastic collision are not required)
blocks.text:
In a one-dimensional collision model with no external resultant force, total signed momentum before equals total signed momentum after. For objects that remain together, their shared final momentum is their combined mass multiplied by their common velocity.

Two trolleys of masses 0.30 kg and 0.20 kg initially moving at +2 m/s and zero have total momentum +0.60 kg m/s. If they remain together and the external resultant is negligible, their common velocity is +1.2 m/s. Opposite initial directions require opposite signs. For a rebound, retain the final velocity sign as well. The supplied masses and directions, rather than a memorised all-positive formula, determine each term. Only the one-dimensional momentum application is needed here.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Constant velocity means zero acceleration and therefore zero resultant force for constant mass. Individual forces can still be present and balanced.

A powered cart can travel steadily while a motor drives it forward and resistance acts backward. If the forward force is 14 N and the motion has constant velocity, the opposing total is also 14 N in the simple collinear model. The resultant is zero, not 14 N. Removing the drive while resistance remains changes the balance and can slow the cart. The error is confusing a named applied force with the total force on the body.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Total momentum conservation requires no external resultant force on the chosen system. An external impulse can change the momentum of that system.

Compare two coasting trolleys interacting with each other and a trolley being pushed by a person outside the selected system. Internal transfers can preserve the combined trolley momentum when the external resultant is negligible. The outside push supplies a momentum change, so the same unchanged-total statement is not justified. Naming the system and its external forces matters more than simply recognising that a collision or movement occurs.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Opposing velocities use opposite signs in a one-dimensional momentum sum. With no external resultant force, that signed sum is the quantity conserved through the interaction.

Choose east as positive. A 2 kg object moving east at 3 m/s contributes +6 kg m/s, while a 1 kg object moving west at 2 m/s contributes −2 kg m/s. The total is +4 kg m/s, not the sum of the speed magnitudes. If the objects remain together with negligible external resultant, divide that signed total by the combined mass. A negative answer in another example would mean common motion west under the same convention.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What is the direction of a normal contact force?
A. Perpendicular to the contact surface
B. Along the surface
C. Geographically north
D. Along the object’s velocity

2. Which interaction is tension?
A. Earth attracting a stone
B. Air slowing a falling object
C. A table pressing perpendicular to a book
D. A taut string pulling a load

3. A cart moves with constant velocity. What is its resultant force in a constant-mass model?
A. Its mass multiplied by its speed
B. Necessarily its weight downward
C. Zero
D. Equal to its forward drive regardless of resistance

4. What is spring extension?
A. The load multiplied by total length
B. Loaded length minus unloaded length
C. Loaded length alone
D. The original length divided by the load

5. Where does the limit of proportionality occur?
A. Where the initial proportional graph trend ends
B. Where the spring necessarily breaks
C. At the first nonzero load for every spring
D. At zero extension only

6. What condition permits a system’s total momentum to be conserved?
A. Every body has zero velocity
B. Every body has equal mass
C. No internal interactions occur
D. No external resultant force

7. Which unit represents momentum?
A. N/m
B. J/s
C. kg m/s
D. kg m/s²

8. Forces of 17 N east and 5 N west act on one body. What is their resultant?
A. 0 N
B. 12 N east
C. 22 N east
D. 12 N west

9. A spring within its proportional range has k = 80 N/m and extension 0.025 m. What is the force?
A. 2.0 N
B. 3200 N
C. 80.025 N
D. 0.0003125 N

10. A 4 kg object has a 10 N resultant force. What is its acceleration?
A. 40 m/s²
B. 0.4 m/s²
C. 10 m/s²
D. 2.5 m/s²

11. A 0.30 kg trolley moves at 4 m/s east. What is its momentum?
A. 0.075 kg m/s east
B. 1.2 kg m/s west
C. 1.2 kg m/s east
D. 13.3 kg m/s east

12. An average resultant of 8 N acts east for 0.25 s. What momentum change does it cause?
A. 0 N s
B. 2 N s east
C. 32 N s east
D. 8.25 N s east

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: The normal direction is defined by the surface. B: That can describe friction instead. C: A surface normal is not a compass direction. D: Normal contact direction is not set by velocity.

2. Key D. A: That is gravitational force. B: That is drag. C: That is normal contact. D: The string transmits a pull along itself.

3. Key C. A: That gives momentum, not force. B: Other vertical forces can balance weight. C: Zero acceleration implies zero resultant. D: The other forces must be included.

4. Key B. A: This is not a length change. B: It is the increase in length. C: This includes the original length. D: This has a different meaning and unit.

5. Key A. A: The force/extension ratio ceases to be constant. B: Breaking is a different event. C: The initial proportional region can extend over many loads. D: The zero point does not define the end of the proportional range.

6. Key D. A: A moving system can conserve momentum. B: Equal masses are not required. C: Internal interactions can transfer momentum between bodies. D: This excludes a net external momentum transfer.

7. Key C. A: This can represent spring stiffness. B: This is power. C: Momentum is mass times velocity. D: This is a force unit.

8. Key B. A: The forces are unequal. B: The opposing components subtract. C: This adds opposing magnitudes. D: This reverses the stronger direction.

9. Key A. A: Use F = kx. B: This divides instead of multiplying. C: This adds quantities with different units. D: This reverses the ratio.

10. Key D. A: This multiplies force and mass. B: This reverses the quotient. C: This ignores the stated mass. D: Divide resultant force by mass.

11. Key C. A: This divides mass by velocity. B: This reverses the momentum direction. C: Multiply mass by velocity and retain direction. D: This divides velocity by mass.

12. Key B. A: A nonzero external resultant over time changes momentum. B: Multiply force by its duration. C: This divides by time. D: This adds incompatible quantities.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the name of the pulling force in a taut rope. [1]

(b) State the graph feature indicating the end of spring proportionality. [1]

(c) Explain why balanced forces can act on a cart moving steadily along a straight track. [2]

(d) Calculate k for a spring extended by 0.030 m under 6 N within its proportional range. [2]

(e) Calculate the acceleration of a 2.5 kg body under a resultant force of 15 N west. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Tension.

(b) The trend departs from its initial proportional straight line.

(c) Steady velocity means zero acceleration and zero resultant; a forward drive can be matched by the opposing resistance.

(d) k = F/x = 6/0.030 = 200 N/m.

(e) a = F/m = 15/2.5 = 6.0 m/s² west.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for loading a spring within its proportional range.

| Force / N | Extension / mm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.4 | 4.8 |
| 0.6 | 7.2 |
| 0.8 | 9.6 |
| 1 | 12 |

(a) Draw the graph with Extension / mm on the vertical axis and Force / N on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Use force horizontally and extension vertically. Plot the six idealised readings and a straight trend through the origin within the stated proportional range.

Gradient: 12 ÷ 1 = 12 mm/N. The plotted gradient is extension per force, so it is reciprocal stiffness in these units; k must instead be obtained as force per extension.

Plan: 1. Secure a spring vertically and place a ruler alongside it with a clear pointer or reference on the extending part. 2. Measure and record the unloaded length before applying any load. 3. Apply a known calibrated force gently and read the loaded length after oscillations settle. 4. Subtract the original length to obtain extension and repeat the reading where appropriate. 5. Repeat for several safe forces, keeping the spring within its proportional range.
Control and accuracy: Use the same spring and reference point, read the scale perpendicularly and protect against falling loads or overload.
Table: Record force / N, original length / mm, loaded length / mm and extension / mm, with repeated readings kept separately.
Graph and conclusion: Plot extension against force to test the proportional trend. Read its slope as extension per force; use the reciprocal with consistent unit conversion if stiffness is required.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-6.png)

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which unit represents mass?
A. kg
B. N
C. N/kg
D. Pa

2. Which property is associated with resistance to a change of motion?
A. Density alone
B. Weight alone
C. Speed alone
D. Inertia

3. What is gravitational field strength?
A. Weight times mass
B. The mass of Earth per object
C. Weight per mass
D. Mass per weight

4. At downward terminal velocity, what is the resultant on the falling body?
A. An increasing downward force
B. Zero
C. Its full weight downward
D. Its full weight upward

5. Which expression gives density?
A. Mass / volume
B. Volume / mass
C. Mass × volume
D. Weight / time

6. What should be avoided in a displacement measurement?
A. Reading an initial volume
B. Measuring the mass separately
C. Stating the volume unit
D. Trapped bubbles on the submerged object

7. At approximately what temperature is liquid water densest?
A. 100 °C
B. At every temperature equally
C. 4 °C
D. 0 °C

8. What is the weight of a 0.60 kg sample where g = 10 N/kg?
A. 6.0 kg
B. 6.0 N
C. 0.060 N
D. 600 N

9. A sample weighs 4.5 N in a 10 N/kg field. What is its mass?
A. 0.45 kg
B. 45 kg
C. 4.5 kg
D. 0.45 N

10. A mass of 36 g occupies 12 cm³. What is its density?
A. 0.333 cm³/g
B. 432 g/cm³
C. 24 g/cm³
D. 3 g/cm³

11. A vessel is 22 g empty and 70 g with liquid. What is the liquid mass?
A. 70 g
B. 22 g
C. 48 g
D. 92 g

12. An immersed solid raises water from 28 to 37 cm³. What is its volume?
A. 28 cm³
B. 9 cm³
C. 65 cm³
D. 37 cm³
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Mass is measured in kilograms. B: Newtons measure force. C: This is gravitational field strength. D: This measures pressure.

2. Key D. A: Density concerns mass per volume, not directly the response of the whole mass. B: Inertia does not require a particular gravitational field. C: Mass, rather than existing speed alone, sets this property. D: Mass is associated with inertia.

3. Key C. A: The product has different units. B: This is not the local definition. C: This gives g = W/m. D: This is the reciprocal ratio.

4. Key B. A: The velocity is steady, so acceleration is zero. B: Drag and weight balance. C: That omits the balancing drag. D: The weight direction is downward.

5. Key A. A: It compares the mass with occupied volume. B: This is reciprocal density. C: The product has a different meaning. D: This is neither mass nor volume ratio.

6. Key D. A: That is needed for the difference. B: That is needed for density. C: Units are required, not an error. D: They can increase the apparent displaced volume.

7. Key C. A: This is not the maximum-density temperature. B: Density changes with temperature. C: This is the maximum-density region. D: Water expands as it cools below about 4 °C.

8. Key B. A: This reports force as a mass. B: Multiply mass by field strength. C: This divides by g. D: This mishandles the mass scale.

9. Key A. A: Divide weight by g. B: This multiplies instead of dividing. C: This equates the numerical force and mass. D: This retains a force unit for a mass result.

10. Key D. A: This is reciprocal density. B: This multiplies mass and volume. C: This subtracts unlike quantities. D: Divide 36 by 12.

11. Key C. A: This includes the vessel. B: This is the empty-vessel mass alone. C: Subtract the empty-vessel mass. D: This adds the two measured masses.
