blocks.heading: define the mass of a body as a measure of the matter in it and that mass depends on the number of particles the body contains and the mass of those atoms
blocks.text:
Mass is a measure of the matter in an object. It depends on the particles present and their masses, rather than being the gravitational force on them.

An object can be moved to a different gravitational field without losing material. Its mass then stays the same in the ordinary school model, even though its weight changes. Record mass in kilograms or a clearly stated compatible unit such as grams. A balance compares masses or infers mass from a calibrated force measurement, so its operating principle matters when discussing another location. Distinguish an object’s mass from its apparent support or scale force in a changing-motion situation.

blocks.heading: define inertia as the property of mass which 'resists' change in motion (Newton’s first law of motion)
blocks.text:
Inertia is the resistance of an object’s motion to change, associated with its mass. For the same resultant force, a greater mass produces a smaller acceleration.

A loaded trolley needs a larger resultant force than an otherwise similar empty trolley to obtain the same acceleration. This is not because an additional force called inertia pushes backward. The relationship F = ma already connects the mass with the required force and acceleration. An object continues with its existing velocity when its resultant force is zero. In everyday motion, friction can hide that behaviour by providing a real opposing interaction.

blocks.heading: define gravitational field strength (g) as the gravitational force or weight per unit mass
blocks.text:
Gravitational field strength is gravitational force per unit mass. It can be written g = W/m and has units N/kg.

If a 2 kg object has weight 20 N at a location, the gravitational field strength there is 10 N/kg. A different test mass gives the same field value in the same approximately uniform region. The field strength is not the weight of every object; the weight also depends on mass. State the location or supplied model when using a numerical g value. The familiar near-Earth approximation is useful for school calculations but is not a claim that gravitational fields have equal strengths everywhere.

blocks.heading: state that gravitational field strength (g) is equal to the gravitational acceleration (a)
blocks.text:
Gravitational field strength in N/kg has the same numerical value as free-fall acceleration in m/s² for the local field. This follows by combining W = mg with resultant force = ma when gravity is the relevant resultant.

If air resistance is negligible, a falling object is accelerated by its weight, so ma = mg and its downward acceleration is g. The two forms of unit describe different definitions of the same local gravitational effect. A value near 10 N/kg corresponds to approximately 10 m/s². Do not apply the free-fall acceleration directly to a falling object whose air resistance is substantial; the gravitational field remains present but the resultant force is then smaller than weight.

blocks.heading: describe qualitatively the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field with and without air resistance, including reference to terminal velocity
blocks.text:
Without appreciable air resistance, an object falls with the local gravitational acceleration. With resistance, increasing drag can reduce the downward resultant until weight and drag balance at terminal velocity.

Just after release from rest, drag may be small, so the downward acceleration is close to g. As speed grows, drag increases and the downward acceleration becomes smaller. At terminal velocity, the resultant is zero because drag balances weight; the object continues downward at a steady speed. Its weight has not vanished. Opening a parachute increases drag and can produce an upward resultant while the person is still moving downward, reducing that speed toward a new terminal value.

blocks.heading: recall and use the equation weight = mass × gravitational field strength and know that near the Earth’s surface g is approximately 10 N/kg
blocks.text:
Weight is the gravitational force on an object, given by W = mg. Use kilograms with g in N/kg to obtain weight in newtons.

A 0.75 kg object has weight 7.5 N in a field of 10 N/kg. An object of the same mass would have a different weight where g differs. Convert a mass given in grams before multiplying by an SI field strength. A force measured in newtons must not be reported as a mass in kilograms without using the field relation. Near Earth’s surface, g ≈ 10 N/kg is the stated school approximation unless another value is supplied.

blocks.heading: determine the mass of an object from its weight (using a balance or a spring)
blocks.text:
A known weight can be used to infer mass by dividing by the local gravitational field strength. A spring balance responds to force and must be interpreted using its calibration.

If a force instrument reports a weight of 3.2 N and the field strength is 10 N/kg, the inferred mass is 0.32 kg. Check the instrument zero and use an appropriate range. An electronic balance often displays grams or kilograms directly after calibration, but this does not make mass and force the same quantity. When comparing measurements between different gravitational environments, distinguish a true comparison of masses from a force-based device calibrated for a particular field.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Mass and weight are different quantities, so changing gravitational field strength changes weight without necessarily changing mass. For the same unchanged object, W = mg links the changed field to the changed force.

A sealed object of mass 3 kg moved from a field of 10 N/kg to one of 2 N/kg retains 3 kg of mass in this model. Its weight changes from 30 N to 6 N. Reporting the new weight as 6 kg confuses a force with matter quantity. The mass could change if material were added or removed, but that is a separate physical change, not the effect of the field alone.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which unit represents mass?
A. kg
B. N
C. N/kg
D. Pa

2. Which property is associated with resistance to a change of motion?
A. Density alone
B. Weight alone
C. Speed alone
D. Inertia

3. What is gravitational field strength?
A. Weight times mass
B. The mass of Earth per object
C. Weight per mass
D. Mass per weight

4. At downward terminal velocity, what is the resultant on the falling body?
A. An increasing downward force
B. Zero
C. Its full weight downward
D. Its full weight upward

5. Which expression gives density?
A. Mass / volume
B. Volume / mass
C. Mass × volume
D. Weight / time

6. What should be avoided in a displacement measurement?
A. Reading an initial volume
B. Measuring the mass separately
C. Stating the volume unit
D. Trapped bubbles on the submerged object

7. At approximately what temperature is liquid water densest?
A. 100 °C
B. At every temperature equally
C. 4 °C
D. 0 °C

8. What is the weight of a 0.60 kg sample where g = 10 N/kg?
A. 6.0 kg
B. 6.0 N
C. 0.060 N
D. 600 N

9. A sample weighs 4.5 N in a 10 N/kg field. What is its mass?
A. 0.45 kg
B. 45 kg
C. 4.5 kg
D. 0.45 N

10. A mass of 36 g occupies 12 cm³. What is its density?
A. 0.333 cm³/g
B. 432 g/cm³
C. 24 g/cm³
D. 3 g/cm³

11. A vessel is 22 g empty and 70 g with liquid. What is the liquid mass?
A. 70 g
B. 22 g
C. 48 g
D. 92 g

12. An immersed solid raises water from 28 to 37 cm³. What is its volume?
A. 28 cm³
B. 9 cm³
C. 65 cm³
D. 37 cm³

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: Mass is measured in kilograms. B: Newtons measure force. C: This is gravitational field strength. D: This measures pressure.

2. Key D. A: Density concerns mass per volume, not directly the response of the whole mass. B: Inertia does not require a particular gravitational field. C: Mass, rather than existing speed alone, sets this property. D: Mass is associated with inertia.

3. Key C. A: The product has different units. B: This is not the local definition. C: This gives g = W/m. D: This is the reciprocal ratio.

4. Key B. A: The velocity is steady, so acceleration is zero. B: Drag and weight balance. C: That omits the balancing drag. D: The weight direction is downward.

5. Key A. A: It compares the mass with occupied volume. B: This is reciprocal density. C: The product has a different meaning. D: This is neither mass nor volume ratio.

6. Key D. A: That is needed for the difference. B: That is needed for density. C: Units are required, not an error. D: They can increase the apparent displaced volume.

7. Key C. A: This is not the maximum-density temperature. B: Density changes with temperature. C: This is the maximum-density region. D: Water expands as it cools below about 4 °C.

8. Key B. A: This reports force as a mass. B: Multiply mass by field strength. C: This divides by g. D: This mishandles the mass scale.

9. Key A. A: Divide weight by g. B: This multiplies instead of dividing. C: This equates the numerical force and mass. D: This retains a force unit for a mass result.

10. Key D. A: This is reciprocal density. B: This multiplies mass and volume. C: This subtracts unlike quantities. D: Divide 36 by 12.

11. Key C. A: This includes the vessel. B: This is the empty-vessel mass alone. C: Subtract the empty-vessel mass. D: This adds the two measured masses.

12. Key B. A: This is the starting water volume. B: Use the volume increase. C: This adds the levels. D: This includes the original water.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: Relate density to mass and volume using density = mass / volume
blocks.text:
Density is mass per volume, ρ = m/V. The chosen mass and volume must refer to the same material sample.

A sample of mass 54 g and volume 20 cm³ has density 2.7 g/cm³. A larger piece of the same uniform material has a greater mass and volume in the same ratio under the same conditions. Density is not total mass alone: a small dense object can have less mass than a large low-density object. Common units are kg/m³ and g/cm³; one g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³. In a mass-versus-volume graph, the gradient can give density; swapping the axes gives its reciprocal.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to determine the density of a liquid and of a regularly shaped solid
blocks.text:
Density determination requires separate measurements of a sample’s mass and volume. For a liquid, subtract the empty-container mass; for a regular solid, calculate volume from measured dimensions.

For a liquid, weigh the empty dry vessel, then the vessel with the measured liquid. Their mass difference is the liquid mass. Read the liquid volume using a suitably graduated cylinder. For a cuboid solid, measure length, width and height with an appropriate instrument and multiply them. A cylinder instead requires its radius and height. Check that the volume is the material volume of interest rather than an unrelated container capacity. Divide the sample mass by that volume and state the resulting unit.

blocks.heading: describe the determination of the density of an irregularly shaped solid by the method of displacement
blocks.text:
An irregular solid’s volume can be measured by displacement of a suitable liquid. The liquid-volume increase equals the volume immersed when the object is fully submerged without trapped bubbles or significant liquid absorption.

Read the initial volume, lower the object carefully and read the new level. A change from 35 cm³ to 43 cm³ corresponds to an immersed volume of 8 cm³. Measure the object’s mass separately and divide by that displaced volume. Choose a liquid that does not dissolve or react with the sample in the intended experiment. If the object floats or absorbs the liquid, the simple fully submerged nonabsorbing method needs modification rather than an uncritical subtraction.

blocks.heading: describe floating and sinking in terms of different densities
blocks.text:
An object’s average density relative to a fluid helps predict floating or sinking. For a simple fully immersed comparison, an object denser than the fluid tends to sink, while a lower-average-density object can float partly immersed.

A hollow boat can float even though some of its construction material is denser than water, because its overall volume includes enclosed air. Use the average density of the whole floating object rather than the density of one piece of its material. An object of approximately equal density can remain suspended when other effects are small. The amount immersed at equilibrium adjusts until the fluid’s support balances the object’s weight.

blocks.heading: state that the density of water around 4  C is a maximum and explain how this is an advantage to aquatic life
blocks.text:
Liquid water has its maximum density at approximately 4 °C. Cooling below that region makes it less dense, and ice is also less dense than liquid water.

As surface water cools toward 4 °C, its increased density can make it sink and promote mixing. Water cooled below 4 °C can remain nearer the surface, and ice forms there rather than sinking as a dense solid. A surface ice layer can reduce further heat loss from the liquid underneath. This helps explain how aquatic organisms may remain in liquid water below an icy surface. Do not claim the whole lake must be at exactly 4 °C; actual temperatures depend on mixing and conditions.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which change increases the moment for the same perpendicular force?
A. A larger pivot-to-force-line distance
B. A smaller arm
C. A force line through the pivot
D. A change of force unit alone

2. Which quantity is a scalar?
A. Force
B. Moment
C. Velocity
D. Work

3. In scissors, which part serves as fulcrum?
A. The material
B. The blade tip
C. The joint
D. The fingers

4. Which pair of conditions establishes equilibrium?
A. A large support force alone
B. Zero resultant force and moment
C. Zero force alone
D. Zero moment alone

5. Where is the centre of mass of a freely suspended stationary lamina?
A. On the vertical below the suspension point
B. At the lowest corner
C. At the suspension hole
D. At the largest visible edge

6. Which change usually improves resistance to toppling?
A. Raising the centre of mass
B. Narrowing the base
C. Removing a supporting wheel
D. Widening the support base

7. Which use needs substantial friction?
A. A freely turning pulley bearing
B. A sliding machine guide intended to move easily
C. A brake pad stopping a wheel
D. A lubricated axle bearing

8. What moment does 8 N produce with a 0.15 m perpendicular arm?
A. 0.01875 N m
B. 1.2 N m
C. 53.3 N m
D. 120 N m

9. A 4 N load has a 0.30 m arm. What load balances it on a 0.20 m opposing arm?
A. 6 N
B. 4 N
C. 2.67 N
D. 12 N

10. A force line passes through a pivot. What is its moment about that pivot?
A. The force value in N m
B. The full beam length times force
C. Its weight
D. Zero

11. A light beam supports 3 N and 5 N downward and is stationary. What upward support is required?
A. 15 N
B. Zero
C. 8 N
D. 2 N

12. A force holds a stationary lever. What is its work on the lever during the hold?
A. Force divided by time
B. Zero
C. Force times lever length
D. Equal to its moment in joules

2. Key D. A: It has direction. B: It has a rotational direction. C: It includes direction. D: It is an energy transfer.

3. Key C. A: It supplies the cutting resistance. B: It is away from the pivot. C: The blades rotate about this pivot. D: They provide effort.

4. Key B. A: Its balance with other forces is unspecified. B: Both translation and rotation are balanced. C: A couple can still turn the body. D: Translation can still accelerate.

5. Key A. A: Its weight line passes through the support. B: The lowest point need not be the centre of mass. C: The body generally hangs below that point. D: Edge length does not locate it.

6. Key D. A: This usually reduces the required toppling tilt. B: This places an edge nearer the weight line. C: This may reduce the support region. D: A larger tilt is then needed to move weight beyond it.

7. Key C. A: Friction there resists the intended movement. B: Lower friction is preferred there. C: Friction transfers motion energy away. D: There friction is unwanted.

8. Key B. A: This reverses the ratio. B: Multiply 8 by 0.15. C: This divides by distance. D: This uses centimetres as metres.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the meaning of fulcrum. [1]

(b) State the rotational condition for equilibrium. [1]

(c) Explain why a moment of 6 N m is not necessarily a transfer of 6 J. [2]

(d) Calculate the moment of 9 N with a perpendicular arm of 0.40 m. [2]

(e) Calculate the force at a 0.60 m arm that balances 12 N at a 0.20 m opposing arm. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The pivot about which a lever turns.

(b) The resultant moment is zero.

(c) Moment uses a lever arm; work requires displacement along force. The body may remain stationary despite the moment.

(d) M = Fd = 3.6 N m.

(e) F = (12 × 0.20)/0.60 = 4 N.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for pivot.
(b) One mark for zero net turning effect.
(c) One mark for distinct distance meanings; one for the absence of displacement preventing work.
(d) One mark for force times arm; one for 3.6 N m.
(e) One mark for equal opposing moments; one for 4 N.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for balancing a lever with a fixed opposing moment.

| Effort distance / m | Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹ |
|---:|---:|
| 0.05 | 0.025 |
| 0.1 | 0.05 |
| 0.15 | 0.075 |
| 0.2 | 0.1 |
| 0.25 | 0.125 |
| 0.3 | 0.15 |

(a) Draw the graph with Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹ on the vertical axis and Effort distance / m on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot balancing effort vertically against reciprocal effort arm horizontally; the straight trend is expected for a fixed opposing moment.

Gradient: 0.125 ÷ 0.25 = 0.5 N m. The gradient of effort against reciprocal arm is the fixed opposing moment, because F = M/d. It is not the force or the arm alone.

Plan: 1. Balance a beam about a stable pivot and account for its own weight. 2. Fix a known load at a measured perpendicular arm on one side. 3. Choose an effort position on the other side and measure its arm from the pivot. 4. Adjust the effort force until the beam is horizontal and stationary, then record it. 5. Repeat for a range of effort arms, keeping the opposing moment fixed and securing suspended weights.
Control and accuracy: Keep the load and its arm fixed, use vertical force lines, avoid pivot friction and prevent weights falling onto feet.
Table: Record effort arm / m, reciprocal arm / m⁻¹ and balancing effort / N.
Graph and conclusion: A straight effort-versus-reciprocal-arm line supports Fd approximately constant; compare its gradient with the known opposing moment.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to determine the position of the centre of mass of a plane lamina
blocks.text:
The centre of mass of a suspended lamina lies vertically below its suspension point at rest. Two suspension directions locate it at the intersection of the corresponding vertical lines.

Make a small hole near an edge of a thin irregular card and suspend it freely from a pin. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and mark its vertical line on the settled card. Suspend the card from another edge point and repeat. Their intersection locates the centre of mass; a third line is a useful check. The card must turn freely, not be clamped at an angle. For an irregular shape the intersection need not be at the visual centre and may even fall outside the material.

blocks.heading: describe qualitatively the effect of the position of the centre of mass on the stability of simple objects
blocks.text:
An object tends to topple when its weight’s line of action passes outside its support base. A lower centre of mass or wider base generally permits a greater tilt before this occurs.

Consider a tall loaded trolley turning or standing on a slope. If its weight acts inside the base, a small tilt can produce a restoring moment; outside the edge, weight produces a toppling moment. Lowering a load reduces the horizontal shift of its centre of mass during a given tilt. Widening the base moves the supporting edge farther from the original weight line. Compare like arrangements and distinguish resistance to toppling from resistance to sliding: surface friction also influences what actually happens.

blocks.heading: describe the effect of friction on objects and how friction depends on the surfaces
blocks.text:
Friction opposes relative sliding, or the tendency to slide, between contacting surfaces. Its magnitude depends on the contacting materials, surface condition and normal contact force.

A stationary shoe can experience friction that prevents slipping even without sliding. Friction on a walking person may act forward because it opposes the shoe’s backward tendency relative to the ground. Sliding friction often transfers mechanical energy into internal energy of the surfaces. Roughness can matter, but avoid treating visible roughness as a complete quantitative law for every pair of materials. Compare the same surfaces under controlled load when investigating their friction; distinguish the force needed to start motion from that during steady sliding.

blocks.heading: describe how to reduce friction and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of friction in everyday life
blocks.text:
Lubrication and replacing sliding by rolling can reduce friction in suitable machines. Friction provides useful grip and braking but can also cause wear and unwanted heating.

Oil can separate suitable moving surfaces, reducing direct interaction; ball bearings replace much sliding with rolling. These methods must fit the machine: reducing tyre-road friction would reduce useful grip. Brake pads rely on friction to reduce vehicle motion and transfer energy to the surroundings, so heating there accompanies the intended action. In bearings, the same heating wastes useful mechanical energy and can damage parts. State both the intended purpose and the surface pair when judging whether friction is beneficial.

blocks.heading: describe the moment of a force as a measure of its turning effect and give everyday examples (such as crowbar, wheelbarrow, pliers, scissors, tweezers or tongs)
blocks.text:
A moment measures a force’s turning effect about a pivot. Its size increases with force and with the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action.

A spanner turns a nut because the hand’s force acts at a distance from the nut’s axis. Pushing near the end gives a larger turning effect than pushing near the nut with the same perpendicular force. The effect also depends on direction: pushing along the spanner toward the nut gives little turning effect. A crowbar turns about its contact point; scissors turn about their joint. Name the pivot before identifying a moment, and state clockwise or anticlockwise relative to the view used.

blocks.heading: describe the difference between moment and work (moment is a vector, work is a scalar; and that the distance involved in moment is perpendicular to the force whilst the distance involved in work is in the same direction as the applied force)
blocks.text:
Moment and work can both be expressed using force times a distance, but their distances describe different things. Moment uses perpendicular distance to a pivot; work uses displacement along the force and is an energy transfer.

Moment has a rotational direction and is a vector quantity in the syllabus treatment; work is a scalar. Report a moment in N m and work in joules even though the units have equivalent dimensions. A person holding a stationary spanner may exert a moment without doing mechanical work on the stationary nut. If the nut rotates, a point of application moves and energy can be transferred. The existence of a lever arm does not itself establish a displacement.

blocks.heading: identify load, effort and fulcrum in everyday examples of common machines (e.g. spanner, wheelbarrow)
blocks.text:
The fulcrum is a lever’s pivot, the effort is the applied driving force and the load is the resistance being moved. These names describe roles in the stated arrangement rather than fixed parts of every machine.

In a wheelbarrow the wheel axle acts as fulcrum, the contents provide much of the load, and the hands provide effort at the handles. A spanner has a turning axis at the nut and effort at the hand; the nut resists the rotation. On scissors the pivot is the joint, the fingers supply effort and the material resists cutting at the blades. Locate forces and their lines before measuring distances; the full length of a tool need not equal a particular moment arm.

blocks.heading: recall and use the formula moment = force × perpendicular distance
blocks.text:
The size of a moment is M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular moment arm. With force in newtons and distance in metres, moment is in N m.

Convert centimetres to metres before substitution. A 15 N force with a perpendicular arm of 0.20 m produces 3.0 N m. If the force line passes through the pivot, its moment about that pivot is zero even when the force is large. For a sloping force, measure the shortest perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action rather than simply the length of the lever. Assign a clockwise or anticlockwise direction separately from the size.

blocks.heading: state that, when there is no resultant force and no resultant turning effect, a system is in equilibrium
blocks.text:
Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment. Balancing clockwise and anticlockwise moments alone does not establish translational equilibrium.

A stationary balanced beam has no tendency to accelerate in translation or rotation. Its support force must balance its downward loads, and its moments about a chosen pivot must balance. Two equal opposite forces whose lines do not coincide have zero resultant force but can produce a turning effect. Conversely, a force through the centre can accelerate an object without creating a moment about that centre. Test the two conditions independently; neither replaces the other.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment (involving vertical forces) to verify that there is no net moment on a body in equilibrium
blocks.text:
A balanced beam can test equality of clockwise and anticlockwise moments from vertical forces. Perpendicular distances must be measured from the pivot to the vertical force lines.

First balance a uniform ruler on a pivot near its centre so that its own weight has negligible moment, or include that moment explicitly. Suspend known weights on opposite sides and adjust positions until the ruler rests horizontally. Measure each distance from the pivot, not from the ruler’s end. Calculate the moments in each direction and compare their sums. Repeat with different forces and positions. Keep the support stable, catch falling masses safely and do not use a hand to hold the beam in apparent balance while measuring.

blocks.heading: use the conditions of equilibrium in simple calculations
blocks.text:
A body in equilibrium has equal total clockwise and anticlockwise moments about a chosen pivot. A suitable pivot eliminates the moment of a force acting through it.

For a light beam, a 6 N load 0.40 m to the left has an anticlockwise moment of 2.4 N m. A downward force 0.30 m to the right must therefore be 8 N for rotational equilibrium. The upward support force must also equal the total 14 N downward force. A heavy beam’s own weight must be included at its centre of mass when its force line does not pass through the pivot. Draw the force positions before substituting numbers.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
A lever arm is not the displacement used to calculate work. A force can have a moment about a pivot even when its point of application remains stationary.

A hand holds a horizontal bar at rest by pushing upward 0.50 m from its pivot. The hand force has a moment about the pivot, but the stationary point has no displacement, so no mechanical work is done on the bar by that force during the hold. Muscles can still consume chemical energy internally. Separating the body being studied from the person avoids treating effort felt by a person as proof of work on a stationary object.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What changes in a chemical fuel reaction?
A. Atoms are rearranged
B. Heavy nuclei split as its defining process
C. Light nuclei fuse as its defining process
D. Atoms vanish without products

2. Which source uses hot rocks beneath Earth’s surface?
A. Tidal
B. Wind
C. Photovoltaic
D. Geothermal

3. Which fuel is finite in the syllabus classification?
A. Wind
B. Tidal flow
C. Nuclear fuel
D. Sunlight

4. Which process supplies the Sun’s energy?
A. Fission of reactor fuel
B. Fusion
C. Coal combustion
D. Hydroelectric flow

5. Which device converts suitable DC output to AC for a load?
A. Inverter
B. Water tank
C. Turbine
D. Thermal insulation

6. What is the main useful output of a solar water heater?
A. Electricity from its pipes
B. Nuclear fuel
C. A stronger wind
D. Increased water internal energy

7. Which difficulty is particularly associated with fission products?
A. Dependence on an ocean tide
B. No need to remove waste heat
C. Radioactive waste management
D. Need for a sunny night

8. A farm needs water after dark. Which arrangement stores daytime solar pumping’s useful result?
A. Removing the pump
B. A raised water tank
C. A disconnected empty wire
D. A smaller unshaded panel without storage

9. Which consideration matters for a hydroelectric site?
A. Available flow and height difference
B. Panel-cell colour alone
C. Radioactive half-life of water
D. Having no water

10. A PV refrigerator is operating. Where is energy rejected?
A. Nowhere because cooling destroys energy
B. Into the panel as manufactured sunlight
C. Into a disappearing mass
D. To the surroundings through the hot side

11. A wind project has no fuel combustion during generation. What follows?
A. Its output cannot vary
B. Its blades need no maintenance
C. Its operational combustion emissions are avoided
D. Its construction has zero impact

12. Water rises from 22 to 30 °C in 4 min. What is its average heating rate?
A. 32 °C/min
B. 2 °C/min
C. 7.5 °C/min
D. 8 °C/min
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: The chemical products have a different arrangement. B: That describes fission. C: That describes fusion. D: That fails to conserve matter in this model.

2. Key D. A: This uses tidal movement. B: This uses moving air. C: This uses incident radiation. D: It draws on internal thermal energy.

3. Key C. A: This is a replenished flow. B: This is renewable on human timescales. C: Its usable material is a finite resource. D: It is treated as renewable.

4. Key B. A: That is the conventional reactor pathway. B: Light nuclei join in the Sun. C: The Sun is not a coal furnace. D: This is a water-based terrestrial system.

5. Key A. A: It changes the electrical supply form. B: This stores water rather than changing electrical supply. C: It provides mechanical rotation. D: It reduces heat transfer.

6. Key D. A: Pipes are not photovoltaic cells. B: There is no nuclear conversion here. C: Wind is not the intended output. D: The intended service is heating.

7. Key C. A: This is not its energy source. B: Cooling remains necessary. C: Some products need containment over long periods. D: Reactor generation does not require sunlight.

8. Key B. A: This removes the lifting mechanism. B: The stored water can later flow down. C: This stores no useful pumping output. D: It still lacks night illumination.

9. Key A. A: Both affect usable water-energy input. B: This is not a hydroelectric criterion. C: This is not the relevant energy source. D: Flow is required for generation.

10. Key D. A: Energy is conserved. B: That is not the cooling pathway. C: The cooling model does not remove material. D: The removed heat plus input energy must leave.

11. Key C. A: Wind changes. B: A moving machine still needs maintenance. C: This is the supported claim. D: Materials and construction can have impacts.

12. Key B. A: This multiplies rise by time. B: The rise is 8 °C over 4 min. C: This divides final temperature by time. D: This omits division by the interval.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the energy form carried by wind. [1]

(b) State the useful energy output of a PV panel. [1]

(c) Explain how insulation helps a solar water tank. [2]

(d) Calculate the average heating rate when water warms by 9 °C in 6 min. [2]

(e) Explain why storing water can suit a pump with variable solar output. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Kinetic energy.

(b) Electrical energy.

(c) It reduces energy transfer from hotter water to cooler surroundings, retaining more of the collected energy.

(d) Rate = temperature rise/time = 1.5 °C/min.

(e) Water can be raised while sunlight is available. The tank then supplies water later without the pump operating at that instant.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for kinetic energy.
(b) One mark for electrical output.
(c) One mark for reduced transfer; one for retaining useful internal energy.
(d) One mark for dividing rise by time; one for 1.5 °C/min.
(e) One mark for collecting the useful result during supply; one for later delivery independent of instantaneous output.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for model solar water heater over a short interval with steady illumination.

| Time / min | Water temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 21 |
| 2 | 22.6 |
| 4 | 24.2 |
| 6 | 25.8 |
| 8 | 27.4 |
| 10 | 29 |

(a) Draw the graph with Water temperature / °C on the vertical axis and Time / min on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot temperature vertically against elapsed time horizontally over the short steady-input interval; fit a rising line.

Gradient: 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 °C/min. The gradient is the temperature increase per minute over this interval, not an energy efficiency. A steady rate is an approximation over the stated short interval.

Plan: 1. Put a measured mass of water in a small solar collector and record its initial temperature. 2. Fix the collector angle and expose it to steady illumination. 3. Start a timer and stir gently before each temperature reading. 4. Record temperature at regular intervals using the same immersed thermometer position. 5. Repeat with the same water mass and comparable illumination, stopping before unsafe temperatures.
Control and accuracy: Hold collector area, angle and water mass fixed; minimise draught changes, avoid looking into intense lamps and handle warm water carefully.
Table: Record elapsed time / min and water temperature / °C; add temperature rise / °C if comparing runs.
Graph and conclusion: The temperature-time gradient compares heating rates under the controlled conditions; efficiency would additionally need input and useful energy measurements.

blocks.heading: Matching renewable systems to the service
blocks.text:
Renewable systems can supply electrical or thermal energy to meet different end uses. Matching the conversion pathway to the intended service reduces unnecessary conversions.

Solar resources offer strong opportunities in Namibia, but actual output depends on location, weather, shading and equipment. The 2018 syllabus gives a world irradiance ranking; that dated ranking is not used here as a current comparison. Heating water directly may avoid generating electricity merely to heat it again. A pump or refrigerator needs the corresponding mechanical or electrical conversion.

blocks.heading: Explain renewable electricity generation
blocks.text:
Renewable electricity generation requires a conversion device suited to the source. Photovoltaic cells use radiation directly, while wind and hydroelectric machines commonly drive generators mechanically.

A small system may include a controller, storage battery and inverter where AC is required. Storage shifts the use of energy to a later time; it is not an additional primary source. Allow for conversion losses and actual demand.

blocks.heading: Explain renewable heating and greenhouses
blocks.text:
Solar collectors can heat water, and transparent greenhouse covers admit useful solar radiation. Absorption raises internal energy, while reduced heat loss helps maintain a warmer interior.

A solar heater uses an absorber, water path and insulated storage. A greenhouse admits radiation that warms surfaces; its enclosure reduces loss by moving warm air away. Ventilation may be needed to prevent overheating. These systems use thermal pathways rather than requiring photovoltaic conversion first.

blocks.heading: Explain renewable water pumping
blocks.text:
Renewable energy can operate a water pump through mechanical or electrical conversion. A wind rotor may drive a pump directly, while a photovoltaic system can drive an electric motor.

Pumping raises water’s gravitational potential energy. A storage tank can retain the benefit of pumping when sunshine or wind is available, reducing the need to store electricity for later pumping. The required lifting height and water flow influence system size.

blocks.heading: Explain renewable refrigeration and air-conditioning
blocks.text:
Renewable electricity can drive a refrigerator or air-conditioner’s compressor. A refrigerator transfers energy from a cooler region to a warmer region using an external energy input.

Cooling does not mean a panel emits coldness. The machine removes thermal energy from the intended region and rejects that energy plus its input energy elsewhere. Solar electricity can supply the compressor; an appropriately designed thermal absorption system can instead use heat input. Output variability and storage must match the cooling duty.

blocks.heading: describe a basic solar photovoltaic (PV) system, a basic solar water heater and basic wind energy systems stating the energy changes involved
blocks.text:
Basic renewable systems contain a collector or rotor and a useful energy-output path. Tracking input, intermediate transfer and output distinguishes PV, water-heating and wind systems.

A PV panel supplies electrical output, a thermal collector raises water temperature, and a wind rotor supplies shaft motion that may drive a generator or pump. Diagrams should label the useful output and losses to the surroundings. A generator and an inverter perform different jobs: the former converts mechanical input, while the latter changes the electrical supply form.

blocks.heading: Describe a basic photovoltaic system and its energy changes
blocks.text:
A basic PV system includes illuminated cells connected to an electrical load. A controller and battery can be included for managed storage, with an inverter when an AC load requires it.

Draw energy flow from radiation to electrical output, then to the intended device. Shade, orientation and illumination affect output. A battery adds a chemical storage stage; it must not be depicted as creating energy independently.

blocks.heading: Describe a basic solar water heater and its energy changes
blocks.text:
A solar water heater uses an absorber to transfer incident radiation to water. An insulated tank limits the loss of the heated water’s internal energy.

A dark collector with pipes and a transparent cover can improve useful collection. Water may circulate by a pump or, in a suitable arrangement, by density-driven convection. In a short steady-input test, temperature rise per time measures a heating rate rather than efficiency unless input and useful energy are also known.

blocks.heading: Describe a basic wind energy system and its energy changes
blocks.text:
A basic wind generator has a rotor coupled to a generator. It converts some air-motion energy through rotational mechanical energy into electrical output.

Wind pumps may instead transmit shaft motion directly to a pumping mechanism. Braking, support and control protect a real machine under changing winds. The rotational stage matters: wind does not directly charge a battery without conversion equipment.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: Energy-source pathways
blocks.text:
Energy sources supply energy by different physical processes. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms; fission splits heavy nuclei, while fusion in the Sun joins light nuclei.

Distinguish the source from the device that converts its energy. Falling water and wind can turn turbines linked to generators; solar radiation can heat a surface or produce electrical output in a photovoltaic cell. Geothermal systems draw on Earth’s internal energy. Wave motion and tidal flow offer different water-based supplies. Follow each energy pathway rather than calling electricity a primary fuel.

blocks.heading: Outline chemical and fuel energy
blocks.text:
Fuel stores chemical energy. A fuel reaction rearranges atoms and can release energy to the surroundings.

Combustion transfers energy from a fuel-and-oxygen system, often heating water to drive a turbine. The atoms are rearranged into products rather than converted wholesale into energy. Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are finite; biomass can be renewable when regrowth replaces consumption.

blocks.heading: Outline energy from hydroelectric water, waves and tides
blocks.text:
Water can provide energy through falling from a height, wave motion or tidal movement. Hydroelectricity typically converts raised water’s gravitational energy through turbine motion to electrical energy.

A dam maintains a height difference that makes a flow through turbines useful. Waves are mainly driven by winds over water. Tides arise from gravitational interactions involving the Moon and Sun, so their regular rise and fall differ from weather-driven waves. Appropriate coasts or height differences are needed.

blocks.heading: Outline geothermal energy
blocks.text:
Geothermal energy comes from Earth’s hot interior. A suitable system can transfer this energy to water or steam for heating or generation.

Accessible hot rocks can heat circulating water. Steam may drive a turbine connected to a generator. Suitability depends on local geology and drilling costs, so a renewable source is not equally practical at every location.

blocks.heading: Outline nuclear fission as an energy source
blocks.text:
Fission of heavy nuclei can release energy in a nuclear reactor. The resulting heating can drive a steam-turbine generator.

Fuel supply is finite. Controlling the chain reaction and removing heat are essential engineering tasks. Radioactive products require containment and management; a low operational carbon output does not remove those concerns. This source account concerns conversion and consequences, without isotope equations.

blocks.heading: Outline solar thermal and photovoltaic energy
blocks.text:
Solar radiation can provide heating or photovoltaic electrical output. The Sun’s energy is supplied by fusion of light nuclei in its interior.

A dark collector absorbs radiation and transfers energy to water in a solar thermal system. A photovoltaic cell instead produces electrical output when illuminated. These are different conversions: a water heater is not a photovoltaic panel merely because both use sunlight.

blocks.heading: Outline wind energy
blocks.text:
Wind energy uses the kinetic energy of moving air. A wind turbine turns this motion into rotational motion and then electrical output through a generator.

Output depends strongly on wind conditions and site. A wind-driven mechanical pump can transfer energy to water without first generating electricity. Identify the actual arrangement rather than assuming every rotating wind machine has the same output.

blocks.heading: compare advantages and disadvantages of the use of different sources of energy, including environmental considerations and the distinction between finite (non- renewable sources such as oil, coal and nuclear) and renewable sources (such as solar, hydroelectricity, geothermal and wind energy)
blocks.text:
An energy-source decision combines supply, environmental effects and practical requirements. No source choice can be justified by a renewable label alone.

Compare a remote pump with an evening urban demand. Solar equipment may suit daytime pumping, but evening supply needs storage or another source. A fossil-fuel generator can operate on demand while creating combustion emissions and consuming finite fuel. Hydroelectric schemes require suitable water and terrain and can alter habitats. State the criteria for the actual task.

blocks.heading: Compare finite and renewable supplies
blocks.text:
A finite energy resource is consumed faster than natural processes replace it on human timescales. A renewable flow or resource is replenished naturally on a relevant timescale.

Coal and oil stores are finite, and nuclear fuel is also non-renewable in this classification. Solar, wind and replenished hydroelectric supplies are renewable. Renewable does not mean unlimited power at one instant; drought, darkness or calm weather can restrict output.

blocks.heading: Compare environmental effects of energy sources
blocks.text:
Energy sources have different environmental effects across construction, operation and disposal. Operational emissions alone are not a complete account of environmental impact.

Fossil combustion releases carbon dioxide and may release air pollutants. Nuclear generation produces radioactive waste requiring management. Wind and solar avoid fuel combustion during generation but involve materials, land and eventual disposal. Reservoirs can flood land and change river ecology. A useful comparison names a particular impact for each source rather than saying a source has no environmental effect.

blocks.heading: Compare reliability and practical suitability of energy sources
blocks.text:
Reliability depends on whether output can meet demand when needed. Site, storage, transmission and maintenance affect the suitability of a source.

Tidal timing is predictable but output varies during a cycle. Wind and solar vary with weather and daylight. Stored fuel can support dispatchable generation if fuel and maintenance are available. Hydroelectric output depends on water resources. A remote site may favour a local system that avoids a long transmission line.

blocks.heading: discuss radioactive isotopes as the source of nuclear energy, its conversion to electrical energy and the problems associated with this process (no nuclide formulas are required)
blocks.text:
Nuclear fuel can release energy through controlled fission, heating a working fluid. A turbine and generator convert part of that energy into electrical output, with other energy transferred to the surroundings.

A reactor is an energy-conversion system, not a device that produces electricity directly from a nucleus into the grid. Heat removal, containment, radiation protection, long-lived waste management and eventual decommissioning are important difficulties. Compare these with the benefit of substantial generation without fuel combustion at the station. Do not confuse reactor fission with fusion in the Sun.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What changes in a chemical fuel reaction?
A. Atoms are rearranged
B. Heavy nuclei split as its defining process
C. Light nuclei fuse as its defining process
D. Atoms vanish without products

2. Which source uses hot rocks beneath Earth’s surface?
A. Tidal
B. Wind
C. Photovoltaic
D. Geothermal

3. Which fuel is finite in the syllabus classification?
A. Wind
B. Tidal flow
C. Nuclear fuel
D. Sunlight

4. Which process supplies the Sun’s energy?
A. Fission of reactor fuel
B. Fusion
C. Coal combustion
D. Hydroelectric flow

5. Which device converts suitable DC output to AC for a load?
A. Inverter
B. Water tank
C. Turbine
D. Thermal insulation

6. What is the main useful output of a solar water heater?
A. Electricity from its pipes
B. Nuclear fuel
C. A stronger wind
D. Increased water internal energy

7. Which difficulty is particularly associated with fission products?
A. Dependence on an ocean tide
B. No need to remove waste heat
C. Radioactive waste management
D. Need for a sunny night

8. A farm needs water after dark. Which arrangement stores daytime solar pumping’s useful result?
A. Removing the pump
B. A raised water tank
C. A disconnected empty wire
D. A smaller unshaded panel without storage

9. Which consideration matters for a hydroelectric site?
A. Available flow and height difference
B. Panel-cell colour alone
C. Radioactive half-life of water
D. Having no water

10. A PV refrigerator is operating. Where is energy rejected?
A. Nowhere because cooling destroys energy
B. Into the panel as manufactured sunlight
C. Into a disappearing mass
D. To the surroundings through the hot side

11. A wind project has no fuel combustion during generation. What follows?
A. Its output cannot vary
B. Its blades need no maintenance
C. Its operational combustion emissions are avoided
D. Its construction has zero impact

12. Water rises from 22 to 30 °C in 4 min. What is its average heating rate?
A. 32 °C/min
B. 2 °C/min
C. 7.5 °C/min
D. 8 °C/min

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: The chemical products have a different arrangement. B: That describes fission. C: That describes fusion. D: That fails to conserve matter in this model.

2. Key D. A: This uses tidal movement. B: This uses moving air. C: This uses incident radiation. D: It draws on internal thermal energy.

3. Key C. A: This is a replenished flow. B: This is renewable on human timescales. C: Its usable material is a finite resource. D: It is treated as renewable.

4. Key B. A: That is the conventional reactor pathway. B: Light nuclei join in the Sun. C: The Sun is not a coal furnace. D: This is a water-based terrestrial system.

5. Key A. A: It changes the electrical supply form. B: This stores water rather than changing electrical supply. C: It provides mechanical rotation. D: It reduces heat transfer.

6. Key D. A: Pipes are not photovoltaic cells. B: There is no nuclear conversion here. C: Wind is not the intended output. D: The intended service is heating.

7. Key C. A: This is not its energy source. B: Cooling remains necessary. C: Some products need containment over long periods. D: Reactor generation does not require sunlight.

8. Key B. A: This removes the lifting mechanism. B: The stored water can later flow down. C: This stores no useful pumping output. D: It still lacks night illumination.

9. Key A. A: Both affect usable water-energy input. B: This is not a hydroelectric criterion. C: This is not the relevant energy source. D: Flow is required for generation.

10. Key D. A: Energy is conserved. B: That is not the cooling pathway. C: The cooling model does not remove material. D: The removed heat plus input energy must leave.

11. Key C. A: Wind changes. B: A moving machine still needs maintenance. C: This is the supported claim. D: Materials and construction can have impacts.

12. Key B. A: This multiplies rise by time. B: The rise is 8 °C over 4 min. C: This divides final temperature by time. D: This omits division by the interval.

(a) Kinetic energy.

blocks.heading: give examples of energy in different forms, its conversion and conservation and apply the principle of energy conservation to simple examples (e.g. the kinetic energy changing to potential energy in a pendulum and the sum of the two is constant if air resistance is negligible)
blocks.text:
Energy is conserved across a complete system and its surroundings. A decrease in one energy store is balanced by increases elsewhere or by transfers across the chosen boundary.

A pendulum exchanges gravitational potential and kinetic energy. At the highest points it has maximum gravitational energy and momentarily zero speed; near the bottom its speed and kinetic energy are greatest. If air resistance and pivot friction are negligible, the sum of these two stores stays constant. With resistance, the mechanical sum falls while internal energy of the surroundings rises. Define the boundary before deciding whether energy has been lost from a particular store.

blocks.heading: describe energy transfer in terms of work done and make calculations involving F × d
blocks.text:
Doing mechanical work transfers energy through a force acting over a displacement. For a constant force parallel to motion, transferred energy is Fd.

Pulling a trolley with 7 N over 3 m transfers 21 J through that force. This is not necessarily its gain in kinetic energy: other forces may transfer energy to internal stores. At steady speed, kinetic energy is unchanged even though the pulling force does positive work. Distinguish the work by one force from net work by the resultant force.

blocks.heading: describe kinetic energy as energy of motion and potential energy as energy of position (e.g. gravitational potential energy and strain potential energy)
blocks.text:
Kinetic energy is associated with motion; potential energy is associated with position or configuration. Gravitational and strain energy are different potential energy stores.

A raised load stores gravitational energy relative to a chosen reference height. A stretched spring stores strain energy because of its deformation. Releasing either can produce motion and kinetic energy. More than one store may be present at once: an object falling from a height generally has both gravitational potential and kinetic energy before it reaches the reference level.

blocks.heading: Describe kinetic energy
blocks.text:
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. For a given mass, increasing speed increases kinetic energy.

The relationship Ek = ½mv² shows that doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, rather than two. The speed is squared, so kinetic energy is nonnegative and does not record motion direction. A moving trolley can transfer its kinetic energy by doing work on a resisting object.

blocks.heading: Describe gravitational potential energy
blocks.text:
Gravitational potential energy depends on position in a gravitational field. Near Earth’s surface, raising a mass through a height increases its gravitational store by mgh.

Height is measured vertically, not along a sloping path. A long gentle ramp and a short steep ramp reaching the same height give the same gravitational energy gain for the same mass in the same field. The work input may differ when friction is included. The reference level sets the quoted store, while a change in height sets its change.

blocks.heading: Describe strain potential energy
blocks.text:
Strain potential energy is stored when a body is elastically deformed. It can be released when the body returns toward its original shape.

A stretched spring and a compressed spring can both store strain energy. Stretching beyond the elastic range can leave permanent deformation and dissipate energy. Do not equate deformation length directly with energy: work depends on the force acting throughout the deformation. This topic uses the qualitative store and its transfers rather than assuming an unstated spring-energy formula.

blocks.heading: Using kinetic and gravitational energy equations
blocks.text:
Near a uniform gravitational field, gravitational energy change is mgh and kinetic energy is ½mv². Equating an energy decrease with an increase requires accounting for other transfers.

For an object released from rest through height h with negligible resistance, mgh = ½mv². The mass cancels, giving v² = 2gh. If drag is appreciable, some gravitational energy is transferred to internal energy and the kinetic gain is smaller. Do not equate the two stores merely because both formulas are available.

blocks.heading: Use gravitational potential energy Ep = mgh
blocks.text:
A near-surface gravitational energy change is ΔEp = mgΔh. Use kilograms, N/kg and metres for an answer in joules.

A 3 kg load raised by 1.2 m where g = 10 N/kg gains 36 J. A downward displacement gives a decrease in the gravitational store. State whether reporting the signed change or its magnitude. The same school formula assumes the field does not vary appreciably over the height.

blocks.heading: Use kinetic energy Ek = ½mv²
blocks.text:
Kinetic energy is Ek = ½mv². Use mass in kg and speed in m/s to obtain joules.

For 4 kg moving at 3 m/s, square the speed first: Ek = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J. When finding speed from energy, rearrange v² = 2Ek/m and take the square root. A negative speed squared does not imply negative energy; kinetic energy uses speed rather than signed velocity.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which store is associated with motion?
A. Kinetic
B. Gravitational alone
C. Strain alone
D. Chemical alone

2. Which distance belongs in W = Fd for a parallel force?
A. Perpendicular arm to a pivot
B. Width of the object
C. Distance to Earth’s centre
D. Displacement along the force

3. What does an efficiency below 100% mean?
A. Output exceeds input
B. Power must be zero
C. Some input is not useful output
D. Energy is destroyed

4. Which unit measures power?
A. kg
B. W
C. J
D. N

5. What is the main ideal effect of a single fixed pulley?
A. Changing effort direction
B. Halving effort in that simple arrangement
C. Creating input energy
D. Eliminating displacement

6. Why does a real swinging pendulum slow?
A. Energy disappears
B. Gravity vanishes
C. Mass becomes zero
D. Energy transfers to surroundings

7. A small external gear drives a larger one. How does the larger gear turn?
A. Slower in the same direction
B. Without a turning effect
C. Slower and oppositely
D. Faster and in the same direction

8. What is Ek for 2 kg at 3 m/s?
A. 6 J
B. 9 J
C. 3 J
D. 18 J

9. What energy is gained by 4 kg raised 0.5 m with g = 10 N/kg?
A. 20 J
B. 2 J
C. 80 J
D. 200 J

10. A 5 N force acts along 4 m. What work does it do?
A. 1.25 J
B. 0.8 J
C. 9 J
D. 20 J

11. Useful output is 90 J from 150 J input. What is efficiency?
A. 40%
B. 90%
C. 60%
D. 167%

12. What average power transfers 240 J in 8 s?
A. 240 W
B. 30 W
C. 1920 W
D. 0.033 W

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: It depends on mass and speed. B: This depends on height. C: This depends on deformation. D: This concerns material configuration.

2. Key D. A: This belongs to moment. B: It need not be a displacement. C: That is not the work distance here. D: This is the work distance.

3. Key C. A: That reverses the comparison. B: Useful transfer may still occur. C: Other stores or surroundings receive it. D: Total energy is conserved.

4. Key B. A: This measures mass. B: One watt is one joule per second. C: This measures energy. D: This measures force.

5. Key A. A: It does not reduce force in the simple model. B: Two load-supporting sections are not provided. C: A machine cannot create energy. D: Rope and load still move.

6. Key D. A: This violates conservation. B: Gravity continues acting. C: The object remains present. D: Drag and friction reduce mechanical energy.

7. Key C. A: External contact reverses direction. B: Teeth transmit a turning force. C: Its larger circumference requires more tooth movement per turn. D: Both parts of this description are wrong.

8. Key B. A: This uses mv rather than energy. B: Half times 2 times 3 squared is 9. C: This fails to square speed. D: This omits the half.

9. Key A. A: Use mgh. B: This omits g. C: This divides by height. D: This misplaces a factor of ten.

10. Key D. A: This divides force by distance. B: This reverses that ratio. C: Adding unlike quantities does not give work. D: Multiply force by displacement.

11. Key C. A: This is the non-useful fraction. B: This ignores total input. C: The useful fraction is 0.6. D: This reverses the ratio.

12. Key B. A: This ignores duration. B: Divide energy by time. C: This multiplies by time. D: This uses time per energy.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: Work done
blocks.text:
Work done by a constant force is force multiplied by displacement in the force direction. The displacement component, rather than the lever arm, is relevant.

A force perpendicular to motion does no work through that displacement. Holding a stationary bag does no mechanical work on the bag during the hold because its displacement is zero, though the person uses energy internally. For an opposing force, energy is transferred out of the moving object’s mechanical store. These distinctions keep work separate from everyday meanings of effort.

blocks.heading: Recall and use work = force × displacement in the force direction, W = Fd
blocks.text:
For parallel constant force and displacement, W = Fd. Rearrange as F = W/d or d = W/F when the physical conditions fit.

If 48 J is transferred by a constant 12 N force along the motion, the displacement is 4 m. Use the force responsible for the stated transfer. An effort force and a resultant force need not be equal; using the resultant computes net mechanical work, while using one applied force computes that force’s contribution.

blocks.heading: explain that energy is the ability to do work and that the joule [J] is the unit of both work and energy
blocks.text:
Energy is the capacity to do work in the syllabus description. Both energy and work are measured in joules.

A battery, raised load and moving object have different energy stores but can each transfer energy to other systems. Work describes one transfer mechanism, rather than an additional substance stored in a body. Use the same joule unit when comparing an energy decrease with work done.

blocks.heading: state the unit of work as 1 J = 1 N m
blocks.text:
One joule equals one newton metre of work. It is the work done by 1 N acting over 1 m in its direction.

Keep both quantities in SI units before combining them. A force of 1 N moving its application point through 1 cm does 0.01 J, not 1 J. Although a moment may also use N m, it describes turning effect rather than energy transfer.

blocks.heading: identify examples of levers, gears and pulleys and explain how they are used for making the effort easier (NOTE: the work stays the same but the force required becomes less)
blocks.text:
Ideal machines can reduce effort by increasing the distance through which the effort moves. In a lossless arrangement, input work equals output work.

A lever, gear system or movable pulley can trade a smaller force for a greater effort distance. This does not create energy. Real friction increases the input work needed for a given useful output. A fixed pulley may mainly change force direction without reducing its size; identify the arrangement before making an effort claim.

blocks.heading: Explain how a lever trades force against distance
blocks.text:
A lever with a longer effort arm can require less effort for a fixed load moment. The effort point then moves farther than the load point for the same rotation.

Balance moments to compare force sizes, then compare point movements through the rotation. For an ideal lever, halving effort while doubling its movement leaves work unchanged. A real lever has friction and deformation losses. The longer arm is a moment arm, while actual movement is used for work.

blocks.heading: Explain the action of gears
blocks.text:
Meshing gears transfer rotational motion and change turning effect and rotation rate. A larger driven gear turns more slowly and can provide greater turning effect than a smaller driving gear in an ideal pair.

Each tooth engages corresponding motion at the contact. Adjacent external gears rotate in opposite directions. The increase in turning effect is accompanied by fewer turns over the same time; it does not create power. Real friction reduces useful output. A bicycle’s gear choice changes the force-distance or turning-effect-speed trade.

blocks.heading: Explain how a pulley reduces required effort
blocks.text:
A movable pulley can share a load between supporting rope sections. Reducing effort requires pulling a greater rope length in the ideal arrangement.

With two parallel supporting sections carrying equal tension, the ideal effort is half the supported load, while twice the load’s rise must be pulled through the free end. A single fixed pulley changes direction with no ideal force reduction. Pulley mass and friction must be included when they matter.

blocks.heading: define efficiency as the percentage of useful energy output from the total energy input
blocks.text:
Efficiency is the percentage of total input energy transferred into the intended useful output. The useful output depends on the purpose of the device.

Heating is useful in a heater but often unwanted in a motor. Define the output before computing the fraction. An efficiency below 100% means some input reaches other stores or surroundings; it does not mean energy is destroyed. Equivalent useful-output-power over input-power ratios can be used for a common steady interval.

blocks.heading: Use efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input × 100%
blocks.text:
Percentage efficiency is useful output energy divided by total input energy, multiplied by 100%. Use matching energy units and include the whole stated input.

If a motor takes in 250 J and gives 175 J of useful mechanical energy, its efficiency is 70%. The remaining 75 J is transferred elsewhere, commonly as internal energy. Reverse the relationship carefully: input energy equals useful output divided by the efficiency expressed as a fraction.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the SI unit of energy. [1]

(b) State what 1 W means. [1]

(c) Explain how a lossless machine reduces effort. [2]

(d) Calculate the energy gained by a 3 kg load raised 2 m where g = 10 N/kg. [2]

(e) Calculate average power when that 60 J lift takes 5 s. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Joule, J.

(b) A transfer rate of 1 J/s.

(c) The smaller effort acts through a greater displacement. The input and output work are equal.

(d) ΔEp = mgh = 60 J.

(e) P = E/t = 12 W.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: define power as the rate of doing work or the rate of energy conversion (1 J s -1 = 1 W)
blocks.text:
Power is the rate of energy transfer or doing work. One watt is one joule per second.

Two people can do equal work lifting equal loads to the same height, but the faster lift has greater average power. Power describes how quickly energy transfers, not the total energy transferred. A high-power device operating briefly may use less energy than a lower-power device operating for a long time.

blocks.heading: Use power = energy transferred / time = work done / time
blocks.text:
Average power is P = E/t or W/t over the stated interval. With energy in joules and time in seconds, power is in watts.

A lift transferring 360 J in 12 s has an average power of 30 W. Rearranging gives E = Pt for constant power. On an energy-time graph, the gradient is power; a straight line means constant rate. If power varies, the whole-interval ratio gives an average rather than each instantaneous value.

Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which quantity is force per area?

B. Density

2. Which unit equals a pascal?

B. kg/m³
C. J/s
D. N/m²

3. A fixed force acts over twice the area. What happens to pressure?
A. It quadruples
B. It stays the same
C. It halves
D. It doubles

4. What is transmitted through an ideal hydraulic liquid?
A. An increase in mass
B. Applied pressure change
C. Equal piston force regardless of area
D. Newly created work

5. At greater altitude, what generally happens to atmospheric pressure?
A. It falls
B. It rises due to more overlying air
C. It becomes density
D. It is fixed by container shape

6. In an open U-tube, gas pushes its side lower. How does gas pressure compare with atmosphere?
A. Lower
B. Equal with a nonzero level difference
C. Impossible to compare directions
D. Higher

7. What does a pressure difference tend to do to air?
A. Remove its mass
B. Stop molecular motion
C. Drive it toward lower pressure
D. Drive it toward higher pressure by itself

8. What pressure is 30 N over 0.010 m²?
A. 300 Pa
B. 3000 Pa
C. 0.30 Pa
D. 3 Pa

9. For ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, what is Δp over 0.20 m?
A. 2000 Pa
B. 200 Pa

blocks.heading: Pressure definition
blocks.text:
Pressure is perpendicular force per unit area. Its SI unit is the pascal, equal to N/m².

Force and pressure are different quantities. The same weight spread over a larger contact area gives a smaller average pressure. A sharp edge concentrates a force onto a small area and can produce a large pressure. The force component normal to the surface is relevant; a force parallel to a surface is not substituted directly into the normal-pressure relationship.

blocks.heading: Use pressure = force / area, P = F/A; convert pascal and kilopascal units
blocks.text:
Average pressure is P = F/A. Force must be in N and area in m² for pressure in Pa; 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.

A 60 N force over 0.020 m² gives 3000 Pa or 3 kPa. Area conversions are squared: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m². Convert a measured rectangular area either by converting both lengths first or by correctly converting the final area. Dividing by an area in cm² gives N/cm², not Pa. Rearranging gives force = pressure × area.

blocks.heading: interpret the relationship between pressure, force and area: explain, for example, what happens to the pressure when either the force or the area is changed
blocks.text:
For a fixed area, pressure increases in proportion to perpendicular force. For a fixed force, increasing the contact area decreases average pressure.

A bag’s broad strap spreads its support force and reduces pressure on a shoulder. A nail tip does the reverse by applying the driving force to a small area. State which quantity is held fixed: doubling force and area together leaves their ratio unchanged. These examples concern average contact pressure; real local distributions need not be perfectly uniform.

blocks.heading: describe and explain the transmission of pressure in hydraulic systems with particular reference to hydraulic brakes on vehicles and hydraulic jacks
blocks.text:
An applied pressure change is transmitted through an enclosed nearly incompressible fluid. At the same level in an ideal hydraulic system, a larger piston area gives a larger force for the same pressure.

With P = F/A, input force F1 over area A1 gives an additional pressure transmitted to output area A2, producing F2 = F1 A2/A1 in the ideal model. A jack multiplies force but the smaller piston moves farther, so useful work is not created. Brake fluid transmits a pedal-induced pressure to wheel mechanisms. Trapped air compresses and can make the response less effective; this is an explanatory model, not a repair procedure.

blocks.heading: state that the pressure beneath a liquid surface is related to depth and to density using appropriate examples
blocks.text:
Pressure increases with depth in a stationary liquid. At the same depth increase and field strength, a denser liquid gives a larger pressure increase.

A lower hole in a water container can eject a jet more strongly because its pressure above the outside atmosphere is greater. Compare points at equal vertical depths rather than equal distances along a sloping wall. Container shape does not enter the simple hydrostatic pressure difference. Surface pressure must be added when finding an absolute pressure rather than a difference.

blocks.heading: derive, from the definitions of pressure and density, the equation Δp = ρgΔh
blocks.text:
For a stationary uniform-density liquid, Δp = ρgΔh follows from the weight of a vertical liquid column. A column of cross-sectional area A and height Δh has volume AΔh and mass ρAΔh.

The extra force supporting this column is its weight, ρAΔhg. Divide by its area using pressure = force/area: Δp = ρAΔhg/A = ρgΔh. The cancellation explains why the pressure difference does not depend on the chosen column area. The derivation assumes static liquid, approximately constant density and gravitational field. For water of density 1000 kg/m³ over 0.40 m with g = 10 N/kg, the difference is 4000 Pa.

blocks.heading: recall and use the equation Δp = ρgΔh
blocks.text:
Hydrostatic pressure difference is Δp = ρgΔh. Use vertical height difference in metres and density in kg/m³ for Pa.

A difference between two submerged points is not automatically the total pressure at the lower point. If the upper point is an open surface, the expression gives pressure above atmospheric pressure. A negative upward depth change gives a decrease in pressure; reporting its magnitude without direction can hide this meaning. Use one consistent height convention.

blocks.heading: describe the atmospheric pressure changes with changes of altitude
blocks.text:
Atmospheric pressure generally decreases as altitude increases. A higher location has less overlying air weight per area.

Air is compressible, so the change over a large height is not represented accurately by treating the whole atmosphere as a constant-density liquid. The qualitative explanation is that fewer overlying air molecules contribute weight above a higher level. A local pressure reading also varies with weather, so altitude is not its sole influence.

blocks.heading: use and describe the use of a manometer and perform calculations on the manometer
blocks.text:
A manometer uses a liquid-level difference to measure a pressure difference. The larger pressure pushes its connected liquid surface lower, and Δp = ρgΔh uses the vertical separation of levels.

For a U-tube with one arm open, compare the gas side with atmospheric pressure. If the gas pushes its side down, its pressure exceeds atmosphere by the calculated liquid-column difference. If its side is higher, the gas pressure is below atmosphere. Read both levels and subtract their heights; the length along the curved tube is irrelevant. A school demonstration should use a suitable safe liquid and low pressures, rather than mercury.

blocks.heading: perform calculations involving interconversion of units of pressure (mm Hg, Pa)
blocks.text:
A pressure in mm Hg describes the pressure difference supported by that height of mercury under specified conditions. For these conversions, a supplied school approximation is 1 mm Hg ≈ 133 Pa.

Multiply a mm Hg value by the stated Pa-per-mm-Hg factor to obtain Pa. For the reverse direction, divide by that factor. For example, 50 mm Hg corresponds to approximately 6650 Pa using 133 Pa per mm Hg. The conversion is a numerical exercise, not a recommendation to use mercury in a student apparatus. State rounding consistently with the supplied factor.

blocks.heading: state that a wind is caused by high and low pressure systems
blocks.text:
A pressure difference can drive air from higher toward lower pressure. This pressure-gradient effect contributes to wind.

Real wind direction also depends on Earth’s rotation, friction and local terrain, so it need not travel in a straight line from a high-pressure centre to a low-pressure centre. For the basic model, a pressure difference across a region produces a resultant force on the air. Do not describe wind as a flow from low to high pressure caused by the pressure difference alone.
