items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for ripple-tank waves at fixed water depth.

| Period / s | Wavelength / cm |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 2 |
| 0.15 | 3 |
| 0.2 | 4 |
| 0.25 | 5 |
| 0.3 | 6 |
| 0.35 | 7 |

(a) Draw the graph with Wavelength / cm on the vertical axis and Period / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot wavelength vertically against reciprocal frequency horizontally at fixed depth.

Gradient: 5 ÷ 0.25 = 20 m/s. The gradient is wave speed because λ = c(1/f). This interpretation assumes approximately unchanged speed over the tested range.

Plan: 1. Set a ripple tank to a measured uniform depth. 2. Drive plane waves at a known frequency and wait for a stable pattern. 3. Measure the distance across several neighbouring crest intervals and divide by the interval count. 4. Repeat for several frequencies while keeping depth fixed. 5. Repeat measurements and use a fixed projected scale or calibrated imaging to reduce reading uncertainty.
Control and accuracy: Keep depth and geometry fixed, avoid reflections contaminating the reading and separate low-voltage equipment from spills.
Table: Record frequency / Hz, reciprocal frequency / s, multi-interval distance / m, interval count and wavelength / m.
Graph and conclusion: A straight wavelength-versus-reciprocal-frequency line supports approximately constant wave speed; its slope gives that speed.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-16.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: define a pulse as a single disturbance
blocks.text:
A pulse is a single disturbance that propagates. It differs from a continuing periodic train of disturbances.

One quick movement of a rope end produces a pulse. Repeated movements produce a wave train. The disturbance transfers energy while the rope elements mainly move about their equilibrium positions rather than travelling with the pulse.

blocks.heading: define oscillations or simple harmonic motion as any repeated to-and-fro motion of a fluid or elastic solid, e.g. a tuning-fork, pendulum or stretched string
blocks.text:
An oscillation is repeated motion to and fro about an equilibrium position. One complete cycle returns to the same state of position and direction.

A pendulum, tuning fork and stretched string can oscillate. The school syllabus groups simple oscillations here; the stricter term simple harmonic motion additionally requires a particular restoring-effect relation, so not every possible repeated motion has that special form. Count full cycles rather than one outward journey.

blocks.heading: describe what is meant by wave motion (propagation), an oscillation which transfers energy from one place to another without any net movement of the medium, as illustrated by vibration in ropes, springs and by experiments using water waves
blocks.text:
Wave propagation transfers energy from place to place without net transport of the medium in the basic wave model. The disturbance travels while individual medium particles oscillate locally.

Mark a point on a rope: its motion can be up and down while the pulse travels horizontally. A floating marker can similarly reveal local surface motion in a water-wave demonstration. Real water can have currents as well, but bulk current is a separate effect from the ideal wave description.

blocks.heading: state typical values of the speed of sound and light in air, water and glass and the speed of light in a vacuum
blocks.text:
Wave speeds depend on wave type and medium. Useful approximate values are sound: air 340 m/s, water 1500 m/s, glass 5000 m/s; light: vacuum or air 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, water 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s, typical glass 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

These are representative school values, not exact constants for every sample. Temperature affects sound speed and glass composition affects both sound and light speeds. Use a supplied value in a calculation. Sound and light respond differently to the same medium, so their speed ordering must not be transferred from one type to the other.

blocks.heading: explain why sound travels faster in solids than in gases, using ideas about molecules
blocks.text:
Sound often travels faster in solids than in gases because their mechanical response transmits disturbances more rapidly. Close spacing and strong particle interactions in a typical solid promote rapid transfer of a compression disturbance.

Spacing alone is not a complete speed law: stiffness and inertia both matter. The qualitative particle picture compares typical glass with air rather than claiming every solid has an identical speed. Particles do not themselves travel from source to listener at the quoted wave speed.

blocks.heading: Different arrival times of light and sound
blocks.text:
Light travels much faster than sound in air. For a distant event, the visual signal generally arrives well before its sound.

A flash and thunder are produced during the same lightning event, but the sound takes appreciably longer to reach a distant observer. The delay estimates distance using sound speed when the light travel time is negligible at this scale. This is a propagation-time model, not an instruction to remain outside during a storm.

blocks.heading: distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves (in terms of the direction of vibration of the particles and the direction of travel of the wave) and give examples of each
blocks.text:
A transverse disturbance oscillates perpendicular to propagation; a longitudinal disturbance oscillates parallel to it. A rope wave is a transverse example and sound in air is longitudinal.

Longitudinal motion produces compressions and rarefactions rather than a literal up-and-down travelling shape. A displacement-distance sine graph can represent either type, so the graph shape alone does not establish particle direction. Compare the oscillation direction with the energy-transfer direction.

blocks.heading: give the meaning of speed c, frequency f, period T, wavelength  and amplitude
blocks.text:
Speed, frequency, period, wavelength and amplitude describe different aspects of a wave. A displacement-distance graph gives spatial information, while a displacement-time graph gives temporal information.

Measure wavelength between neighbouring points in the same phase on a spatial snapshot; measure period between equivalent states at one position over time. Amplitude is measured from equilibrium, not from crest to trough. Keeping the horizontal-axis quantity clear prevents reading metres as seconds.

blocks.heading: Define wave speed
blocks.text:
Wave speed is the distance a disturbance travels per time. Its SI unit is m/s.

Track a crest or pulse between two positions over a measured interval. Do not use the local up-down speed of a rope particle as the propagation speed.

blocks.heading: Define frequency
blocks.text:
Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second. Its unit is hertz, Hz.

Count complete cycles over a suitable time and divide by the duration. Ten cycles in two seconds gives 5 Hz. This is not the time for one cycle.

blocks.heading: Define period
blocks.text:
Period is the time for one complete oscillation. Its SI unit is the second.

Timing several cycles and dividing by their number can reduce the relative effect of reaction-time uncertainty. Check that each count represents a full return to the same state.

blocks.heading: Define wavelength
blocks.text:
Wavelength is the distance between adjacent points in the same phase. It can be measured between neighbouring crests or neighbouring compressions.

Crest to trough is half a wavelength for a simple sinusoidal wave, not a full wavelength. Measure along propagation, not along the curved length of a rope.

blocks.heading: Define amplitude
blocks.text:
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. Crest-to-trough displacement is twice amplitude for a symmetric sinusoidal wave.

Amplitude describes the size of oscillation, not its period or wavelength. A wave can have small amplitude and high frequency independently. Label the undisturbed level before measuring it.

blocks.heading: Wave equations
blocks.text:
Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by c = fλ. Since f = 1/T, the same relation can be written c = λ/T.

One period advances a repeating wave pattern by one wavelength. This links a spatial interval with a time interval. A period in seconds cannot be inserted directly as though it were a frequency in hertz. Convert to a reciprocal or use the equivalent wavelength-over-period form.

blocks.heading: Use wave speed = frequency × wavelength
blocks.text:
Wave speed is frequency multiplied by wavelength. Use hertz and metres for m/s.

A 5 Hz ripple with wavelength 0.040 m has speed 0.20 m/s. If wavelength is supplied in centimetres, convert first. For a fixed wave speed, a higher source frequency gives a shorter wavelength. This requires a medium and regime where the speed is effectively unchanged.

blocks.heading: Use frequency = 1/period
blocks.text:
Frequency and period are reciprocals. f = 1/T when T is in seconds and f is in hertz.

A period of 0.25 s corresponds to 4 Hz. To find period from frequency, use T = 1/f. Shorter period means more cycles fit into a second. State the unit after taking the reciprocal because the new quantity is not a time.

blocks.heading: define the term wave front in wave motion, as the line containing adjacent points that are in the same phase
blocks.text:
A wavefront joins adjacent points in the same phase. A ray indicates propagation normal to a wavefront in the simple uniform-medium model.

Successive crest fronts are separated by a wavelength. A wavefront is not the path of one water particle. In a plan view of a ripple tank, circular fronts indicate spreading from a point source and straight parallel fronts indicate plane waves.

blocks.heading: draw circular and plane wave fronts on the surface of water
blocks.text:
A point source produces circular wavefronts in a uniform water region; a straight source can produce plane fronts. Propagation arrows are perpendicular to the local fronts.

Use a plan view and show several successive fronts at equal intervals for a steady source and speed. Circular fronts have increasing radii about one centre. Plane fronts are parallel straight lines. Their spacing represents wavelength, not amplitude; plan-view front drawings do not show vertical water height.

blocks.heading: Draw circular wavefronts
blocks.text:
Circular water wavefronts are concentric curves about a point source. Equal radial spacing represents a constant wavelength in a uniform region.

Draw three circles of radii 1, 2 and 3 arbitrary length units about one marked source. Add radial outward arrows perpendicular to the curves. Do not show separate circles with unrelated centres or take circumference as wavelength.

blocks.heading: Draw plane wavefronts
blocks.text:
Plane wavefronts are parallel straight lines. A constant wavelength is shown by equal perpendicular spacing.

A straight vibrating bar in a ripple tank can generate an approximately plane wave train. Show the propagation arrow normal to the lines, not along them. The length of each drawn line is chosen for visibility and is not the wavelength.

blocks.heading: use the term wave front to describe the observation of water waves in a ripple tank undergoing: - reflection at a plane surface (wave fronts reflect at the same angle to the surface) - refraction due to a change in depth, changing the speed, and the wavelength but not the frequency
blocks.text:
Water-wave reflection changes propagation direction at a boundary. Refraction from a depth change can alter speed, wavelength and direction while source frequency stays fixed.

At a straight barrier, incident and reflected ray angles measured from the normal are equal. Into shallower water, the usual ripple-tank wave speed falls; at unchanged frequency its wavelength shortens. Oblique incidence bends the propagation toward the normal. At normal incidence the spacing changes without a direction change.

blocks.heading: Describe reflected wavefronts
blocks.text:
Reflected plane wavefronts obey equal incidence and reflection angles. Ray directions are normal to fronts and are measured relative to the barrier normal.

Draw a horizontal barrier with a vertical normal at the reflection point. An incident ray travels down-right and the reflected ray up-right at equal normal angles. Place fronts perpendicular to each ray, keeping their spacing equal in the same water region. Arrows must show the incident ray toward the barrier and reflected ray away.

blocks.heading: Describe refracted wavefronts when water depth changes
blocks.text:
Into shallower water, ripple wavefront spacing becomes smaller at fixed frequency. For oblique incidence, the ray bends toward the boundary normal.

Show closer front spacing on the shallow side and a smaller ray-normal angle. The fronts are perpendicular to their rays. A frequency label must stay unchanged across the boundary because the same source generates both trains. The direction change is absent for normal incidence, although the spacing still changes.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Period and frequency are reciprocals rather than interchangeable inputs. Wave speed can be calculated as wavelength divided by period.

For a wave with period 0.20 s and wavelength 0.060 m, frequency is 5 Hz and speed is 0.30 m/s. Multiplying 0.20 by 0.060 treats a time as a cycle rate and gives the wrong quantity and unit. Dimensional checks expose this conceptual mismatch.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What is a pulse?
A. A single disturbance
B. A repeated train by definition
C. A fixed material object
D. The distance between crests

2. In a transverse wave, oscillations are oriented how?
A. Parallel to propagation
B. Without any motion
C. Only toward the source
D. Perpendicular to propagation

3. Which distance gives amplitude?
A. Crest to next crest
B. Source to observer
C. Equilibrium to maximum displacement
D. Crest to trough

4. What do points on a wavefront share?
A. A material path
B. Phase
C. The same source distance in every wave type
D. A fixed temperature label

5. Which is a typical vacuum light speed?
A. 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
B. 340 m/s
C. 1500 m/s
D. 5 m/s

6. What does an ideal rope wave mainly transfer along the rope?
A. The whole rope material continuously
B. New rope mass
C. Only a colour change
D. Energy

7. Which remains unchanged at a stationary depth boundary?
A. Speed necessarily
B. Direction for every incidence
C. Source frequency
D. Wavelength necessarily

8. For f = 4 Hz and λ = 0.08 m, what is speed?
A. 3.2 m/s
B. 0.32 m/s
C. 50 m/s
D. 0.02 m/s

9. A period is 0.5 s. What is frequency?
A. 2 Hz
B. 0.5 Hz
C. 5 Hz
D. 0.25 Hz

10. With sound speed 340 m/s, what distance corresponds to an approximately 2 s light-sound delay?
A. 170 m
B. 340 m
C. 0.006 m
D. 680 m

11. Four complete wavelengths span 20 cm. What is one wavelength?
A. 20 cm
B. 4 cm
C. 5 cm
D. 80 cm

12. A ripple enters shallower water and slows at unchanged frequency. What happens to wavelength?
A. It becomes amplitude
B. It decreases
C. It increases
D. It must stay fixed

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: This distinguishes it from a repeated wave train. B: A pulse is single. C: A disturbance propagates. D: That is wavelength.

2. Key D. A: That defines longitudinal. B: Oscillation is present. C: They alternate about equilibrium. D: This defines transverse.

3. Key C. A: That is wavelength. B: That is a travel distance. C: This is its definition. D: That is twice amplitude for a symmetric wave.

4. Key B. A: A front is not one particle’s trajectory. B: The front joins adjacent equal-phase points. C: Plane fronts need no single finite source centre. D: That is not the defining property.

5. Key A. A: This is the school approximation. B: This is typical air sound speed. C: This is typical water sound speed. D: This is far too slow.

6. Key D. A: That is not the wave model. B: No matter is created. C: The disturbance is mechanical. D: Rope elements oscillate locally.

7. Key C. A: Depth can change it. B: Oblique refraction can bend the ray. C: The same source drives both regions. D: It changes with speed.

8. Key B. A: This introduces a factor of ten. B: Multiply frequency and wavelength. C: This divides f by wavelength. D: This divides wavelength by frequency.

9. Key A. A: Take the reciprocal. B: Period and frequency differ. C: This misreads the decimal. D: Squaring the period is inappropriate.

10. Key D. A: This divides by time. B: This ignores the 2 s interval. C: This reverses time and speed. D: Sound distance is speed times delay.

11. Key C. A: This ignores the number of intervals. B: This substitutes the number of waves as a length. C: Divide total distance by four. D: This multiplies instead.

12. Key B. A: These are different measures. B: λ = c/f. C: That reverses the speed dependence. D: Frequency alone does not fix wavelength.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the unit of frequency. [1]

(b) State the meaning of period. [1]

(c) Explain the motion of a marked rope point as a transverse wave passes. [2]

(d) Calculate speed for f = 8 Hz and λ = 0.025 m. [2]

(e) Calculate period at 8 Hz. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Hz.

(b) Time for one complete oscillation.

(c) It oscillates across the propagation direction. The disturbance and energy travel along the rope without net transport of that marked element.

(d) c = fλ = 0.20 m/s.

(e) T = 1/f = 0.125 s.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for ripple-tank waves at fixed water depth.

| Period / s | Wavelength / cm |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 2 |
| 0.15 | 3 |
| 0.2 | 4 |
| 0.25 | 5 |
| 0.3 | 6 |
| 0.35 | 7 |

(a) Draw the graph with Wavelength / cm on the vertical axis and Period / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot wavelength vertically against reciprocal frequency horizontally at fixed depth.

Gradient: 5 ÷ 0.25 = 20 m/s. The gradient is wave speed because λ = c(1/f). This interpretation assumes approximately unchanged speed over the tested range.

Plan: 1. Set a ripple tank to a measured uniform depth. 2. Drive plane waves at a known frequency and wait for a stable pattern. 3. Measure the distance across several neighbouring crest intervals and divide by the interval count. 4. Repeat for several frequencies while keeping depth fixed. 5. Repeat measurements and use a fixed projected scale or calibrated imaging to reduce reading uncertainty.
Control and accuracy: Keep depth and geometry fixed, avoid reflections contaminating the reading and separate low-voltage equipment from spills.
Table: Record frequency / Hz, reciprocal frequency / s, multi-interval distance / m, interval count and wavelength / m.
Graph and conclusion: A straight wavelength-versus-reciprocal-frequency line supports approximately constant wave speed; its slope gives that speed.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which is normally seen mainly by reflected sunlight?
A. The Moon
B. The Sun
C. A glowing lamp filament
D. A flame

2. What is a penumbra?
A. A region with every direct source ray blocked
B. A mirror image
C. A light source
D. A partially illuminated shadow region

3. What is the usual pinhole-image orientation?
A. Determined by the screen’s colour alone
B. No image can form using a small opening alone
C. Inverted
D. Upright due to reflection

4. Which description fits tracing paper?
A. Reflects all light with no transmission
B. Transmits scattered light
C. Transmits a clear view like an ideal clear sheet
D. Emits its own light necessarily

5. What is the nature of a plane-mirror image?
A. Virtual
B. Real on a screen behind the mirror
C. Necessarily inverted top to bottom
D. Larger than the object

6. What is the normal?
A. A line along the surface
B. The source-to-eye distance
C. The image height
D. A perpendicular to the surface at incidence

7. Which qualitative benefit can a convex viewing mirror provide?
A. Light creation
B. Complete removal of glare everywhere
C. A wider field of view
D. Larger undistorted images at every position

8. Incidence is 28° to the normal. What is reflection angle?
A. 14°
B. 28°
C. 62°
D. 56°

9. An incident ray is 20° to a mirror surface. What is its normal angle?
A. 70°
B. 20°
C. 40°
D. 110°

items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot reflected angle vertically against incident angle horizontally; both are measured from the normal.

Gradient: 50 ÷ 50 = 1 degree/degree, dimensionless. The gradient is the ratio of reflection-angle change to incidence-angle change. A slope near one with near-zero intercept supports r = i.

Plan: 1. Place a plane mirror along a marked line on paper and mark an incidence point. 2. Draw a normal perpendicular to the mirror line. 3. Direct a narrow ray-box beam to the point and mark incident and reflected paths using separated points. 4. Remove the apparatus and use a protractor to measure both angles from the normal. 5. Repeat across several angles and repeat alignments to assess reading variation.
Control and accuracy: Keep the mirror upright and on its line, use thin marks, avoid parallax and do not direct a beam into eyes.
Table: Record incidence angle / degree and reflection angle / degree for each trial.

blocks.heading: explain the use of apparatus such as a ray-box, mirror, glass window, Perspex strips, protractor and rectangular block to investigate what happens when light falls on different objects that are translucent, transparent and opaque
blocks.text:
Transparent, translucent and opaque describe different transmission behaviour. Reflection and absorption may accompany transmission at a surface.

A ray box, test sheet and screen let you compare how much light passes and whether it stays sufficiently directed to show a clear image. Use matched lighting and distances. A transparent sample transmits a clear view; a translucent sample scatters transmitted light; an opaque sample has negligible visible transmission in the stated thickness.

blocks.heading: Investigate transparent materials
blocks.text:
A transparent material transmits light with enough direction preserved to see a clear image. Some reflection or absorption can still occur.

Place clear glass or Perspex in a narrow ray path and observe the transmitted ray and a target viewed through it. The ray may change direction at boundaries, so transparent does not mean no optical effect. Use safe low-intensity light and do not stare into a beam.

blocks.heading: Investigate translucent materials
blocks.text:
A translucent material transmits light but scatters it strongly enough to obscure a clear view. Its transmitted screen patch can be broader or more diffuse than a clear sample’s.

Compare tracing paper with a clear sheet under the same illumination. A target may disappear as a distinct image even though light still passes. Do not classify it as opaque merely because a sharp ray cannot be followed through it.

blocks.heading: Investigate opaque materials
blocks.text:
An opaque material transmits negligible visible light through its stated thickness. Incident light can instead be reflected or absorbed.

Put card in the ray path and compare the screen behind it with an unobstructed reference. A shadow indicates blocked direct transmission. A mirror is opaque despite reflecting strongly, so opacity is not the same as blackness or total absorption.

blocks.heading: draw a ray diagram to show the formation of the image of a point on an object produced by a plane mirror
blocks.text:
A plane-mirror image is located where backward extensions of reflected rays meet. The light itself remains in front of the reflecting surface in this construction.

For a vertical mirror at x = 0 and a point at (−2, 1), the image is at (2, 1) in arbitrary length units. Draw rays to two separated mirror points, reflect them using equal normal angles, then extend the outgoing rays backward using dashed lines. Dashed extensions distinguish the virtual construction from real propagation.

blocks.heading: give the characteristics (position, nature, size and lateral inversion) of an optical image formed by a plane mirror
blocks.text:
A plane mirror gives an upright virtual image of the same size as the object. Its image is the same perpendicular distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, with lateral inversion in the syllabus description.

Position is measured perpendicular to the mirror, not along a slanting eye-to-image line. The image is virtual because the reflected rays do not actually meet behind the mirror. The familiar left-right appearance arises from front-back reversal and how an object is compared with its reflected orientation.

blocks.heading: Describe plane-mirror image position and nature
blocks.text:
A plane-mirror image is virtual and lies as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. This is a perpendicular distance comparison.

An object 15 cm in front has an image 15 cm behind, giving an object-image separation of 30 cm. A screen behind an opaque mirror cannot collect that virtual image because the reflected rays do not converge there.

blocks.heading: Describe plane-mirror image size and lateral inversion
blocks.text:
A plane-mirror image is upright and the same size as its object. It shows lateral inversion in the usual reflected-view description.

A written symbol can reveal the changed orientation. The mirror does not magnify merely because it is larger; a larger mirror can admit rays from a greater field without changing the image-size ratio. Keep image size distinct from how much of the image is visible.

blocks.heading: identify and measure the angles of incidence and of reflection (angle of incidence is equal to angle of reflection) and the normal at the point a ray strikes the surface
blocks.text:
The normal is perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the ray’s incidence point. Incidence and reflection angles are measured between their rays and this normal.

A ray 25° to the surface is 65° to the normal. Read a protractor from the correct baseline and mark the incidence point before drawing the normal. Confusing the surface with the normal can give complementary angles that are consistently wrong despite a neat diagram.

blocks.heading: describe advantages and disadvantages of reflection, including everyday applications of reflection such as the uses of different kinds of mirrors and the reflecting surfaces behind lights
blocks.text:
Reflection can provide useful viewing or light direction but can also cause glare. Mirror shape affects whether rays remain spread, converge or diverge.

A plane mirror provides a familiar undistorted reflected view. A convex mirror offers a wider field with smaller images, useful for surveillance; a concave reflector can direct light when a source is suitably placed. These are qualitative applications, not a new curved-mirror calculation topic. Unwanted reflected light from a bright surface can reduce visibility.

blocks.heading: recall and use the law: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
blocks.text:
For reflection at a plane surface, angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Both angles use the same normal.

If the incident ray is 38° to the normal, the reflected ray is also 38° to the normal. The angle between the two rays in front of the mirror is then 76°. A normal-incidence ray retraces its path; do not measure its 90° surface angle as the incidence angle.

blocks.heading: perform simple constructions, measurements and calculations on a ray diagram
blocks.text:
Ray constructions require a labelled surface, incidence point, normal and directional rays. Geometry can relate surface angles, normal angles and the separation of rays.

For an incident ray 40° to a horizontal mirror surface, incidence is 50° to the vertical normal. Draw the reflected ray at the same 50° normal angle on the other side. Its surface angle is again 40° and the two rays enclose 100° in front of the surface. Arrowheads show propagation toward and away from the mirror.

blocks.heading: outline the difference between luminous and illuminated objects
blocks.text:
A luminous object emits its own visible light. An illuminated object is seen by light received from another source and redirected toward the eye.

A switched-on lamp is luminous, while a book beside it is illuminated. The Moon is mainly seen by reflected sunlight rather than producing its own visible light. Light must enter the eye for either to be seen. Avoid describing ordinary vision as rays leaving the eye to touch the object.

blocks.heading: explain that light travels in straight lines and how this leads to the - formation of shadows - appearance of the image (pin-hole camera) - eclipses of the sun and moon, including the terms umbra and penumbra
blocks.text:
In a uniform medium, the ray model represents light travelling along straight lines. Blocking or selecting these paths explains shadows, pinhole images and eclipses.

A ray traces a propagation direction rather than a physical thin rod. Use boundary rays from the source edges to identify the illuminated and shadow regions. Refraction and reflection change direction at interfaces; they do not contradict straight propagation between interactions.

blocks.heading: Explain shadows and straight-line propagation
blocks.text:
An opaque object can block direct light paths to form a shadow. An extended source can form an umbra with no direct source light and a penumbra receiving light from part of the source.

Draw rays from both edges of the source past the edges of the obstacle. Where all direct source rays are blocked, the umbra forms. Where only some are blocked, the penumbra forms. A point-source approximation gives a sharper boundary than a broad source. Scattered room light can make a real shadow less dark without changing which direct paths are blocked.

blocks.heading: Explain image formation in a pinhole camera
blocks.text:
A pinhole selects narrow straight-line paths from an object to a screen. The resulting image is inverted because rays from opposite object regions cross at the opening.

A ray from the object top passes through the hole to the lower screen; one from the bottom reaches the upper screen. A smaller hole reduces overlap and can sharpen the image, but also reduces brightness until other effects become important. A larger screen distance can enlarge the image while spreading the admitted light over more area.

blocks.heading: Explain solar and lunar eclipses using umbra and penumbra
blocks.text:
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon lies between Sun and Earth and its shadow reaches Earth. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth lies between Sun and Moon and the Moon enters Earth’s shadow.

The umbra corresponds to complete blocking of direct sunlight and the penumbra to partial blocking. The required alignment does not happen at every lunar cycle because the orbital planes differ. In a diagram, place the light source first and trace the outermost rays. Direct observation of the Sun requires appropriate specialist protection; the model can be studied using safe lamps and balls.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. At normal incidence into glass, what can change?
A. Speed and wavelength
B. Frequency because the source changes
C. Direction must turn by 90°
D. The light becomes sound

2. Critical angle concerns which direction?
A. Air toward higher-index glass
B. Any direction with zero incidence
C. Only parallel mirrors
D. Higher index toward lower index

3. What locates a virtual image?
A. Its visibility alone
B. The lens colour alone
C. Backward extensions of outgoing rays
D. Actual convergence on a screen

4. Which corrects short sight in the basic model?
A. A flat coloured card
B. A diverging lens
C. A converging lens
D. An opaque screen over the eye

5. Which colour deviates more in a usual glass prism?
A. Violet
B. Red
C. All colours equally
D. No colour can emerge

6. Where does the eye form its optical image?
A. Outside the pupil
B. On the front of a corrective lens
C. At a virtual point behind the head
D. Retina

7. Which distant object is suitable for a classroom focal-length estimate?
A. A fingertip inside the focal distance
B. A mark on the lens surface
C. A distant building
D. The Sun viewed through the lens

8. What is n for sin i = 0.75 and sin r = 0.50?
A. 1.25
B. 1.5
C. 0.667
D. 0.25

9. Vacuum speed is 3 × 10⁸ m/s and material speed 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s. What is n?
A. 1.25
B. 0.8
C. 5.4
D. 0.6

10. A ray is 25° to the surface. What is its normal angle?
A. 25°
B. 50°
C. 115°
D. 65°

11. An object lies inside a converging lens’s focal length. What image results?
A. Equal-sized real
B. A real image on the opposite-side screen
C. Upright enlarged virtual
D. Reduced inverted real

12. Glass-to-air incidence exceeds its critical angle. What occurs in the ideal model?
A. Frequency doubles
B. Total internal reflection
C. Refraction at 90° exactly
D. No interaction with the boundary
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Frequency remains fixed and no bending is required. B: The source has not changed. C: There is no bending at normal incidence. D: The wave type remains electromagnetic.

2. Key D. A: This is not the total-internal-reflection direction. B: The threshold is not normal incidence. C: It is a refractive-interface concept. D: That permits the limiting 90° refracted ray.

3. Key C. A: Both image types can be seen. B: That does not establish image nature. C: Actual rays do not meet there. D: That locates a real image.

4. Key B. A: It does not provide the needed correction. B: It reduces premature convergence. C: This generally adds convergence. D: That blocks useful light.

5. Key A. A: Its refractive index is larger than red’s in this case. B: Red is less deviated in this comparison. C: That would give no dispersion. D: A transmitted spectrum can form.

6. Key D. A: The image forms inside the eye. B: That lens helps adjust convergence. C: This is not the normal retinal image. D: This is its receiving surface.

7. Key C. A: It does not approximate a distant source. B: It is not a distant object. C: Its approximately parallel rays can form a safe screen image. D: Concentrated sunlight presents a hazard.

8. Key B. A: This adds them. B: Divide the sines. C: This reverses the ratio. D: This subtracts them.

9. Key A. A: Use vacuum speed over material speed. B: This reverses the ratio. C: Adding speeds does not give index. D: A speed difference is not the index.

10. Key D. A: This uses the wrong reference. B: Doubling is not the conversion. C: The intended acute angle is 65°. D: Use the complementary angle.

11. Key C. A: That fits the 2f case. B: Actual rays do not converge there. C: Outgoing rays diverge and extensions meet. D: That fits an object beyond 2f.

12. Key B. A: Reflection does not require that frequency change. B: The transmission condition is exceeded. C: That occurs at the critical angle, not above. D: The light is reflected.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the name of the point where axis-parallel rays meet after a converging lens. [1]

(b) State whether an image formed by actual ray convergence is real or virtual. [1]

(c) Explain the conditions for total internal reflection. [2]

(d) Calculate n for sin i = 0.66 and sin r = 0.44. [2]

(e) Calculate light speed in a material of n = 1.5 when vacuum speed is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Principal focus.

(b) Real.

(c) Light travels from higher to lower index and its internal incidence exceeds the critical angle.

(d) n = 0.66/0.44 = 1.5.

(e) v = c0/n = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for principal focus.
(b) One mark for real.
(c) One mark for index direction; one for angle above critical.
(d) One mark for sine ratio; one for 1.5.
(e) One mark for dividing vacuum speed by index; one for 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for ray-box investigation of refraction through a rectangular block.

| sin r | sin i |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 0.15 |
| 0.2 | 0.3 |
| 0.3 | 0.45 |
| 0.4 | 0.6 |
| 0.5 | 0.75 |
| 0.6 | 0.9 |

(a) Draw the graph with sin i on the vertical axis and sin r on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot sin i vertically against sin r horizontally using angles measured from the entry normal.

Gradient: 0.75 ÷ 0.5 = 1.5 dimensionless. The sin i against sin r gradient is the air-to-block refractive index. Reversing the axes would give its reciprocal.

Plan: 1. Trace a rectangular transparent block and mark a chosen entry point. 2. Direct a narrow ray at that point and mark incident and emergent paths. 3. Remove the block, join internal entry and exit points and construct the entry normal. 4. Measure i and r from that normal and calculate their sines in degree mode. 5. Repeat for several incidence angles and repeat alignments while using the same block.
Control and accuracy: Keep the same wavelength or source and block, use thin lines, separate marking points well and avoid eye exposure to intense beams.
Table: Record i / degree, r / degree, sin i and sin r, with the sine columns unitless.
Graph and conclusion: Fit sin i against sin r; a straight near-origin trend supports the relation and its slope estimates the relative refractive index.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-18.png)

Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).

blocks.heading: relate that light travels in straight lines to explain divergent, convergent and parallel rays or beams of light
blocks.text:
Divergent rays spread apart, convergent rays approach a meeting point and parallel rays maintain separation. Each ray is locally straight in a uniform medium between optical interactions.

The beam describes a collection of propagation directions. A single ray has no widening width in the simple model. Follow arrowheads to decide whether a set approaches or leaves a point; the same drawn lines without direction can represent different propagation.

blocks.heading: Describe divergent rays
blocks.text:
Divergent rays spread apart as they propagate. Their backward extensions may indicate a real source or a virtual image.

Light leaving a small source diverges through space. The growing beam does not mean each ray bends outward continually in uniform air; the rays leave with different directions. Mark outward arrowheads when constructing the beam.

blocks.heading: Describe convergent rays
blocks.text:
Convergent rays approach one another along propagation. Actual convergence can form a real image.

A converging lens can redirect an incoming beam toward a point. After crossing, the same rays diverge again. Identify whether the crossing is of actual rays or merely backward extensions before calling an image real.

blocks.heading: Describe parallel rays
blocks.text:
Parallel rays travel in the same direction with fixed separation in a uniform medium. A distant source can provide an approximately parallel bundle across a small optical instrument.

Parallel does not mean horizontal on every page: a tilted parallel bundle is still parallel. A converging lens focuses rays parallel to its principal axis at its principal focus in the thin-lens model.

blocks.heading: define refraction of light as the change in direction of light entering or leaving a medium with different optical density
blocks.text:
Refraction is the change of propagation on entering a medium with a different light speed, usually including a direction change at oblique incidence. At normal incidence the speed and wavelength can change without bending.

Optical density describes a speed-related property, not simply mass density. Light entering typical glass from air slows and bends toward the normal if incidence is oblique. Source frequency remains unchanged across a stationary interface. Distinguish the transmitted refracted ray from the reflected ray that stays in the first medium.

blocks.heading: draw and describe the refraction of a ray of light as it passes through a rectangular block and a triangular prism
blocks.text:
A rectangular block with parallel faces can produce a sideways-displaced emergent ray parallel to the incident ray. A triangular prism generally gives a net angular deviation.

At each face draw its own normal. Air-to-glass transmission bends toward the normal and glass-to-air transmission away when a refracted ray exists. The parallel faces of a rectangular block undo the angular change but leave displacement. Nonparallel prism faces do not undo it in that way.

blocks.heading: Trace refraction through a rectangular block
blocks.text:
Refraction through a parallel-sided block has two boundary changes. For the same outside medium, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but can be laterally displaced.

Trace the block outline, incidence point and ray directions. Draw normals perpendicular to both faces. The internal ray bends toward the first normal; the exiting ray bends away from the second. Compare the outside directions only after applying both interactions.

blocks.heading: Trace refraction through a triangular prism
blocks.text:
A prism refracts light at its nonparallel faces. For a typical glass prism in air, the transmitted ray is deviated toward the prism’s base.

Draw normals at both points rather than using one common vertical line. At entry the ray bends toward the local normal; at exit it bends away if it transmits. An internal incidence above the critical angle would instead give total internal reflection, so not every chosen path can leave the intended face.

blocks.heading: measure the angle of refraction r as light enters and leaves a rectangular block
blocks.text:
A refraction angle is measured from the transmitted ray to the normal in that ray’s medium. At the second face, construct a new normal at the new incidence point.

Mark two points on each visible ray, remove the block and join the marks to its traced boundary. Join the internal entry and exit points. Use a protractor centred on the interface point and aligned with the normal. Measure acute ray-normal angles, not angles from the surface.

blocks.heading: Use refractive index n = sin i / sin r, with both angles measured from the normal
blocks.text:
For air-to-material transmission, relative refractive index is n = sin i/sin r. Both angles are measured from the normal using degree-mode trigonometry when angles are in degrees.

If i = 30° and r ≈ 19.5°, n is approximately 1.50. Do not divide the angles themselves; the relation uses their sines. A plot of sin i vertically against sin r horizontally has gradient n. Swapping these axes gives 1/n.

blocks.heading: give the meaning of critical angle
blocks.text:
Critical angle is the incidence angle in the optically denser medium for which the refracted ray lies along the boundary. The refraction angle is then 90° to the normal in the less optically dense medium.

The definition concerns light going toward a lower-index medium, such as glass to air. Above this incidence angle, no propagating refracted ray leaves the surface in the school model and total internal reflection occurs. It is not the angle from the surface and not an air-to-glass threshold.

blocks.heading: describe internal and total internal reflection
blocks.text:
Internal reflection can return part of incident light inside a medium. Total internal reflection requires travel toward a lower-index medium and incidence above the critical angle.

Below the threshold, both reflected and refracted rays can exist. At the threshold the refracted ray runs along the boundary. Above it the incident light is internally reflected in the ideal model. Optical fibres and suitable prisms can use this effect to guide or turn light without a metal mirror coating.

blocks.heading: recall and use the definition of refractive index in terms of speed or wavelength
blocks.text:
Absolute refractive index is vacuum light speed divided by light speed in the material. For the same frequency, it is also vacuum wavelength divided by material wavelength.

Frequency remains fixed at a stationary interface, so c = fλ links reduced speed with reduced wavelength. For vacuum speed 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and material speed 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s, n = 1.5. The index has no unit because it is a ratio of matching quantities.

blocks.heading: describe the action of a thin converging lens on a parallel beam of light
blocks.text:
A thin converging lens brings an axis-parallel beam toward its principal focus. The simple construction applies to suitable near-axis rays.

The lens is thicker at its centre in the usual glass-in-air form. A ray through the optical centre is treated as undeviated in the thin-lens approximation. Real lenses have finite apertures and imperfections, so the ideal point is a model. Diverging lenses are mentioned later for sight correction without a separate image-calculation treatment.

blocks.heading: define the principal focus (focal point) of a converging lens
blocks.text:
A converging lens’s principal focus is the point where axis-parallel incident rays converge after refraction. Focal length is the distance from the lens’s optical centre to that point.

A lens has a principal focus on each side for propagation from the corresponding direction. Label the principal axis and the relevant far-side focus before drawing a parallel ray. A focus is a property of the lens model; an object’s image is not necessarily at the focus.

blocks.heading: describe how to measure the focal length of a converging lens using a distant object
blocks.text:
A distant object gives nearly parallel incident rays across a small lens. Its sharp real image forms approximately one focal length behind a converging lens.

Use a distant building or tree, never the Sun. Move a screen behind the lens until a sharp image appears, then measure optical-centre-to-screen distance. Repeat with another distant object or position and estimate uncertainty. The approximation improves when object distance greatly exceeds focal length.

blocks.heading: draw ray diagrams for the formation of real image and a virtual image by a single lens
blocks.text:
A converging lens can form a real image for an object beyond its focus and a virtual image for an object inside it. Principal rays locate the image by actual intersection or backward extension.

Draw one ray from the object top parallel to the axis, refracted through the far focus. Draw another through the optical centre, undeviated in the thin-lens model. When they meet on the far side the image is real; when outgoing rays diverge, extend them backward to locate a virtual image on the object side.

blocks.heading: Construct a real image with a converging lens
blocks.text:
For an object beyond a converging lens’s focal point, actual rays can form an inverted real image. The image may be reduced, equal-sized or enlarged depending on object distance.

With focal length 2 cm and an object 6 cm away, a principal-ray construction gives an image 3 cm on the far side, half as tall and inverted. These values are a diagram stimulus, not a requirement to derive an extra lens equation. Position the screen where actual rays meet.

blocks.heading: Construct a virtual image with a converging lens
blocks.text:
An object inside a converging lens’s focal length forms an upright enlarged virtual image in the thin-lens model. The image lies on the object side, where backward extensions of outgoing rays meet.

For focal length 2 cm and a 1 cm tall object 1 cm from the lens, the construction gives a 2 cm tall virtual image 2 cm on the object side. Use dashed extensions: actual rays do not travel backward to that point after leaving the lens. This is the basic magnifying-glass arrangement.

blocks.heading: distinguish between a real and a virtual image
blocks.text:
A real image is formed by actual convergence of light rays. A virtual image is located by backward extensions rather than actual convergence at that location.

A real image can be received on a screen placed at its image location. A virtual image can be seen by an eye receiving the diverging rays, but cannot be collected on a screen placed at the apparent location. Visibility alone does not establish that an image is real.

blocks.heading: give the characteristics of an optical image formed by a converging lens
blocks.text:
A converging lens’s image characteristics depend on object distance relative to focal length. Beyond 2f the real image is reduced; at 2f equal-sized; between f and 2f enlarged; inside f the image is virtual and enlarged.

Real images in these basic cases are inverted. The inside-f virtual image is upright. At the focal position, ideal outgoing rays are parallel and no finite image position is obtained on a nearby screen. State the object condition before predicting image size or nature.

blocks.heading: describe the use of a single lens in a camera and the human eye, drawing ray diagrams to show how each forms an image and compare the functioning of the human eye with the functioning of the camera
blocks.text:
A camera and eye use converging optics to form real inverted images on receiving surfaces. A camera sensor or film corresponds to the retina as the image-receiving surface.

Use the real-image ray construction with a receiving surface at the convergence point. For the same simplified geometry, the surface is 3 cm behind the lens in the 6 cm object, 2 cm focal-length model. The eye changes optical power by accommodation; a simple camera can instead change lens-to-sensor separation. Aperture control regulates admitted light, not the fundamental real-image criterion.

blocks.heading: Describe a camera lens and image
blocks.text:
A simple camera forms a real inverted image on film or an electronic sensor. Focusing places the image plane at that receiving surface.

For a nearby object, the required lens-to-sensor separation differs from the distant-object setting. A simple camera moves the lens relative to the fixed sensor. The aperture controls light admission; a shutter controls exposure time. These roles should not be confused with focusing.

blocks.heading: Describe the eye lens and image
blocks.text:
The eye forms a real inverted image on the retina. Accommodation changes the shape and optical power of the eye’s lens.

The cornea also contributes refraction, but the simplified syllabus comparison emphasises the lens and retina. The lens becomes more strongly converging for nearer objects in normal accommodation. The retina detects the image; the brain’s interpretation does not make the optical image upright on the retina.

blocks.heading: Compare camera and eye focusing
blocks.text:
A simple camera can focus by moving its lens relative to its receiving surface. The eye mainly accommodates by changing lens power while retina position is approximately fixed.

Both require actual ray convergence at the receiving surface. Compare the changed feature rather than merely saying each has a lens. More complex cameras can have internal moving groups, but the elementary comparison concerns the simple model.

blocks.heading: describe short sight and long sight and describe the correction of these eye defects (diverging lenses are only mentioned at this stage)
blocks.text:
Short sight and long sight are different failures to focus an intended object on the retina. The corrective lens type depends on whether the uncorrected convergence is too early or too late.

Short sight commonly blurs distant objects because their image would lie in front of the retina; a diverging correction reduces convergence. Long sight can blur near objects because the required image would lie behind the retina; a converging correction adds convergence. This is an educational optical model rather than an individual prescription.

blocks.heading: Describe and correct short sight
blocks.text:
In short sight, distant-object rays would focus in front of the retina without correction. A diverging corrective lens can reduce the incoming bundle’s convergence.

The correction lets the eye form its image farther back on the retina. Keep the ray account qualitative here; a separate treatment of diverging-lens formulae and image calculations is outside this topic’s intended depth. The defect concerns focus location, not a claim that the retina emits light.

blocks.heading: Describe and correct long sight
blocks.text:
In long sight, near-object rays can be insufficiently converged to focus on the retina. A converging corrective lens supplies additional convergence.

Without suitable accommodation or correction, the ideal focus for those near rays would be behind the retina. The corrective lens shifts the focus toward the retinal surface. Describe the near-object condition; the optical defect is not simply inability to see any distant object.

blocks.heading: describe applications of the refraction of light in nature such as the rainbow, size and position of objects under water and mirages to explain: - the passage of light through a prism (dispersion) and identify the colours of the spectrum produced from white light - how rainbows can be formed by the internal reflection of light in water - how mirages are formed as an optical illusion that uses the phenomena of reflection and refraction
blocks.text:
Refraction explains several natural apparent-position and colour effects. Dispersion, internal reflection and changing air index add specific features to different examples.

A prism separates white light because its index depends on wavelength. Water droplets combine refraction and internal reflection to form a rainbow. A submerged object can appear shallower because emerging rays bend, while a mirage involves direction changes through air layers of different refractive index. Use the mechanism appropriate to each case rather than attributing all to reflection alone.

blocks.heading: Explain prism dispersion and the visible colour order
blocks.text:
Dispersion separates white light because a material’s refractive index varies with wavelength. The visible sequence from red to violet is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

In the usual glass-prism case, violet deviates more than red. White light already contains the different colour components; the prism separates their directions rather than manufacturing the colours. A narrow incident slit makes the separated spectrum easier to distinguish on a screen.

blocks.heading: Explain rainbow formation
blocks.text:
A primary rainbow involves refraction into droplets, one internal reflection and refraction out. Dispersion directs different colours toward the observer at different angles.

Many droplets at suitable viewing directions contribute light. The observer normally has the Sun behind and droplets ahead. Red appears on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge of the primary bow. The internally reflected part need not be described as total internal reflection for the usual primary-rainbow path.

blocks.heading: Explain apparent underwater position and size
blocks.text:
Light from an underwater object bends away from the normal on entering air. An observer traces the emerging directions backward and sees an apparent position closer to the surface in the usual near-normal view.

The apparent depth differs from actual depth. Refraction can also change apparent size because ray directions and angular extent change, but the result depends on viewing geometry. Do not use a blanket claim that every underwater object is enlarged by one fixed factor. A ray sketch should show dashed backward extensions to the apparent point.

blocks.heading: Explain mirage formation qualitatively
blocks.text:
A mirage can result when air temperature layers create a refractive-index gradient. Rays can curve through successive small refractions and reach the eye from an unexpected direction.

Above a hot road, lower warmer air commonly has a lower index. A ray from the sky can bend upward through this gradient and enter an observer’s eye, giving an apparent sky-like patch on the road. The layered model can include limiting internal-reflection behaviour; a literal pool of water is not needed.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Reflection returns light into the incident region, while refraction concerns transmission with changed propagation in another medium. Both processes can occur at the same interface.

At an air-glass boundary, some light can reflect in air and some can enter glass with changed speed. Calling the transmitted bent ray reflected mixes up the side of the interface on which it propagates. Track the ray and the medium instead of naming any direction change reflection.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Optical incidence and refraction angles use the normal, not the surface. A stated surface angle must be complemented to 90° before use as a normal angle.

A transmitted ray 60° to a flat surface is 30° to its normal. Substituting 60° as the refraction angle into the index relation changes the sine ratio. A diagram with its normal drawn explicitly prevents mixing the two references.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
An image can be visible even if no actual rays meet at its apparent position. Virtual images are located by extensions, whereas real images use actual convergence.

A magnifying-glass virtual image can be seen through the lens, but a screen placed at its apparent location does not collect it. Visibility means rays enter the eye; it does not mean those rays originated or met at the apparent point.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. At normal incidence into glass, what can change?
A. Speed and wavelength
B. Frequency because the source changes
C. Direction must turn by 90°
D. The light becomes sound

2. Critical angle concerns which direction?
A. Air toward higher-index glass
B. Any direction with zero incidence
C. Only parallel mirrors
D. Higher index toward lower index

3. What locates a virtual image?
A. Its visibility alone
B. The lens colour alone
C. Backward extensions of outgoing rays
D. Actual convergence on a screen

4. Which corrects short sight in the basic model?
A. A flat coloured card
B. A diverging lens
C. A converging lens
D. An opaque screen over the eye

5. Which colour deviates more in a usual glass prism?
A. Violet
B. Red
C. All colours equally
D. No colour can emerge

6. Where does the eye form its optical image?
A. Outside the pupil
B. On the front of a corrective lens
C. At a virtual point behind the head
D. Retina

7. Which distant object is suitable for a classroom focal-length estimate?
A. A fingertip inside the focal distance
B. A mark on the lens surface
C. A distant building
D. The Sun viewed through the lens

8. What is n for sin i = 0.75 and sin r = 0.50?
A. 1.25
B. 1.5
C. 0.667
D. 0.25

9. Vacuum speed is 3 × 10⁸ m/s and material speed 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s. What is n?
A. 1.25
B. 0.8
C. 5.4
D. 0.6

10. A ray is 25° to the surface. What is its normal angle?
A. 25°
B. 50°
C. 115°
D. 65°

11. An object lies inside a converging lens’s focal length. What image results?
A. Equal-sized real
B. A real image on the opposite-side screen
C. Upright enlarged virtual
D. Reduced inverted real

12. Glass-to-air incidence exceeds its critical angle. What occurs in the ideal model?
A. Frequency doubles
B. Total internal reflection
C. Refraction at 90° exactly
D. No interaction with the boundary

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: Frequency remains fixed and no bending is required. B: The source has not changed. C: There is no bending at normal incidence. D: The wave type remains electromagnetic.

2. Key D. A: This is not the total-internal-reflection direction. B: The threshold is not normal incidence. C: It is a refractive-interface concept. D: That permits the limiting 90° refracted ray.

3. Key C. A: Both image types can be seen. B: That does not establish image nature. C: Actual rays do not meet there. D: That locates a real image.

4. Key B. A: It does not provide the needed correction. B: It reduces premature convergence. C: This generally adds convergence. D: That blocks useful light.

5. Key A. A: Its refractive index is larger than red’s in this case. B: Red is less deviated in this comparison. C: That would give no dispersion. D: A transmitted spectrum can form.

6. Key D. A: The image forms inside the eye. B: That lens helps adjust convergence. C: This is not the normal retinal image. D: This is its receiving surface.

7. Key C. A: It does not approximate a distant source. B: It is not a distant object. C: Its approximately parallel rays can form a safe screen image. D: Concentrated sunlight presents a hazard.

8. Key B. A: This adds them. B: Divide the sines. C: This reverses the ratio. D: This subtracts them.

9. Key A. A: Use vacuum speed over material speed. B: This reverses the ratio. C: Adding speeds does not give index. D: A speed difference is not the index.

10. Key D. A: This uses the wrong reference. B: Doubling is not the conversion. C: The intended acute angle is 65°. D: Use the complementary angle.

11. Key C. A: That fits the 2f case. B: Actual rays do not converge there. C: Outgoing rays diverge and extensions meet. D: That fits an object beyond 2f.

12. Key B. A: Reflection does not require that frequency change. B: The transmission condition is exceeded. C: That occurs at the critical angle, not above. D: The light is reflected.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the name of the point where axis-parallel rays meet after a converging lens. [1]

(b) State whether an image formed by actual ray convergence is real or virtual. [1]

(c) Explain the conditions for total internal reflection. [2]

(d) Calculate n for sin i = 0.66 and sin r = 0.44. [2]

(e) Calculate light speed in a material of n = 1.5 when vacuum speed is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Principal focus.

(b) Real.

(c) Light travels from higher to lower index and its internal incidence exceeds the critical angle.

(d) n = 0.66/0.44 = 1.5.

(e) v = c0/n = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which sequence increases in frequency?
A. Infrared, visible, ultraviolet
B. Ultraviolet, visible, infrared
C. Visible, infrared, ultraviolet
D. Infrared, ultraviolet, visible

2. What do radio and gamma waves share in vacuum?
A. Frequency
B. Wavelength
C. Identical application
D. Speed

3. Which band is named for satellite telephone links in this course?
A. Ocean waves
B. Mechanical rope pulses
C. Microwaves
D. Sound

4. Which use is associated with ultraviolet?
A. Supplying a mechanical rope
B. Controlled sterilisation
C. Producing sound in a vacuum
D. Measuring mass by buoyancy

5. Which common controller uses infrared?
A. A television remote
B. A simple mechanical lever
C. A water manometer
D. A plumb line

6. What supports fibre guidance?
A. Sound bouncing between water walls
B. Light needing air to exist
C. Glass moving to the destination
D. Total internal reflection

7. Which visible colour has longer wavelength?
A. Both have identical wavelength
B. Neither can be a wave
C. Red compared with violet
D. Violet compared with red

8. Vacuum frequency doubles. What happens to wavelength?
A. It becomes zero
B. It halves
C. It doubles
D. It stays fixed

9. A region absorbs more X-rays. What happens to transmitted detector signal there?
A. It decreases
B. It increases from absorption alone
C. It becomes a sound wave
D. It is unrelated to absorption

10. A warm body moves past an appropriate infrared detector. What can it detect?
A. Only visible colour
B. The absence of all radiation
C. The body’s mass directly
D. A change in infrared input

11. An oven door interlock is faulty. Which principle follows?
A. Assume microwaves are harmless at any intensity
B. Use the fault as a source of extra cooking power
C. Do not bypass the protective interlock
D. Remove shielding to improve access

12. Why can an internal crack change a radiograph?
A. It removes the need for shielding
B. It changes attenuation along a path
C. It makes gamma travel slower than sound
D. It necessarily emits visible light
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: This is the correct neighbouring order. B: This decreases in frequency. C: The first step goes downward. D: The last step goes downward.

2. Key D. A: Their frequencies differ. B: Their wavelengths differ. C: Their interactions lead to different uses. D: Both travel at the common vacuum light speed.

3. Key C. A: They do not provide that signal path. B: These require a rope. C: They can carry the communication signal. D: Sound cannot cross a vacuum.

4. Key B. A: It does not provide the stated medium. B: Its interaction can damage microorganisms. C: That is not a UV role. D: That is unrelated.

5. Key A. A: It sends coded infrared pulses. B: It transfers force directly. C: It measures pressure mechanically. D: It uses gravity.

6. Key D. A: This is not optical guidance. B: Light can travel through a vacuum. C: The signal moves, not the fibre. D: Suitable core and cladding indices confine light.

7. Key C. A: Their frequencies and wavelengths differ. B: Both are electromagnetic radiation. C: Red has lower frequency in vacuum. D: This reverses the relation.

8. Key B. A: A finite frequency gives finite wavelength. B: The speed remains c = fλ. C: That would quadruple the product. D: Then speed would change.

9. Key A. A: Fewer photons reach the detector. B: Absorption removes photons from that path. C: The radiation type does not change this way. D: Differential absorption produces contrast.

10. Key D. A: The detector responds to infrared. B: Warm bodies emit radiation. C: The signal is radiative, not a direct mass measurement. D: Warm-body emission supports detection.

11. Key C. A: They can heat tissue. B: That is not the interlock’s role. C: It is part of containing operation. D: That defeats protection.

12. Key B. A: Exposure control still matters. B: The detector receives different transmitted radiation. C: That is not the imaging mechanism. D: The detector uses transmitted radiation.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

(a) Ultraviolet.

(b) 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

(c) Different materials attenuate differently, so the detector receives a spatially varying transmitted signal.

(d) This allows the travelling core light to approach a lower-index boundary. At sufficient incidence angle total internal reflection can confine it.

blocks.heading: state the components of the electromagnetic spectrum and place them in the correct order of frequency and wavelength
blocks.text:
In increasing frequency, the school spectrum order is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Wavelength decreases along that order for a common vacuum speed.

These names divide a continuous spectrum into useful regions. Since c = fλ, a higher frequency at fixed speed requires a shorter wavelength. Learn the order with an explicit direction rather than memorising a sequence without knowing which end is higher. Boundaries between adjacent named bands are conventions rather than physical gaps.

blocks.heading: Locate radio waves in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Radio waves occupy the low-frequency, long-wavelength end relative to the other named bands. Microwaves lie next in the stated increasing-frequency order.

A radio transmitter uses a selected frequency rather than emitting an undifferentiated whole spectrum. A longer wavelength does not make it a sound wave.

blocks.heading: Locate microwaves in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Microwaves occupy between radio and infrared in the school sequence. They have higher frequency and shorter wavelength than the radio region listed before them.

Microwaves are often treated as a radio-frequency subregion in wider classifications. In this course sequence they have a separate label for communication and heating applications.

blocks.heading: Locate infrared in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Infrared occupy between microwaves and visible light. Its frequency is below visible red and its wavelength is longer.

Infrared is invisible to the ordinary human eye. A warm object can emit infrared without glowing visibly red. Its thermal applications depend on absorption and emission.

blocks.heading: Locate visible light in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Visible light occupy between infrared and ultraviolet. Within visible light, red has lower frequency and longer wavelength than violet.

The eye responds to a limited part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Visible is a response-based region, not the only radiation capable of transferring energy.

blocks.heading: Locate ultraviolet in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Ultraviolet occupy between visible light and X-rays. It has higher frequency and shorter wavelength than visible violet.

Ultraviolet is outside ordinary vision. Different UV subregions have different absorption and biological effects; the school ordering is the broad comparison needed here.

blocks.heading: Locate X-rays in the spectrum
blocks.text:
X-rays occupy between ultraviolet and gamma in the school sequence. They have short wavelengths and high frequencies.

X-ray and gamma energy ranges can overlap in detailed classifications, where origin distinguishes the names. The syllabus ordering describes their typical regions and should not be treated as a claim of perfectly sharp universal boundaries.

blocks.heading: Locate gamma rays in the spectrum
blocks.text:
Gamma rays occupy the high-frequency, short-wavelength end of the school sequence. They are electromagnetic radiation, not helium nuclei or electrons.

Gamma radiation is associated with nuclear transitions in the basic nuclear account. Its high penetration is useful for certain imaging and industrial tasks but creates exposure concerns.

blocks.heading: Shared electromagnetic properties
blocks.text:
The named electromagnetic waves in this spectrum are transverse and travel in vacuum at approximately 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Their frequencies and wavelengths differ despite this common vacuum speed.

They can cross a vacuum and do not require air. In a material their speeds can depend on the material and wavelength; the vacuum statement must not be copied unqualified to every substance. A radio signal and a visible-light signal travelling the same vacuum distance take equal propagation times in this model.

blocks.heading: describe the role of electromagnetic waves in: - radio and television communications (radio waves) - satellite television and telephones (microwaves) - electrical appliances, remote controllers for televisions and intruder alarms (infrared) - sterilisation (ultra violet) - medicine and security (X-rays) - optical fibres (visible light and infrared) - killing cancerous cells and detecting cracks in metals (gamma rays)
blocks.text:
Electromagnetic applications depend on propagation, detection, absorption and penetration. The useful interaction determines the selected band rather than frequency alone being a universal measure of suitability.

Communication uses a controlled signal that can be transmitted and received. Imaging can exploit different absorption through a material. Heating uses absorbed energy, while sterilisation or treatment uses radiation’s biological effects under controlled conditions. Match the named application to its mechanism rather than giving only a band name.

blocks.heading: Explain radio-wave communication
blocks.text:
Radio communication transmits information by controlled changes in an electromagnetic carrier. A receiver detects the signal and recovers its information.

An aerial emits and receives the selected radio signal. Sound from a broadcast microphone is converted into an electrical information signal; it does not itself travel through space as a sound wave to the receiving radio. The receiver converts the recovered information into sound if required.

blocks.heading: Explain microwave satellite and telephone links
blocks.text:
Microwaves can carry information between suitable transmitters, receivers and satellites. A directed beam and suitable receiving equipment support a communication link.

The link sends encoded information electromagnetically, rather than transporting an object through the air. Line of sight and alignment can matter. The same broad band has other applications, so describing microwave heating alone does not explain its communication role.

blocks.heading: Explain infrared applications
blocks.text:
Infrared can transfer heating energy or carry a coded control signal. Warm-body emission can also be detected by suitable sensors.

A remote control emits pulses detected by its receiver. A thermal intruder detector senses changes in incoming infrared associated with a warm body. A heater instead relies on absorption that raises internal energy. These uses share a wave region but differ in whether the desired outcome is information or heating.

blocks.heading: Explain ultraviolet sterilisation
blocks.text:
Suitable ultraviolet radiation can damage microorganisms and is used in controlled sterilisation systems. The same interaction can harm living tissue.

The educational link is between radiation absorption and damage to cellular material. Effective equipment must manage exposure, shielding and the treated region; this example does not supply a do-it-yourself dose or procedure. Do not confuse germ reduction by UV with merely warming a surface.

blocks.heading: Explain X-ray medicine and security
blocks.text:
X-ray imaging exploits different transmission through materials. A detector records the spatial pattern of transmitted radiation.

In the simple bone-radiograph example, bone absorbs more strongly than surrounding soft tissue, so the detector receives different signals. Security imaging uses related material-dependent transmission. Radiograph contrast does not mean X-rays reflect from bones like light from a mirror. The examples describe physics rather than decisions about individual medical examinations.

blocks.heading: Explain visible and infrared optical fibres
blocks.text:
Visible and infrared signals can be guided along optical fibres. Total internal reflection in a suitable core-cladding system helps confine the light.

The core has higher refractive index than its surrounding cladding. Rays meeting the boundary under the required conditions remain guided. Coded pulses carry information; the glass is not moved along with the message. Real signal loss means repeaters or other system design may be needed over long paths.

blocks.heading: Explain gamma-ray treatment and industrial use
blocks.text:
Gamma radiation can affect cells and penetrate materials sufficiently for some industrial inspections. Controlled treatment uses cell damage, while crack detection uses transmission differences.

In industrial radiography a defect changes the radiation reaching a detector, making internal structure visible. The same penetration that permits inspection requires exposure control. Cancer-treatment use is a syllabus example of a specialist application; it is not an instruction about individual treatment choice or dose.

blocks.heading: describe the main dangers of the electromagnetic spectrum
blocks.text:
Electromagnetic hazards depend on frequency, intensity, duration and the material exposed. Heating can damage tissue, while sufficiently energetic radiation can cause ionisation and cellular damage.

Intense visible light can harm eyes; infrared and microwaves can cause excessive heating. Ultraviolet can damage skin and eyes, and X-rays and gamma rays are ionising. A useful answer names a mechanism and affected tissue rather than calling every band equally dangerous under every exposure. Lower photon energy does not imply unlimited intensity is harmless.

blocks.heading: outline the safety issues regarding the use of a microwave oven and X-rays
blocks.text:
Microwave ovens use shielding and interlocks to contain operation, while X-ray systems control exposure with shielding and restricted access. Equipment protection should not be bypassed.

A metal enclosure and designed door structure limit escaping microwave radiation. X-ray work uses appropriate barriers and exposure management because the beam can penetrate and ionise tissue. These are the intended safety principles in the syllabus, not repair or operating instructions for high-energy equipment.
