items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What produces ordinary sound at a source?
A. Vibration
B. A permanent absence of motion
C. Light travelling in vacuum alone
D. A static shadow

2. How are air-sound oscillations oriented?
A. Perpendicular by definition
B. Only in circles around the ear
C. Without particle interaction
D. Parallel to propagation

3. Which is the usual approximate human hearing range?
A. 20 000 Hz–200 000 Hz
B. Only one fixed frequency
C. 20 Hz–20 000 Hz
D. 2 Hz–20 Hz

4. Which mainly determines simple-tone pitch?
A. The signal’s colour
B. Frequency
C. Amplitude alone
D. The wall distance alone

5. Which mainly changes loudness at fixed frequency and conditions?
A. Amplitude
B. Period alone
C. The number of graph axes
D. Wavelength alone

6. Why is a medium required for sound?
A. Sound is visible light
B. A vacuum carries air molecules faster
C. No source can vibrate in a vacuum
D. Material interactions transmit the disturbance

7. Which animal is known for echo-based sensing?
A. A mirror as a living receiver
B. A stationary rock choosing a path
C. Bat
D. A plant leaf as a hearing organ

8. A wall is 17 m away. What is the outward-and-return path?
A. 289 m
B. 34 m
C. 17 m
D. 8.5 m

9. For a 0.40 s echo delay and c = 340 m/s, how far away is the wall?
A. 68 m
B. 136 m
C. 850 m
D. 34 m

10. A trace has period 2 ms. What is frequency?
A. 0.5 Hz
B. 2 Hz
C. 2000 Hz
D. 500 Hz

11. At unchanged microphone settings, one trace is twice as tall with the same period. What is supported?
A. Half the speed of sound
B. Same amplitude and higher pitch
C. Greater amplitude and same frequency
D. Twice the frequency

12. Moving farther from a reflecting wall has what effect on echo delay?
A. It removes the return path by definition
B. It increases
C. It decreases for the same sound speed
D. It becomes frequency
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: It disturbs the surrounding medium. B: A disturbance requires change. C: This is not the mechanical sound mechanism. D: This is an optical effect.

2. Key D. A: That would be transverse. B: That is not the basic model. C: Interactions transmit the disturbance. D: The wave is longitudinal.

3. Key C. A: This is above the usual upper reference. B: People can detect a range. C: This is the school reference for a healthy young ear. D: This lies mostly below that range.

4. Key B. A: Sound has no visible colour. B: Higher frequency gives higher pitch. C: This chiefly changes loudness. D: This may alter echo delay.

5. Key A. A: Larger variations generally sound louder. B: That changes frequency. C: Display format does not create loudness. D: This does not set amplitude.

6. Key D. A: It is not electromagnetic radiation. B: A vacuum lacks the medium. C: A source can vibrate without transmitting airborne sound. D: It is a mechanical wave.

7. Key C. A: A mirror is not an animal. B: This is not biological sensing. C: It uses returning sound. D: This is not the named animal mechanism.

8. Key B. A: Squaring does not give path length. B: The sound travels there and back. C: This counts only one leg. D: This halves an already one-way distance.

9. Key A. A: Use d = ct/2. B: This is the round-trip distance. C: This divides speed by time. D: This halves the correct distance again.

10. Key D. A: This treats milliseconds as seconds. B: This confuses period and frequency. C: This reverses the intended arithmetic. D: Convert to 0.002 s, then take reciprocal.

11. Key C. A: The display does not show that. B: This reverses both comparisons. C: Height and timing measure different features. D: Period is unchanged.

12. Key B. A: A suitable wall can still reflect. B: The path becomes longer. C: That reverses the distance effect. D: Delay is a time.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State whether air sound is transverse or longitudinal. [1]

(b) State the sound property associated chiefly with pitch. [1]

(c) Explain why sound cannot cross an empty vacuum gap. [2]

(d) Calculate the return delay for a wall 51 m away when c = 340 m/s. [2]

(e) Calculate wall distance for a 0.50 s return delay at 340 m/s. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Longitudinal.

(b) Frequency.

(c) It needs particles to transmit a mechanical disturbance. The vacuum contains no such medium.

(d) t = 2d/c = 0.30 s.

(e) d = ct/2 = 85 m.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for longitudinal.
(b) One mark for frequency.
(c) One mark for material interactions; one for their absence.
(d) One mark for double path divided by speed; one for 0.30 s.
(e) One mark for halving the round-trip distance; one for 85 m.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for echo timing with a supplied average air sound speed model.

| Round-trip time / s | Reflector distance / m |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 17 |
| 0.2 | 34 |
| 0.3 | 51 |
| 0.4 | 68 |
| 0.5 | 85 |
| 0.6 | 102 |

(a) Draw the graph with Reflector distance / m on the vertical axis and Round-trip time / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot echo delay vertically against one-way wall distance horizontally.

Gradient: 85 ÷ 0.5 = 170 s/m. The delay-distance gradient is 2/c. The inferred sound speed is c = 2/gradient, not the gradient itself.

Plan: 1. Choose a large flat wall and a quiet safe measuring line perpendicular to it. 2. Measure the distance from the sound source and nearby microphone to the wall. 3. Produce a brief moderate pulse and record direct and echoed signals. 4. Measure their time separation electronically and repeat at that distance. 5. Repeat over a range of distances while retaining the same source-receiver arrangement.
Control and accuracy: Keep air conditions similar, avoid competing reflectors, do not use harmful sound levels and account for electronic timing offsets.
Table: Record one-way distance / m, repeated return delays / s and mean delay / s.
Graph and conclusion: Fit delay against distance; use c = 2/gradient and inspect any nonzero intercept for a systematic timing offset.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-20.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: describe the production of sound by vibrating sources, how sound moves through the air and how the ear receives sound waves
blocks.text:
Sound links a vibrating source, a mechanical disturbance in a medium and a receiver. In air, the disturbance is a longitudinal pattern of pressure variations.

A loudspeaker cone pushes and pulls nearby air, forming alternating compressions and rarefactions. Neighbouring regions pass the disturbance onward while molecules oscillate locally. At the ear, pressure variations cause the eardrum to vibrate. This connects source and receiver without requiring the source’s original air molecules to travel the whole distance.

blocks.heading: Describe a vibrating sound source
blocks.text:
A vibrating body can act as a sound source by disturbing its surroundings. Examples include a tuning fork, string and loudspeaker cone.

Motion must couple to a medium to produce the corresponding travelling sound. A tuning fork has alternating prong motion; a string can transfer vibration to an instrument body that moves a larger air region. The source’s frequency is linked to the emitted sound’s frequency in a stationary simple arrangement.

blocks.heading: Explain sound propagation in air
blocks.text:
Sound in air propagates through successive compressions and rarefactions. Air molecules oscillate approximately parallel to propagation.

A compression is a relatively high-pressure, high-density region; a rarefaction is lower pressure and density. They are features travelling through the air rather than separate permanent groups of molecules. Random thermal motion continues alongside the small organised acoustic oscillation.

blocks.heading: Describe reception of sound by the ear
blocks.text:
Incoming pressure variations can vibrate the eardrum. The ear transfers that motion through internal structures and converts it into nerve signals.

The outer ear guides sound toward the eardrum. The middle-ear bones help transmit vibration to the inner ear, where sensory structures respond. The optical idea of light entering the eye must not be substituted for this mechanical pressure pathway.

blocks.heading: suggest the approximate range of audible frequencies for the healthy human ear (20 Hz to 20 000 Hz)
blocks.text:
A commonly quoted healthy-young-human hearing range is approximately 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Actual limits vary with age, exposure and the individual.

Below the lower reference is infrasound; above the upper reference is ultrasound. A frequency being outside human hearing does not mean no wave exists or that another animal cannot detect it. These are approximate physiological reference values, not exact limits for every listener.

blocks.heading: discuss the effect of noise levels on human hearing
blocks.text:
High sound exposure can damage hearing. Risk depends on sound level and exposure duration.

Noise can interfere with communication and sustained or intense exposure can harm the ear’s sensory structures. Increasing amplitude is not merely a change in pitch. The syllabus principle is to reduce harmful exposure through source control, distance, reduced duration and appropriate protection, rather than assuming discomfort is the sole sign of damage.

blocks.heading: discuss the frequency of vibration in relation to the pitch of the sound
blocks.text:
Higher sound frequency is associated with higher perceived pitch. Changing amplitude alone does not set the pitch.

With the same oscilloscope time scale, more complete cycles across the screen mean a higher frequency. A shorter period corresponds to higher pitch for comparable simple tones. Complex sounds can contain several frequency components, so the simple comparison concerns otherwise similar tones.

blocks.heading: discuss the amplitude of vibration in relation to the loudness of the sound
blocks.text:
For comparable sounds and listening conditions, greater vibration amplitude is associated with greater loudness. Pitch is mainly related to frequency rather than amplitude.

A taller oscilloscope trace on unchanged gain indicates a larger signal amplitude. To compare loudness from traces, keep microphone position and amplifier settings fixed. Perceived loudness also depends on frequency and the listener, so amplitude is the intended controlled-variable comparison rather than a complete hearing law.

blocks.heading: describe displayed waveforms on a cathode-ray or a PC oscilloscope
blocks.text:
An oscilloscope displays a signal against time, with vertical deflection linked to microphone output. At fixed settings, trace height compares amplitude and cycle spacing compares period.

For a model trace at times 0 to 4 ms, draw two complete cycles of amplitude 1 V and another of amplitude 2 V with the same 2 ms period. The second is louder under matched recording conditions but has the same pitch. Time-base units are essential: 2 ms corresponds to 0.002 s and a frequency of 500 Hz. Voltage is a microphone signal, not particle displacement in metres.

blocks.heading: explain that a medium (solid, liquid and gas) is required in order to transmit sound waves
blocks.text:
Sound requires a material medium because it is a mechanical disturbance. A vacuum has no particles to transmit ordinary sound.

A bell may continue vibrating inside an evacuated enclosure while its airborne sound becomes much weaker as air is removed. Residual sound can travel through supports, so the demonstration needs isolation and does not imply the bell stops moving. Light from it can still cross the vacuum because light is electromagnetic.

blocks.heading: design and conduct an experiment to show how sound is reflected and how echoes are produced
blocks.text:
Sound can reflect from a boundary and return as an echo. A distinct echo needs sufficient delay and suitable strength relative to the original sound.

Use a brief pulse near a large flat reflecting wall and record the direct and returned signals. Change distance to show the delay changing. Absorbing surfaces can reduce the return. A reflected sound arriving too soon may blend with the original rather than being heard as a separate echo. Keep sound levels moderate and choose a quiet safe space.

blocks.heading: discuss how humans and animals make use of echoes
blocks.text:
Echo timing can locate reflecting boundaries or objects. Animals such as bats and dolphins use reflected sound to gain information about their surroundings.

Human applications include sonar and distance sensing. A time delay gives a travel distance if speed is known, while return strength can add information about the target. The outward and return paths must both be included in the simple ranging model.

blocks.heading: describe a measurement of the speed of sound in air using an echo from a vertical flat surface
blocks.text:
For a source and receiver together a distance d from a flat wall, the echo path is approximately 2d. Sound speed is c = 2d/t for the measured outward-and-return delay.

Measure the perpendicular wall distance and use a recorder or electronic timing to distinguish direct and echoed pulses. At 34 m with a 0.20 s delay, the estimate is 340 m/s. Repeat at several distances; a plot of echo delay against one-way distance has slope 2/c, so speed is twice the reciprocal gradient. Correct for an electronic timing offset if present.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Loudness is associated with amplitude under comparable conditions, not wavelength alone. Wavelength and frequency are linked through wave speed and chiefly support the pitch comparison.

Two tones in the same air can have equal wavelength and frequency yet different amplitudes. The larger-amplitude one is generally louder with matched observation conditions. Saying a longer wavelength makes a sound louder confuses two independent descriptors.

blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State whether air sound is transverse or longitudinal. [1]

(b) State the sound property associated chiefly with pitch. [1]

(c) Explain why sound cannot cross an empty vacuum gap. [2]

(d) Calculate the return delay for a wall 51 m away when c = 340 m/s. [2]

(e) Calculate wall distance for a 0.50 s return delay at 340 m/s. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Longitudinal.

(b) Frequency.

(c) It needs particles to transmit a mechanical disturbance. The vacuum contains no such medium.

(d) t = 2d/c = 0.30 s.

(e) d = ct/2 = 85 m.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for echo timing with a supplied average air sound speed model.

| Round-trip time / s | Reflector distance / m |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 17 |
| 0.2 | 34 |
| 0.3 | 51 |
| 0.4 | 68 |
| 0.5 | 85 |
| 0.6 | 102 |

(a) Draw the graph with Reflector distance / m on the vertical axis and Round-trip time / s on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot echo delay vertically against one-way wall distance horizontally.

Gradient: 85 ÷ 0.5 = 170 s/m. The delay-distance gradient is 2/c. The inferred sound speed is c = 2/gradient, not the gradient itself.

Plan: 1. Choose a large flat wall and a quiet safe measuring line perpendicular to it. 2. Measure the distance from the sound source and nearby microphone to the wall. 3. Produce a brief moderate pulse and record direct and echoed signals. 4. Measure their time separation electronically and repeat at that distance. 5. Repeat over a range of distances while retaining the same source-receiver arrangement.
Control and accuracy: Keep air conditions similar, avoid competing reflectors, do not use harmful sound levels and account for electronic timing offsets.
Table: Record one-way distance / m, repeated return delays / s and mean delay / s.
Graph and conclusion: Fit delay against distance; use c = 2/gradient and inspect any nonzero intercept for a systematic timing offset.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What signs of charge are used?
A. Positive and negative
B. North and south
C. Hot and cold
D. Light and heavy

2. What unit measures charge?
A. A
B. V
C. W
D. C

3. What do two negative charges do?
A. Become magnetic north poles
B. Necessarily vanish
C. Repel
D. Attract solely due to opposite signs

4. Which is a typical conductor?
A. A vacuum as a metal wire
B. Copper
C. Dry plastic
D. Dry glass

5. What does a precipitator collect?
A. Charged particles from a gas
B. Uncharged pollutant gas molecules as its defining action
C. Only sound waves
D. Newly made protons

6. Field direction is defined using which test charge?
A. Negative
B. Neutral only
C. No specified sign
D. Positive

7. Can a neutral electroscope deflect when a charged rod approaches without contact?
A. Only if protons leave the cap
B. Only because it becomes hot
C. Yes, by redistribution
D. No, only contact has electric effects

8. A material gains electrons. What net charge can result?
A. No possible charge change
B. Negative
C. Positive from gaining negative charge
D. Magnetic south

9. A charged rod attracts neutral paper. What is supported?
A. Polarisation can account for attraction
B. The paper must already have opposite net charge
C. The rod must be neutral
D. Charge has been created without transfer

10. A field points right. Which way is electric force on an electron?
A. Right by the positive convention
B. Zero due to electron charge
C. Out of the page necessarily
D. Left

11. With a negative rod nearby, an earthed conductor loses electrons. What must be disconnected first to retain the intended charge?
A. The conductor’s atoms
B. Every electron
C. Earth connection
D. The rod’s influence first

12. Where is the simple uniform-plate-field model most appropriate?
A. Inside a distant uncharged rod
B. Near the central region between broad plates
C. Far outside the pair
D. At every edge with no curvature
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: These are the two signs. B: These name magnetic poles. C: These describe thermal comparisons. D: These describe different properties.

2. Key D. A: Ampere measures current. B: Volt measures energy per charge. C: Watt measures power. D: Coulomb is the charge unit.

3. Key C. A: Charge is not a magnetic pole. B: Repulsion does not destroy charge. C: Like signs repel. D: Their signs are the same.

4. Key B. A: It is not a solid electron-conducting wire. B: It has mobile electrons. C: It is an ordinary insulator. D: It is ordinarily an insulator.

5. Key A. A: An electric force moves them to collectors. B: It does not guarantee complete gas-pollutant removal. C: Those are not charged particles. D: That is not its process.

6. Key D. A: Its force is opposite the defined direction. B: It has no simple qE force. C: A direction convention requires one. D: This is the direction convention.

7. Key C. A: Electrons redistribute in the metal. B: The intended effect is electrostatic. C: Its net charge can remain zero. D: Fields act without contact.

8. Key B. A: Electron imbalance changes net charge. B: Electrons add negative charge. C: That reverses the sign. D: This is not a charge sign.

9. Key A. A: Opposite nearer induced charge can dominate. B: Attraction alone does not prove that. C: A charged rod can attract neutral material. D: The observation does not require that.

10. Key D. A: That convention applies to positive test charge. B: An electron is charged. C: That is not set by this electric field. D: Its charge is negative.

11. Key C. A: Atoms do not need removal. B: Only a small imbalance is required. C: Then remove the rod. D: Charge can return through Earth.

12. Key B. A: That is another arrangement. B: Edge effects are smaller there. C: The field pattern differs. D: Real edge fields curve.

blocks.heading: describe simple experiments to show the production of charges by friction and detection of electrostatic charges (using an electroscope)
blocks.text:
Rubbing suitable materials can transfer electrons between them. An electroscope detects effects of charge redistribution through leaf or pointer deflection.

Charge is separated, not created from nothing. One body can gain electrons and become negative while the other loses electrons and becomes positive. A neutral electroscope can deflect when a charged object approaches because its charges redistribute; this does not by itself identify the approaching sign. A known initial charge can support a carefully interpreted sign comparison.

blocks.heading: Show frictional charging
blocks.text:
Frictional charging involves electron transfer between suitable contacted materials. The paired system retains its total charge if no charge enters or leaves elsewhere.

Rub a suitable dry plastic rod with cloth and test its interaction with small neutral paper pieces. Attraction demonstrates an electric effect but does not prove the paper initially has opposite net charge: polarisation can attract a neutral object. Avoid humid conditions that allow charge to leak away rapidly.

blocks.heading: Detect charge using an electroscope
blocks.text:
An electroscope’s conducting parts allow mobile charge to redistribute. Like charges on the movable leaf and stem can produce repulsion and deflection.

Bring a charged rod near the cap without contact and observe deflection. Remove it and note whether the initial state returns. Contact can leave net charge on the instrument, unlike simple temporary induction in an isolated neutral electroscope. Keep the instrument dry and discharge it between neutral-start trials.

blocks.heading: state that there are positive and negative charges
blocks.text:
Electric charge has positive and negative signs. A neutral object has balanced total positive and negative charge, not an absence of charged particles.

Protons carry positive charge and electrons negative charge. Ordinary charging changes the electron balance in this model; the positive nuclei remain within the material. Neutrality concerns the total, so a neutral conductor can still have locally separated induced charges.

blocks.heading: state that charge is measured in coulomb
blocks.text:
Electric charge is measured in coulombs. The SI symbol for coulomb is C.

Charge is a quantity, while current is its flow rate. A transferred charge of 2 C is not a current of 2 A unless the time relation is specified. Keep the charge unit separate from the letter C sometimes used for heat capacity in a different topic.

blocks.heading: state that unlike charges attract and that like charges repel
blocks.text:
Like net charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged body can also attract a neutral polarisable body.

Repulsion between two tested objects is strong evidence that both have like charges in the simple electrostatic test. Attraction alone does not identify opposite signs because induced charge separation can bring the nearer opposite charge closer. Explain the relative distances when using this neutral-attraction mechanism.

blocks.heading: state that electrostatics is used in. photocopying, electrostatic precipitator and ink-jet printing
blocks.text:
Electrostatic forces can position toner, remove airborne particles or steer charged ink droplets. Each application requires charge and an electric field arranged for the desired motion.

A photocopier attracts toner to a patterned surface. A precipitator charges particles and collects them on suitable electrodes. A continuous ink-jet design can deflect charged droplets between plates. Not every printer uses the same mechanism, so the last example concerns that specified design.

blocks.heading: Describe electrostatic photocopying
blocks.text:
Electrostatic photocopying uses a charge pattern to attract toner selectively. The toner is then transferred and fixed to paper.

Illumination changes the charge pattern on a suitable drum so toner marks the intended regions. Transfer moves the pattern to the paper, and fixing makes it persist. The electric role is selective attraction, not merely warming every part of the sheet.

blocks.heading: Describe electrostatic precipitation
blocks.text:
An electrostatic precipitator charges suspended particles and attracts them to collecting surfaces. This can remove particulate matter from a gas stream.

The gas flows through a controlled field region, particles acquire charge and then move toward a suitable electrode. Collected material must be removed so it does not simply accumulate indefinitely. This removes particles rather than guaranteeing removal of every gaseous pollutant.

blocks.heading: Describe ink-jet printing
blocks.text:
In a charged-droplet ink-jet system, an electric field deflects charged droplets. Changing charge or the field changes the droplet path in the intended design.

Droplets enter a region between charged plates and experience a force depending on sign. Neutral droplets are not deflected by the same simple qE mechanism. The example concerns electrostatic steering rather than every possible commercial ink-jet mechanism.

blocks.heading: explain lightning as discharge from a cloud
blocks.text:
Lightning is a large electrical discharge associated with charge separation in clouds and their surroundings. A sufficiently strong field can ionise air and create a conducting path.

Before the discharge, the air is a poor conductor under ordinary conditions. Once ionised, charge can move rapidly along a channel, transferring energy and heating the air. The resulting rapid expansion contributes to thunder. The event does not mean protons leave every object and fly upward as the usual charging mechanism.

blocks.heading: describe an electric field as a region in which an electric charge experiences a force due to its charge
blocks.text:
An electric field is a region where a charge experiences an electric force due to its charge. Field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge.

The test charge should be small enough not to disturb the source arrangement appreciably. A negative charge experiences force opposite to the defined field direction. A field can exist before the test charge is introduced; the test reveals it rather than creating the source field.

blocks.heading: distinguish between electrical conductors and insulators using the simple electron model and give typical examples
blocks.text:
Conductors have charges able to move through the material relatively readily. In ordinary solid-metal conductors, mobile electrons carry charge; an insulator lacks comparable free movement.

Copper is a conductor; dry plastic and glass are typical insulators under ordinary conditions. An insulator can still polarise, meaning its charges shift slightly within bound structures. Insulation is conditional: a sufficiently strong electric field can cause breakdown. This does not remove the usefulness of the ordinary classification.

blocks.heading: state the direction of the electric lines of force and describe simple electric field patterns, including the electric field around a point charge and between two parallel plates with opposite charges
blocks.text:
Electric field lines indicate the force direction on a positive test charge. They point away from positive sources and toward negative sources.

A point source gives a radial pattern. Far from plate edges, oppositely charged parallel plates give an approximately uniform field with straight parallel equally spaced lines. Curving near edges is a limitation of the ideal central-region drawing. Lines do not cross because the field cannot have two directions at one point.

blocks.heading: Draw the electric field around a point charge
blocks.text:
A positive point charge has radially outward electric field lines. A negative point charge has the same radial geometry with inward arrowheads.

Draw several evenly distributed rays about the charge and label its sign. Line spacing increases farther away, representing weaker field in a qualitative diagram. Do not draw closed circles, which would indicate tangential rather than radial field direction.

blocks.heading: Draw the field between oppositely charged parallel plates
blocks.text:
The central field between opposite parallel plates is approximately uniform. Its direction is from the positive plate toward the negative plate.

Draw equal-length parallel plates, label their signs and show straight parallel equally spaced lines between central regions. Use arrows across the gap rather than along the metal. Near edges the real field curves, so the simple construction is a central-region approximation.

blocks.heading: State electric field direction
blocks.text:
Field direction follows positive-test-charge force. Electron force is opposite to the field direction.

For plates with positive on the left and negative on the right, the field arrow points right, while a free electron accelerates left if other forces are negligible. Do not reverse the definition merely because electron motion is being discussed.

blocks.heading: describe and explain charging by induction
blocks.text:
Charging a conductor by induction uses an external field, charge redistribution and a controlled connection to Earth. The order of removing the earth connection and inducing object determines the final state.

Bring a negative rod near an isolated conductor without touching. Electrons are repelled; connect the conductor to Earth so some electrons leave. Disconnect Earth while the rod remains, then remove the rod. The conductor is left positive and its charge redistributes. Removing the rod before disconnecting Earth can allow charge to return and defeats the intended result.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Positive frictional charging ordinarily means loss of electrons. The simple rubbing model does not transfer protons between the materials.

The nuclei remain bound in the materials while electrons are exchanged. Removing some negative charge leaves the pre-existing positive charge in excess. Describing the outcome as proton gain confuses a net charge imbalance with the mobile particle responsible.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What signs of charge are used?
A. Positive and negative
B. North and south
C. Hot and cold
D. Light and heavy

2. What unit measures charge?
A. A
B. V
C. W
D. C

3. What do two negative charges do?
A. Become magnetic north poles
B. Necessarily vanish
C. Repel
D. Attract solely due to opposite signs

4. Which is a typical conductor?
A. A vacuum as a metal wire
B. Copper
C. Dry plastic
D. Dry glass

5. What does a precipitator collect?
A. Charged particles from a gas
B. Uncharged pollutant gas molecules as its defining action
C. Only sound waves
D. Newly made protons

6. Field direction is defined using which test charge?
A. Negative
B. Neutral only
C. No specified sign
D. Positive

7. Can a neutral electroscope deflect when a charged rod approaches without contact?
A. Only if protons leave the cap
B. Only because it becomes hot
C. Yes, by redistribution
D. No, only contact has electric effects

8. A material gains electrons. What net charge can result?
A. No possible charge change
B. Negative
C. Positive from gaining negative charge
D. Magnetic south

9. A charged rod attracts neutral paper. What is supported?
A. Polarisation can account for attraction
B. The paper must already have opposite net charge
C. The rod must be neutral
D. Charge has been created without transfer

10. A field points right. Which way is electric force on an electron?
A. Right by the positive convention
B. Zero due to electron charge
C. Out of the page necessarily
D. Left

11. With a negative rod nearby, an earthed conductor loses electrons. What must be disconnected first to retain the intended charge?
A. The conductor’s atoms
B. Every electron
C. Earth connection
D. The rod’s influence first

12. Where is the simple uniform-plate-field model most appropriate?
A. Inside a distant uncharged rod
B. Near the central region between broad plates
C. Far outside the pair
D. At every edge with no curvature

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: These are the two signs. B: These name magnetic poles. C: These describe thermal comparisons. D: These describe different properties.

2. Key D. A: Ampere measures current. B: Volt measures energy per charge. C: Watt measures power. D: Coulomb is the charge unit.

3. Key C. A: Charge is not a magnetic pole. B: Repulsion does not destroy charge. C: Like signs repel. D: Their signs are the same.

4. Key B. A: It is not a solid electron-conducting wire. B: It has mobile electrons. C: It is an ordinary insulator. D: It is ordinarily an insulator.

5. Key A. A: An electric force moves them to collectors. B: It does not guarantee complete gas-pollutant removal. C: Those are not charged particles. D: That is not its process.

6. Key D. A: Its force is opposite the defined direction. B: It has no simple qE force. C: A direction convention requires one. D: This is the direction convention.

7. Key C. A: Electrons redistribute in the metal. B: The intended effect is electrostatic. C: Its net charge can remain zero. D: Fields act without contact.

8. Key B. A: Electron imbalance changes net charge. B: Electrons add negative charge. C: That reverses the sign. D: This is not a charge sign.

9. Key A. A: Opposite nearer induced charge can dominate. B: Attraction alone does not prove that. C: A charged rod can attract neutral material. D: The observation does not require that.

10. Key D. A: That convention applies to positive test charge. B: An electron is charged. C: That is not set by this electric field. D: Its charge is negative.

11. Key C. A: Atoms do not need removal. B: Only a small imbalance is required. C: Then remove the rod. D: Charge can return through Earth.

12. Key B. A: That is another arrangement. B: Edge effects are smaller there. C: The field pattern differs. D: Real edge fields curve.

blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the unit of charge. [1]

(b) State the interaction between like charges. [1]

(c) Explain the conducting behaviour of a metal. [2]

(d) Explain positive charging of a rubbed insulating sample in the simple model. [2]

(e) Explain why the earth connection is removed before the inducing rod. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Coulomb.

(b) Repulsion.

(c) It has mobile electrons that can move through the material and carry charge.

(d) Electrons leave the sample. Its remaining positive and negative charges are unbalanced with a positive excess.

(e) It traps the intended net charge on the isolated conductor. If the rod is removed first, electrons can return through the earth connection and restore neutrality.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What does current measure?
A. Charge flow per time
B. Energy per charge
C. Energy per time
D. Stored mass

2. Where is an ammeter placed to measure branch current?
A. Directly across a source
B. Parallel with no regard to the branch
C. Outside the circuit with no connection
D. In series in that branch

3. How is a voltmeter connected across a resistor?
A. As a zero-resistance short
B. To one terminal only
C. In parallel
D. In series only

4. Which feature defines AC?
A. Zero voltage everywhere
B. Periodic direction reversal
C. A fixed positive direction
D. Only electron motion with no field

5. In a metal, electron drift compared with conventional current is what?
A. Opposite
B. Identical direction
C. Perpendicular necessarily
D. Undefined because electrons are neutral

6. Which quantity is source energy per charge?
A. Power
B. Current
C. Resistance alone
D. E.m.f.

7. What does 1 V equal?
A. 1 J/s
B. 1 N/m²
C. 1 J/C
D. 1 C/s

8. What current transfers 10 C in 5 s?
A. 10 A
B. 2 A
C. 50 A
D. 0.5 A

9. A current of 0.4 A flows for 20 s. What charge passes?
A. 8 C
B. 50 C
C. 0.02 C
D. 0.4 C

10. A component transfers 12 J per 3 C. What is V?
A. 36 V
B. 0.25 V
C. 12 V
D. 4 V

11. Three ideal 1.2 V cells are connected series-aiding. What is their open-circuit voltage?
A. 0.4 V
B. 0 V
C. 3.6 V
D. 1.2 V

12. A pulsed current varies but never reverses. How is it classified?
A. No electrical quantity
B. DC
C. AC solely because it varies
D. Static charge with no flow
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: This gives C/s or A. B: This is voltage. C: This is power. D: This is not current.

2. Key D. A: That can create a short circuit. B: It must measure the intended path. C: It cannot measure conduction current there. D: The measured charge flows through it.

3. Key C. A: It should have high resistance. B: A two-point difference needs both connections. C: Its terminals compare the resistor’s endpoints. D: That would alter the circuit strongly.

4. Key B. A: That does not describe a working AC supply. B: Magnitude variation alone is insufficient. C: That is DC. D: This is not the defining feature.

5. Key A. A: Electrons carry negative charge. B: The convention uses positive charge. C: That is not the basic wire relation. D: Electrons are negative.

6. Key D. A: This is energy per time. B: This is charge per time. C: This is voltage per current. D: It describes the source contribution.

7. Key C. A: That is 1 W. B: That is 1 Pa. C: Voltage is energy per charge. D: That is 1 A.

8. Key B. A: This ignores duration. B: Divide charge by time. C: This multiplies them. D: This reverses the ratio.

9. Key A. A: Use It. B: This divides time by current. C: This divides current by time. D: This ignores duration.

10. Key D. A: This multiplies energy and charge. B: This reverses the ratio. C: This ignores the amount of charge. D: Divide energy by charge.

11. Key C. A: This divides by the number. B: They are not opposing one another. C: Their energy-per-charge contributions add. D: That ignores series addition.

12. Key B. A: It is a measurable current. B: One-direction flow is the defining feature. C: Reversal is required for AC. D: Current is flowing.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for measuring open-circuit voltage from identical cells in series.

| Cell count | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.45 |
| 2 | 2.9 |
| 3 | 4.35 |
| 4 | 5.8 |
| 5 | 7.25 |
| 6 | 8.7 |

(a) Draw the graph with Potential difference / V on the vertical axis and Cell count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot open-circuit voltage vertically against the number of series-aiding identical cells horizontally.

Gradient: 7.25 ÷ 5 = 1.45 V per cell. The gradient estimates the open-circuit voltage contribution of one cell. The count axis is dimensionless; the slope can be described as volts per added cell.

Plan: 1. Check a high-resistance voltmeter’s zero, polarity and low-voltage range. 2. Measure one cell’s open-circuit voltage without a load. 3. Join a second identical cell in series-aiding orientation and measure across the outer terminals. 4. Repeat for the stated modest cell counts, checking polarity each time. 5. Repeat measurements and compare individual cells to assess variation.
Control and accuracy: Use similar cells in similar condition, avoid short circuits, keep total voltage within safe classroom limits and do not connect a measuring ammeter across the cells.
Table: Record number of series cells and open-circuit voltage / V, including repeated readings.
Graph and conclusion: An approximately straight near-origin voltage-count relation supports addition of similar source contributions; its gradient estimates one-cell e.m.f. under negligible load.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-22.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

units.title: Current, electromotive force and potential difference — 5.2.2

blocks.heading: state that electromotive force (e.m.f) is measured by the energy dissipated (supplied) by a source in driving unit charge round a complete circuit
blocks.text:
Electromotive force is energy supplied by a source per unit charge. Despite its name, e.m.f. is not a force measured in newtons.

A 1.5 V cell supplies about 1.5 J per coulomb in the specified model. It converts energy from a store such as chemical energy into the circuit’s electrical transfer pathway. For identical series-aiding cells under open-circuit conditions, their voltages add because each contributes energy per charge; a high-resistance voltmeter measures this approximately without substantial load current.

blocks.heading: Use electromotive force = source energy transferred per charge, V = E/Q
blocks.text:
Source e.m.f. is ε = E/Q for the source’s supplied energy. One volt is one joule per coulomb.

A source supplying 18 J to 6 C has e.m.f. 3 V. The denominator is charge, not time. If the source has internal resistance and a load draws current, terminal potential difference can differ from e.m.f.; the basic energy-per-charge definition remains. No internal-resistance calculation is required for this task.

blocks.heading: Use potential difference = component work per charge, V = W/Q
blocks.text:
Potential difference is energy transferred per charge between two points. Across a component, V = W/Q.

If 15 J transfers as 5 C passes a lamp, the potential difference is 3 V. The charge need not disappear after giving energy to the lamp. An analogy can compare the same amount of circulating charge at different energy levels, but it must not imply charge is fuel consumed by the component.

blocks.heading: state that both e.m.f and p.d across a circuit component are measured in volts [V]
blocks.text:
Both e.m.f. and potential difference use volts. They describe energy-per-charge changes with different roles.

The same unit does not make a source and a load identical. A source supplies energy per charge; a component can transfer it to light, internal energy or mechanical output. Label which pair of points or which source is being considered.

blocks.heading: state the correct way to connect a voltmeter
blocks.text:
A voltmeter measures potential difference between its two terminals. It is connected in parallel across the chosen component or pair of points.

An ideal voltmeter has very high resistance so it draws negligible current and disturbs the circuit little. Use a suitable DC range and correct polarity in a cell circuit. Putting it in series would substantially alter the current rather than simply measuring the intended component voltage.

blocks.heading: state that the potential difference between the terminals of a cell enables current to flow around a circuit
blocks.text:
A cell’s terminal potential difference can drive current through a complete conducting path. A broken circuit prevents steady ordinary current around that path.

The voltage can exist across open terminals even when current is negligible. Closing a suitable path allows a field to establish charge drift through its components. A source voltage alone therefore does not prove current is flowing: the path and its properties also matter.

blocks.heading: state the difference between e.m.f. as the total energy per charge and p.d as the work per charge in a part of the circuit and that the e.m.f. and p.d. involve different energy changes
blocks.text:
E.m.f. describes source energy supplied per charge, while a load’s potential difference describes energy transferred per charge there. Both quantities use V or J/C.

A complete circuit’s energy accounting compares source input with transfers across its components. In a simple ideal source and one-load model, their numerical values can match, but their physical roles remain distinct. With several series components, their potential differences share the source contribution.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Energy per charge is potential difference, while energy per time is power. The different denominators give different physical quantities and units.

A component transferring 18 J while 6 C passes has 3 V across it. If the event takes 2 s, its average power is 9 W. Both descriptions can apply to the same event, but one cannot replace charge with time merely because both values appear in a question.

units.title: Current, electromotive force and potential difference — 5.2.1

blocks.heading: state that a current is a flow of charge and that current is measured in amperes [A] using an ammeter
blocks.text:
Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. It is measured in amperes using an ammeter; 1 A = 1 C/s.

A current is not the total amount of charge stored on an object. The same charge crossing a section over a shorter interval corresponds to greater average current. In a metal, electrons provide the mobile charge carriers; the conventional current direction is defined using positive-charge motion.

blocks.heading: state and use the correct way to connect an ammeter
blocks.text:
An ammeter measures the current passing through it. It is connected in series with the branch whose current is measured.

Open the low-voltage circuit and insert the meter so branch charge passes through it. Choose an appropriate range and polarity for DC measurement. An ideal ammeter has negligible resistance; connecting it directly across a source can create a damaging large-current path. Use a current-limited classroom supply and switch off before changing connections.

blocks.heading: Use current I = charge Q / time t
blocks.text:
Average current is I = Q/t. Charge is Q = It when a constant current flows for time t.

A 0.30 A current for 20 s transfers 6 C across a section. Use seconds rather than unconverted minutes and amperes rather than unconverted milliamperes for the SI calculation. A current need not consume charge as it passes through a resistor; the energy transfer and charge flow are different descriptions.

blocks.heading: distinguish between static electricity and current electricity
blocks.text:
Electrostatics concerns charge distributions approximately at rest. Current electricity concerns charge flow through a path.

A rubbed insulating rod can retain a net charge locally, while a complete conducting circuit can support sustained current from a source. An electrostatic discharge is itself a brief current, so the two descriptions are connected rather than unrelated forms of substance. Charge is conserved in both.

blocks.heading: explain and distinguish between - alternating current (a.c) and direct current (d.c) - the direction of the electron flow and the direction of the conventional current
blocks.text:
AC reverses direction periodically, while DC flows in one direction. In a metal, electron drift is opposite to conventional current.

Two different comparisons are involved. AC versus DC describes whether the current’s direction changes with time. Electron versus conventional direction describes the carrier’s sign relative to a defined positive-current direction. A varying one-direction current is still DC, so constant magnitude is not the defining requirement.

blocks.heading: Distinguish alternating and direct current
blocks.text:
Alternating current reverses direction periodically. Direct current keeps one direction, although its magnitude can vary.

On a signed current-time graph, a typical AC trace crosses zero into opposite signs. A pulsed trace that stays on one side is one-direction current despite changing size. A cell is a common classroom DC source. Do not assume that any changing current must be alternating.

blocks.heading: Distinguish electron flow and conventional current
blocks.text:
Conventional current follows the defined direction of positive-charge flow. In a metal circuit, negative electrons drift in the opposite direction.

In the external circuit of a discharging cell, conventional current goes from positive toward negative through the load; electrons drift from negative toward positive. The microscopic random electron motion is superimposed on a much smaller drift. This drift direction is distinct from the speed at which circuit changes propagate.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What does current measure?
A. Charge flow per time
B. Energy per charge
C. Energy per time
D. Stored mass

2. Where is an ammeter placed to measure branch current?
A. Directly across a source
B. Parallel with no regard to the branch
C. Outside the circuit with no connection
D. In series in that branch

3. How is a voltmeter connected across a resistor?
A. As a zero-resistance short
B. To one terminal only
C. In parallel
D. In series only

4. Which feature defines AC?
A. Zero voltage everywhere
B. Periodic direction reversal
C. A fixed positive direction
D. Only electron motion with no field

5. In a metal, electron drift compared with conventional current is what?
A. Opposite
B. Identical direction
C. Perpendicular necessarily
D. Undefined because electrons are neutral

6. Which quantity is source energy per charge?
A. Power
B. Current
C. Resistance alone
D. E.m.f.

7. What does 1 V equal?
A. 1 J/s
B. 1 N/m²
C. 1 J/C
D. 1 C/s

8. What current transfers 10 C in 5 s?
A. 10 A
B. 2 A
C. 50 A
D. 0.5 A

9. A current of 0.4 A flows for 20 s. What charge passes?
A. 8 C
B. 50 C
C. 0.02 C
D. 0.4 C

10. A component transfers 12 J per 3 C. What is V?
A. 36 V
B. 0.25 V
C. 12 V
D. 4 V

11. Three ideal 1.2 V cells are connected series-aiding. What is their open-circuit voltage?
A. 0.4 V
B. 0 V
C. 3.6 V
D. 1.2 V

12. A pulsed current varies but never reverses. How is it classified?
A. No electrical quantity
B. DC
C. AC solely because it varies
D. Static charge with no flow

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: This gives C/s or A. B: This is voltage. C: This is power. D: This is not current.

2. Key D. A: That can create a short circuit. B: It must measure the intended path. C: It cannot measure conduction current there. D: The measured charge flows through it.

3. Key C. A: It should have high resistance. B: A two-point difference needs both connections. C: Its terminals compare the resistor’s endpoints. D: That would alter the circuit strongly.

4. Key B. A: That does not describe a working AC supply. B: Magnitude variation alone is insufficient. C: That is DC. D: This is not the defining feature.

5. Key A. A: Electrons carry negative charge. B: The convention uses positive charge. C: That is not the basic wire relation. D: Electrons are negative.

6. Key D. A: This is energy per time. B: This is charge per time. C: This is voltage per current. D: It describes the source contribution.

7. Key C. A: That is 1 W. B: That is 1 Pa. C: Voltage is energy per charge. D: That is 1 A.

8. Key B. A: This ignores duration. B: Divide charge by time. C: This multiplies them. D: This reverses the ratio.

9. Key A. A: Use It. B: This divides time by current. C: This divides current by time. D: This ignores duration.

10. Key D. A: This multiplies energy and charge. B: This reverses the ratio. C: This ignores the amount of charge. D: Divide energy by charge.

11. Key C. A: This divides by the number. B: They are not opposing one another. C: Their energy-per-charge contributions add. D: That ignores series addition.

12. Key B. A: It is a measurable current. B: One-direction flow is the defining feature. C: Reversal is required for AC. D: Current is flowing.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the unit of current. [1]

(b) State the unit of e.m.f. [1]

(c) Explain e.m.f. versus load potential difference. [2]

(d) Calculate current for 18 C transferred in 60 s. [2]

(e) Calculate potential difference for 45 J transferred per 9 C. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Ampere.

(b) Volt.

(c) E.m.f. is source energy supplied per charge. Load potential difference is energy transferred per charge at the load.

(d) I = Q/t = 0.30 A.

(e) V = W/Q = 5 V.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for measuring open-circuit voltage from identical cells in series.

| Cell count | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.45 |
| 2 | 2.9 |
| 3 | 4.35 |
| 4 | 5.8 |
| 5 | 7.25 |
| 6 | 8.7 |

(a) Draw the graph with Potential difference / V on the vertical axis and Cell count on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot open-circuit voltage vertically against the number of series-aiding identical cells horizontally.

Gradient: 7.25 ÷ 5 = 1.45 V per cell. The gradient estimates the open-circuit voltage contribution of one cell. The count axis is dimensionless; the slope can be described as volts per added cell.

Plan: 1. Check a high-resistance voltmeter’s zero, polarity and low-voltage range. 2. Measure one cell’s open-circuit voltage without a load. 3. Join a second identical cell in series-aiding orientation and measure across the outer terminals. 4. Repeat for the stated modest cell counts, checking polarity each time. 5. Repeat measurements and compare individual cells to assess variation.
Control and accuracy: Use similar cells in similar condition, avoid short circuits, keep total voltage within safe classroom limits and do not connect a measuring ammeter across the cells.
Table: Record number of series cells and open-circuit voltage / V, including repeated readings.
Graph and conclusion: An approximately straight near-origin voltage-count relation supports addition of similar source contributions; its gradient estimates one-cell e.m.f. under negligible load.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-22.png)

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which unit measures resistance?
A. Ω
B. A
C. V
D. C

2. Which condition is required for the stated ohmic relation?
A. A steadily heating filament
B. A different material at every reading
C. No current measurement
D. Fixed temperature and physical conditions

3. Parallel branches share what?
A. Equal resistance by definition
B. A series-only path
C. Potential difference
D. Equal current regardless of components

4. What does a relay use to operate contacts?
A. A changing colour alone
B. An electromagnet
C. A melting link for each normal switch action
D. A permanently open air gap with no mechanism

5. Why does a filament lamp become non-ohmic during a voltage sweep?
A. Its temperature and resistance change
B. Charge is used up
C. Its length must vanish
D. The current has no energy transfer

6. Which symbol identifies an ammeter?
A. V in a circle
B. Unequal parallel plates
C. A circle with a cross
D. A in a circle

7. What is a diode’s rectifying behaviour?
A. Creates charge
B. Measures mass directly
C. Strongly favours one direction
D. Equal constant resistance both ways

8. What resistance gives 6 V at 0.5 A?
A. 6 Ω
B. 12 Ω
C. 3 Ω
D. 0.083 Ω

9. What is 5 Ω in series with 8 Ω?
A. 13 Ω
B. 3.08 Ω
C. 40 Ω
D. 3 Ω

10. What is 4 Ω in parallel with 4 Ω?
A. 8 Ω
B. 4 Ω
C. 16 Ω
D. 2 Ω

11. Two branches carry 0.2 A and 0.6 A. What source current feeds them?
A. 0.12 A
B. 3 A
C. 0.8 A
D. 0.4 A

12. A wire’s diameter doubles at unchanged length, material and temperature. What is its resistance factor?
A. Four
B. One quarter
C. One half
D. Two
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Ohm is V/A. B: Ampere is current. C: Volt is potential difference. D: Coulomb is charge.

2. Key D. A: Its resistance changes. B: That changes the conductor. C: The relation involves current. D: Resistance must remain constant in the comparison.

3. Key C. A: Components need not match. B: Parallel creates separate paths. C: They span the same two nodes. D: Branch resistances can differ.

4. Key B. A: Colour is not the switching force. B: Its coil attracts an armature. C: That describes destructive fuse action. D: A mechanism is needed.

5. Key A. A: Heating changes the current-voltage ratio. B: Charge is conserved. C: No such change occurs. D: The lamp receives energy.

6. Key D. A: That is a voltmeter. B: That is a cell. C: That is a lamp. D: It is the current-measuring instrument.

7. Key C. A: It does not create charge. B: That is unrelated. C: Its characteristic is asymmetric. D: That is not the basic diode behaviour.

8. Key B. A: This ignores current. B: Use V/I. C: This multiplies V and I. D: This reverses the ratio.

9. Key A. A: Series resistances add. B: This is their parallel combination. C: This multiplies without dividing. D: This subtracts.

10. Key D. A: That is series addition. B: The second path increases conductance. C: This multiplies branch values. D: Equal parallel branches halve resistance.

11. Key C. A: This multiplies currents. B: This divides them. C: Branch currents add. D: This subtracts rather than adds.

12. Key B. A: This reverses the area dependence. B: Area rises by four. C: This mistakes diameter for area. D: A thicker wire has lower resistance.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for fixed-temperature metallic resistor at low voltage.

| Current / A | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 0.05 | 0.6 |
| 0.1 | 1.2 |
| 0.15 | 1.8 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.25 | 3 |

(a) Draw the graph with Potential difference / V on the vertical axis and Current / A on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]

(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot voltage vertically against current horizontally for the low-voltage metal resistor.

Gradient: 3 ÷ 0.25 = 12 V/A or Ω. The voltage-current gradient is resistance if temperature and other physical conditions remain fixed. Current-versus-voltage axes would give reciprocal resistance.

Plan: 1. Connect a low-voltage current-limited supply, switch, ammeter and test resistor in series. 2. Connect the voltmeter across the test resistor. 3. Set a small current with a variable resistor and record paired current and voltage readings. 4. Change the setting over a modest range and open the switch between readings to reduce warming. 5. Repeat readings and reverse polarity if the approved apparatus permits a symmetric comparison.
Control and accuracy: Keep the resistor temperature approximately fixed, use suitable meter ranges and never connect an ammeter directly across the supply.
Table: Record current / A and resistor voltage / V with repeat readings.
Graph and conclusion: A straight near-origin V-I graph supports ohmic behaviour under the controlled conditions, and its slope estimates resistance.

Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).

Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).

blocks.heading: state that resistance [R] is the tendency of a conductor to oppose the flow of charges, measured in ohms [Ω], using an ohmmeter
blocks.text:
Resistance measures opposition to charge flow and is quantified as potential difference divided by current. Its unit is the ohm, Ω; an ohmmeter can measure it in an appropriate isolated unpowered component.

A larger resistance gives less current for the same applied potential difference. Do not connect an ordinary resistance-meter mode to a powered circuit. A resistor transfers electrical energy; it does not consume charge. The relation R = V/I can describe an operating point even when the component is not ohmic.

blocks.heading: state that: - resistance is directly proportional to the length of a wire - resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area of a wire - as the temperature of a wire increases, the resistance also increases
blocks.text:
Wire resistance depends on material, length, cross-sectional area and temperature. For the same material and temperature, R is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.

Compare like materials and avoid changing temperature while testing geometry. A longer wire gives a longer interaction path, while a thicker wire provides more conducting paths. Typical metal resistance rises with temperature. Semiconductor components can behave differently, so the temperature statement here is conditioned on metal wire.

blocks.heading: Relate resistance to wire length
blocks.text:
For a uniform wire at fixed material, area and temperature, resistance is proportional to length. Doubling the length doubles resistance under those conditions.

A fair experiment varies the distance between contacts on the same uniform wire. Short readings and small currents reduce warming. Measure the conducting length between contacts rather than the whole spool. Contact resistance can create an offset, especially for short wire lengths.

blocks.heading: Relate resistance to cross-sectional area
blocks.text:
For fixed material, length and temperature, wire resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Doubling diameter quadruples circular area and reduces resistance to one quarter in this model.

The diameter-area distinction matters because A = πd²/4. A twofold diameter change is not merely twofold area. A thicker conductor provides more parallel conducting paths through the same length, explaining the lower resistance qualitatively.

blocks.heading: Relate metal-wire resistance to temperature
blocks.text:
A typical metal wire’s resistance increases as its temperature rises. Greater lattice vibration increases electron scattering in the simple account.

A filament lamp warms substantially as current increases, so its resistance is not constant across its full operating range. This does not mean every semiconductor has the same temperature trend. Temperature control is required when testing a fixed metal’s simple proportional current-voltage relation.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: sketch and interpret graphically and by calculation the relationship between current and voltage in an electrical conductor at a fixed temperature
blocks.text:
An ohmic conductor at fixed temperature has current proportional to voltage. Its current-voltage graph is a straight line through the origin.

Use voltage on the horizontal axis and current on the vertical axis. Points (0 V, 0 A), (1 V, 0.1 A), (2 V, 0.2 A) and (3 V, 0.3 A) describe a 10 Ω resistor. On these axes the gradient is 1/R, not R. If voltage is plotted vertically against current, gradient instead gives R.

blocks.heading: state Ohm’s Law and discuss the temperature limitation on Ohm’s Law
blocks.text:
Ohm’s law states that current is proportional to potential difference for an ohmic conductor when temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. A temperature change can alter the resistance and invalidate one constant proportionality across the readings.

A metal wire can show a straight low-current graph while remaining cool, then depart from it when heating matters. State the fixed conditions alongside the proportionality. The equation R = V/I defines an operating-point resistance more widely; using it alone does not prove the component obeys Ohm’s law.

blocks.heading: Define electrical resistance as potential difference divided by current
blocks.text:
Resistance is potential difference across a component divided by current through it. One ohm equals one volt per ampere.

The voltage and current must refer to the same component and operating point. For a lamp, the ratio can change as it heats. A graph gradient equals resistance only with the appropriate axes and a suitable linear relation; it is not a substitute for checking what is plotted.

blocks.heading: Use resistance R = V/I
blocks.text:
An operating-point resistance is R = V/I. Use volts and amperes for ohms.

A 2.4 V drop with a 0.20 A current gives 12 Ω. Convert milliamperes first: 200 mA is 0.20 A. Rearranging gives V = IR and I = V/R when using the appropriate resistance at that condition.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to measure the resistance of a metallic conductor using a voltmeter and an ammeter and make the necessary calculations
blocks.text:
A voltmeter across a conductor and ammeter in series provide the V and I needed for R = V/I. Low currents and short measurement intervals help keep metal temperature approximately fixed.

Use a current-limited low-voltage source, switch and variable resistor. Set a modest current, record the two readings, then vary the setting and repeat. Open the switch between readings if heating is a concern. Plot the selected characteristic with labelled axes and use its slope consistently. The instruments ideally disturb the circuit little, but real meter effects contribute uncertainty.

blocks.heading: distinguish between ohmic (e.g. fixed resistors) and non-ohmic (e.g. light bulbs and semi-conductors) conductors and sketch their V/I characteristic graphs
blocks.text:
Ohmic and non-ohmic components have different current-voltage characteristics. A fixed-temperature ohmic resistor gives a straight origin line, while lamp heating and diode directionality produce different curves.

Keep the axes consistent when comparing. A lamp current-versus-voltage curve becomes shallower as its hot resistance increases. A diode has little reverse current in the intended safe range and a strongly increasing forward current. This course uses observed semiconductor behaviour without junction theory.

blocks.heading: Describe an ohmic current-voltage characteristic
blocks.text:
An ohmic current-voltage characteristic is linear through the origin at fixed temperature. A non-ohmic characteristic does not maintain one constant current-to-voltage ratio over the stated range.

A larger current-versus-voltage slope indicates lower resistance for two straight ohmic lines on identical axes. The opposite comparison applies if voltage is vertical. Specify axes before interpreting steepness.

blocks.heading: Describe a filament-lamp characteristic
blocks.text:
A filament lamp heats as its operating current increases. Its increasing resistance makes the current-versus-voltage curve flatten compared with a fixed-resistance line.

For positive voltage, the slope becomes smaller at larger voltage in the illustrative characteristic. A similar symmetric behaviour occurs for reversed polarity in the simple filament model. Unlike an ideal fixed-temperature resistor, the lamp’s physical temperature is changing during the sweep.

blocks.heading: Describe a semiconductor characteristic within the stated syllabus scope
blocks.text:
A diode’s observed characteristic favours current in one direction. A resistor can conduct in either direction without the same strong rectifying asymmetry.

Use a safe limited-current model and keep reverse voltage within the component’s intended range. The forward curve rises steeply after its transition region, while reverse current is small in the depicted range. A zero reverse current is an ideal approximation rather than a universal exact claim. No junction or doping theory is required here.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for fixed-temperature metallic resistor at low voltage.

| Current / A | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 0.05 | 0.6 |
| 0.1 | 1.2 |
| 0.15 | 1.8 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.25 | 3 |
| 0.3 | 3.6 |

(a) Draw the graph with Potential difference / V on the vertical axis and Current / A on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot voltage vertically against current horizontally for the low-voltage metal resistor.

Gradient: 3 ÷ 0.25 = 12 V/A or Ω. The voltage-current gradient is resistance if temperature and other physical conditions remain fixed. Current-versus-voltage axes would give reciprocal resistance.

Plan: 1. Connect a low-voltage current-limited supply, switch, ammeter and test resistor in series. 2. Connect the voltmeter across the test resistor. 3. Set a small current with a variable resistor and record paired current and voltage readings. 4. Change the setting over a modest range and open the switch between readings to reduce warming. 5. Repeat readings and reverse polarity if the approved apparatus permits a symmetric comparison.
Control and accuracy: Keep the resistor temperature approximately fixed, use suitable meter ranges and never connect an ammeter directly across the supply.
Table: Record current / A and resistor voltage / V with repeat readings.
Graph and conclusion: A straight near-origin V-I graph supports ohmic behaviour under the controlled conditions, and its slope estimates resistance.
