blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: Recognise a diode symbol and its observed one-direction rectification context; no semiconductor-junction theory
blocks.text:
A diode symbol has a directed triangular element facing a bar representing the cathode side in the chosen school convention. In its observed rectification role it conducts much more readily forward than reverse in the intended range.

Conventional forward current goes from the anode side toward the cathode bar. Recognise the symbol and one-direction use; no semiconductor-junction theory is required. This limited annex supports the observed characteristic taught above.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: draw circuit diagrams with power sources (cell, battery or a.c. mains), switches (closed and open), resistors (fixed and variable), bulbs/lamps, ammeters, voltmeters, fuses, and relays
blocks.text:
Circuit diagrams use standard symbols joined by lines representing conducting connections. A diagram shows electrical topology rather than the physical shape of wires.

A cell, switch and lamp can form a series loop, with an ammeter inserted in that loop and a voltmeter connected across the lamp. Crossing wires need a clear connection convention; show a dot when a junction is intended. The symbol constructions below cover the listed components. Actual mains wiring is not a classroom construction exercise.

blocks.heading: Draw cell and battery symbols
blocks.text:
A cell symbol has one long and one short parallel line. A battery symbol repeats paired lines; the long line marks the positive terminal.

Connecting leads extend away from the two plates in the symbol. Draw the plates with unequal lengths so polarity is clear. A rectangle is a resistor symbol, not a substitute for a cell. For series-aiding batteries, connect the negative end of one cell to the positive end of the next.

blocks.heading: Draw an alternating supply and switching symbols
blocks.text:
An AC source can be shown by a circle containing a wave mark. An open switch has a gap; a closed switch joins its contacts.

Draw a switch as two contacts and a movable arm. Its open position breaks the path, whereas the closed arm completes it. The AC symbol indicates alternating output rather than an ordinary positive-negative cell pair. Use labelled circuit models rather than connecting a classroom drawing to a mains supply.

blocks.heading: Draw fixed and variable resistors
blocks.text:
A fixed resistor can be drawn as a rectangle with a lead at each end. A diagonal arrow across the resistor indicates a variable resistance.

The arrow is a control indicator, not a current arrow through a wire. In rheostat use, a selected portion of a resistance track is included in the circuit. Symbols must show where wires connect so the variable control is not mistaken for a disconnected annotation.

blocks.heading: Draw lamp symbols
blocks.text:
A lamp symbol is a circle containing a cross. Its two leads connect into the circuit path.

Do not confuse the cross with an unconnected crossing of wires: it is inside the lamp’s circle and identifies the component. A lamp has a current-voltage behaviour that can differ from a fixed-temperature resistor because its filament heats.

blocks.heading: Draw ammeter and voltmeter symbols
blocks.text:
An ammeter symbol is a circle containing A; a voltmeter is a circle containing V. Their connection positions differ even though their circle forms look similar.

Ammeter in series measures the branch current. Voltmeter in parallel measures a difference between two nodes. Label the letters clearly and connect both leads. The symbol alone does not show that the ammeter has low resistance or the voltmeter high resistance, but the circuit interpretation uses those ideal properties.

blocks.heading: Draw fuse and relay symbols
blocks.text:
A fuse symbol identifies a sacrificial overcurrent link in its circuit path. A relay symbol shows a coil controlling a mechanically linked switch in a separate path.

Draw the fuse as a small rectangle with its link line through it in the chosen school convention. For a relay, keep the coil circuit electrically distinct from the contacts and use a dashed mechanical link. Energising the coil changes the switch position; it does not imply a direct electrical junction between the two circuits.

blocks.heading: state that the current at every point in a series circuit is the same and use this in calculations
blocks.text:
A steady series circuit has the same current through each component. Charge is conserved rather than used up in successive components.

If two lamps in one unbranched loop carry 0.30 A, both have that current, although their energy transfers may differ. A resistor can reduce the whole circuit current, not remove some current permanently between its two ends. This statement assumes the steady circuit rather than a transient charge build-up.

blocks.heading: state that the current from the source is the sum of the currents in the separate branches of a parallel circuit
blocks.text:
At a steady junction, total entering current equals total leaving current. For two parallel load branches, source current is I1 + I2.

Draw arrows before writing the sum. If 0.20 A and 0.35 A flow outward through two branches, the incoming source supplies 0.55 A. Branch current is not necessarily equal unless branch properties make it so. Recombining the branches restores the same total return current in the simple loop.

blocks.heading: state that sum of the potential difference (p.d.) across the components in a series circuit is equal to the potential difference (p.d) across the power supply and use this in calculations
blocks.text:
Series potential differences add to the supply potential difference around the simple load loop. This expresses energy-per-charge accounting.

With a 9 V ideal supply and two series loads having drops of 4 V and 5 V, the total transfer per coulomb equals the source’s 9 J/C contribution. Equal current does not require equal voltage drops. Ideal connecting wires have negligible drops in this model.

blocks.heading: state that, for a parallel circuit, the potential difference (p.d) is the same across each branch
blocks.text:
Parallel branches connected to the same two nodes share the same potential difference. Their currents can differ because their component properties differ.

A 6 V ideal supply directly across two resistor branches provides 6 V to each. It is not divided into 3 V per branch. Trace both endpoints: branches share voltage when they genuinely span the same two nodes, not merely because they look side by side on paper.

blocks.heading: state that the combined resistance of two or more resistors in parallel is less than that of each resistor by itself
blocks.text:
For positive resistances in parallel, total resistance is smaller than each individual branch resistance. Additional paths increase total current at the same applied voltage.

Two 8 Ω resistors in parallel give 4 Ω. The supply drives twice the current compared with one alone. This is a different rule from series addition; the topology determines which calculation is valid. A short-circuit idealisation is a special limiting case, not an ordinary positive-resistance branch.

blocks.heading: Use series resistance RT = R1 + R2 + … and parallel resistance 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
blocks.text:
Series resistances add directly, while parallel conductances add. The parallel rule is 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … for positive-resistance branches.

Identify whether components share the same current path or the same two endpoints. In mixed circuits, simplify a genuine series or parallel subnetwork before combining the next stage. Do not apply a rule based solely on how close two symbols appear on a diagram.

blocks.heading: Combine series resistances
blocks.text:
Resistances in one series path add. RT = R1 + R2 for two ideal resistors.

The same current passes through both and their voltage drops add: V = IR1 + IR2 = I(R1 + R2). This explains the rule rather than treating it as a disconnected memory fact. Adding another positive series resistance reduces current from an unchanged ideal voltage source.

blocks.heading: Combine parallel resistances
blocks.text:
Parallel resistances combine through the reciprocal rule. For two resistors, RT = R1R2/(R1 + R2).

For 6 Ω and 3 Ω, 1/RT = 1/6 + 1/3 = 0.5, so RT = 2 Ω. Invert the final reciprocal sum; 0.5 here is conductance in reciprocal ohms, not resistance in ohms. The total smaller than the smallest branch is a useful magnitude check.

blocks.heading: discuss the advantage of making a battery from several identical sources of e.m.f. arranged in parallel
blocks.text:
Matched ideal cells connected parallel-aiding have the same voltage as one cell. They can share the load current and provide greater charge capacity in the simple model.

This differs from series-aiding connection, which adds source voltages. Real cells must be appropriately matched and designed for parallel use; mismatched voltages can drive unwanted currents between them. The lesson uses ideal identical sources rather than instructing learners to combine arbitrary batteries.

blocks.heading: explain that increasing the number of cells in series in a circuit increases the current flowing around the circuit and increases the potential difference across components in the circuit
blocks.text:
Adding series-aiding identical cells increases ideal source voltage. For a fixed ohmic external resistance and negligible internal effects, greater voltage gives greater current.

Two ideal 1.5 V cells provide 3 V, compared with 1.5 V for one. At fixed R, I = V/R doubles. A lamp may heat and change resistance, so its actual current need not double exactly. Extra cells also must not exceed component ratings.

blocks.heading: state the use of variable resistors (rheostat), fuses and relays
blocks.text:
A variable resistor controls current, a fuse interrupts excessive current and a relay provides electrically operated switching. Their circuit functions differ even when each appears as a two-terminal part in a simplified path.

Use a rheostat to vary resistance, a correctly rated fuse for the intended overcurrent protection and a relay when one circuit needs to operate a separate contact path. A fuse is not a reusable variable resistor. A relay’s coil and contacts perform different roles and may have different ratings.

blocks.heading: Explain variable-resistor use
blocks.text:
A rheostat varies the resistance included in a circuit. With other conditions fixed, a greater series resistance reduces current.

Choose a suitable current rating and start with a limiting setting. In a classroom circuit it allows several V-I readings without replacing the test conductor.

blocks.heading: Explain fuse use
blocks.text:
A fuse is intended to melt and break its path if excessive current persists. Its rating must match the protected circuit and expected normal operation.

The protection depends on heating of the link and its time-current response. Replacing it with a wire defeats the designed protection.

blocks.heading: Explain relay use
blocks.text:
A relay uses an electromagnet to operate switch contacts. A control circuit can operate a separate load circuit.

Coil current produces magnetic attraction that moves an armature and changes the contact state. Removing current lets a spring restore the normal state in a basic relay.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Parallel resistors do not combine by direct series addition. Their shared voltage and added branch currents require the reciprocal rule.

Two 6 Ω branches across 6 V each carry 1 A, so total current is 2 A and total resistance is 3 Ω. Directly adding them would give 12 Ω and contradict the two-path current. The smaller-than-each-branch check helps reveal the topology confusion.

blocks.heading: define electric power as the rate at which electrical energy is transferred to other sources of energy by an electric circuit, and is measured in watt [W]
blocks.text:
Electrical power is the rate of electrical energy transfer. It is measured in watts, with 1 W = 1 J/s.

An appliance’s power describes transfer rate rather than energy used over its whole operating period. A 20 W lamp transfers 20 J each second at its rated operating condition. Total energy also depends on duration. Energy transferred to light, motion or heating must still be accounted for as energy rather than new energy creation.

blocks.heading: recall and use the equations power = voltage × current [P=VI], and energy = voltage × current × time [E=VIt] and energy = power x time [E=Pt]
blocks.text:
For steady DC quantities, P = VI and E = Pt = VIt. The relations connect energy per charge with charge flow per time.

Multiplying V in J/C by I in C/s gives J/s, or watts. Multiplying by seconds gives energy in joules. Use the stated school DC model; an AC appliance rating cannot generally be analysed by multiplying arbitrary instantaneous or peak values without considering the appropriate quantities. Here rated power supplies the mains energy calculation directly.

blocks.heading: Use electrical power P = VI
blocks.text:
Steady electrical power is P = VI. Use volts and amperes for watts.

A low-voltage motor at 6 V carrying 0.50 A has electrical input power 3 W. Its useful mechanical output can be smaller because other energy transfers occur. Identify input or output when discussing efficiency.

blocks.heading: Use electrical energy E = VIt
blocks.text:
For constant V and I over time t, E = VIt. Use seconds for joules when voltage and current are in SI units.

A 6 V heater carrying 2 A for 30 s receives 360 J. If the readings vary appreciably, one simple product of the starting values does not represent the whole interval accurately. A joulemeter or correctly averaged measurement is then preferable.

blocks.heading: Use electrical energy E = Pt
blocks.text:
At constant power, energy is E = Pt. Watts times seconds gives joules; kilowatts times hours gives kilowatt-hours.

A 0.80 kW appliance running for 2 h uses 1.6 kWh. A kilowatt-hour is energy, not power or power per hour. One kWh equals 3.6 × 10⁶ J because it represents 1000 J/s for 3600 s. Keep the chosen unit path consistent.

blocks.heading: interpret the power rating of bulb/lamps and other electrical appliances and the energy consumption in kilowatt hours
blocks.text:
A rated power describes an appliance’s energy-transfer rate at its stated operating conditions. A kilowatt-hour is the energy transferred by 1 kW operating for 1 h.

A 60 W lamp does not use 60 J in total regardless of duration. It transfers about 60 J each second at its rating. Actual energy use can vary with duty cycle, control setting and operating condition, so a refrigerator’s compressor rating is not proof that it runs continuously for a whole day.

blocks.heading: calculate the cost of using electrical appliances where the unit is the kWh
blocks.text:
Energy cost is energy used in kWh multiplied by the stated price per kWh. A tariff used in a practice problem is an invented given, not a current electricity price.

At an invented N$2.40 per kWh, 1.5 kWh costs N$3.60 before any other charges. Convert watts to kilowatts and minutes to hours before forming kWh. A bill can include fixed charges, but include those only when the problem specifies them.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: Mains and battery supply models
blocks.text:
The syllabus compares mains as a 220 V AC model with low-voltage DC from classroom batteries. The 220 V value here is the syllabus’s given model, not a new specification of local supply conditions.

AC reverses direction while battery DC has one direction. Mains can deliver dangerous current and is not used for the classroom experiments in these notes. The low-voltage investigations use suitable current-limited supplies; a battery can still overheat or damage equipment if short-circuited.

blocks.heading: describe the uses of electricity in heating, lighting (including bulb/lamps in parallel), motors, bell and relay
blocks.text:
Electrical devices transfer energy into heating, lighting or motion and can use magnetic switching. The desired service determines which output is useful.

A heater primarily raises internal energy, a lamp supplies useful light, and a motor supplies mechanical work. An electric bell uses repeated magnetic attraction and release, while a relay changes a contact state. Device diagrams should distinguish the energy path from the control path.

blocks.heading: Describe electrical heating
blocks.text:
A resistive heater transfers electrical energy to internal energy. Its useful role is heating the intended material or surroundings.

A heating element is chosen to tolerate its operating temperature and power. Heat must be transferred to the intended load without overheating the element or nearby material. A classroom demonstration uses a rated low-voltage heater rather than exposed mains conductors.

blocks.heading: Describe parallel domestic lighting
blocks.text:
Parallel lighting puts each lamp branch across the same supply potential difference. Each branch can have its own switch and one open branch need not interrupt the others.

In a series chain, a break stops the shared path and lamps share voltage according to their properties. Parallel connection avoids that dependence for ordinary separately controlled lighting. Trace the nodes to recognise branches rather than relying on the physical spacing of lamps.

blocks.heading: Describe motor use
blocks.text:
An electric motor converts electrical input into mechanical output. Magnetic forces on current-carrying conductors provide its turning effect.

Useful applications include fans and pumps. Heating in wires, friction and sound can reduce the useful fraction of input energy. A fan’s moving air is a useful mechanical output, not a direct creation of coldness.

blocks.heading: Describe electric bell and relay use
blocks.text:
A basic electric bell uses an electromagnet and a make-break contact to sustain repeated impacts. A relay uses an electromagnet to operate separate switch contacts.

In a bell, attraction moves an armature and hammer, breaks the coil circuit, and lets a spring return the armature and reconnect it. A relay need not oscillate: its contacts can remain operated while coil current is present. Distinguish a repeated bell action from the general switching purpose.

blocks.heading: state the dangers of electricity caused by damaged insulation, overheating of electric cables, overloading of sockets (multiple plugs on one socket) and damp conditions
blocks.text:
Damaged insulation, excessive current and damp conditions create different electrical hazards. Protection must address contact, overheating and fault paths rather than relying on one device for every risk.

Exposed live metal can provide a path through a person. An overloaded cable can heat beyond its intended limit, damaging insulation or causing fire. Moisture can lower the resistance of unintended paths. Use these mechanisms to explain hazards in diagrams; learners do not need to create an unsafe circuit to demonstrate them.

blocks.heading: Recognise damaged-insulation hazards
blocks.text:
Damaged insulation can expose a live conductor. Contact can allow current through an unintended path including a person.

Recognise exposed wire, cracked casing and frayed cable as reasons to remove equipment from use and obtain appropriate repair. A normal operating appliance can still be unsafe if its insulation is damaged.

blocks.heading: Recognise cable overheating and socket overload
blocks.text:
Excessive current can overheat cables, connections or sockets. Several loads on one supply path add their current demands.

A socket count alone is not the physical cause: total load and the ratings of the common path matter. A loose connection can also heat locally. A protective rating should not be increased to hide repeated tripping.

blocks.heading: Recognise damp-condition hazards
blocks.text:
Damp conditions can increase electrical-shock risk. Moisture can lower resistance along unintended paths.

The same voltage can drive a larger current through a lower-resistance path. Keep the physics explanation tied to altered conduction rather than saying water simply attracts electricity.

blocks.heading: discuss the importance of safety devices, including earthing, circuit breakers, placing switches in the live wire, circuit breaker settings, double insulation, fuses and fuse ratings
blocks.text:
Earthing, insulation and overcurrent interruption serve complementary protective roles. Correct placement and rating are necessary for a protective device to act as intended.

An earth connection provides a low-resistance fault path from suitable exposed metal. A fuse or overcurrent breaker can interrupt excessive current; a residual-current protective device responds to imbalance and is a different device. Double insulation instead prevents accessible conductive parts becoming live without relying on a protective earth in that design. The syllabus discussion is a circuit model, not a complete installation standard.

blocks.heading: Explain earthing
blocks.text:
Protective earthing connects suitable exposed metal to a low-resistance protective path. A live-to-case fault can then produce a fault current that operates suitable protection.

The earth conductor is not intended to carry the normal load current. It helps keep accessible metal near earth potential and supports automatic disconnection in the model. It does not replace intact insulation or prove a damaged appliance is safe to touch.

blocks.heading: Explain circuit-breaker operation and settings
blocks.text:
An overcurrent circuit breaker opens a circuit when its designed current-time limit is exceeded. Its setting must protect the relevant cable and equipment while allowing intended operation.

Unlike a melted fuse link, many breakers can be reset after the fault is dealt with. A higher setting is not automatically better because it may permit dangerous heating. Do not treat every breaker as a residual-current detector; the response depends on the device type.

blocks.heading: Explain switches in the live wire
blocks.text:
A single-pole switch is placed in the live conductor in the syllabus safety model. Opening it then separates the appliance’s internal load from the live supply side.

A switch only in neutral could stop normal current yet leave internal parts connected to live. Therefore no current and safe isolation are different conditions. Real work requires proper isolation and verification by a competent person, not merely seeing an appliance stop.

blocks.heading: Explain double insulation
blocks.text:
Double insulation provides two effective insulating barriers or an equivalent protective design. It does not rely on an exposed-metal protective-earth path in the intended appliance design.

The commonly used identification is a square within a square. A plastic outer case alone does not prove a device meets the double-insulation design. Compare its protective method with an earthed metal case rather than claiming one visible feature removes every risk.

blocks.heading: Explain fuse operation and rating
blocks.text:
A fuse melts to interrupt an excessive-current path according to its rated behaviour. Choose a specified suitable rating above normal operating current while protecting the cable and equipment.

A school selection question may give available fuse ratings and normal current, then ask for the smallest suitable rating. Real selection must also account for start-up current and device characteristics. A fuse limits overcurrent consequences; it does not make direct live contact safe or protect against every shock current.

blocks.heading: describe how to wire a mains plug safely, state the meaning of the terms live, neutral and earth and be able to identify the wires by colour code
blocks.text:
In the learning model, live supplies energy, neutral forms the normal return and protective earth serves fault protection. Wire identity must be checked against labelled terminals and the specified colour convention.

For the convention used here, live is brown, neutral blue and earth green/yellow. Older or nonstandard wiring may differ, so colour alone cannot establish real-world safety. Plug diagrams are studied with an unplugged training model; work on actual mains equipment requires competent supervision and verified isolation. A cord grip holds the outer sheath rather than bare inner conductors.

blocks.heading: Wire a mains plug safely
blocks.text:
A safe training-plug assembly uses correct labelled terminals, secure insulation and an effective cord grip. The outer cable sheath is held by the grip, with no exposed stray strands.

With the model disconnected from any supply, match each conductor to its labelled terminal using the stated convention, secure the connections, check no bare wire lies outside terminals, clamp the outer sheath and replace the cover. Any fuse must be the specified suitable type and rating. This is an inspection sequence for a supervised training model.

blocks.heading: Identify live, neutral and earth by function and colour
blocks.text:
The colour convention used here is brown live, blue neutral and green/yellow protective earth. The three functions remain distinct even when a load is switched off.

Live is the conductor disconnected by the model’s single-pole switch; neutral carries the normal return current; earth is protective. These descriptions refer to the stated model and do not certify a real cable by appearance. Label the function as well as the colour in a revision diagram.

blocks.heading: discuss how electrical energy in the home can be conserved
blocks.text:
Reducing unnecessary operating time and using efficient devices can reduce electrical energy use for the same intended service. Energy savings follow E = Pt and the useful-output efficiency.

Switch off an unused light, use suitable efficient lighting, and limit unnecessary heating or cooling. Compare devices providing the same service rather than assuming a lower power always meets the same need. A lower-power heater taking much longer may not save the energy expected from power alone.

blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

items.prompt: Explain why a simple DC motor uses a split-ring commutator.
items.canonical_answer: It reverses the coil current as the sides exchange positions each half-turn. The force directions then preserve the rotational sense instead of opposing continued motion.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What do unlike magnetic poles do?
A. Attract
B. Repel
C. Become positive electric charge
D. Lose all field by approaching

2. What changes during magnetisation in the dipole model?
A. Protons move to one end
B. The sample loses every atom
C. Electrons become magnetic north only
D. Alignment increases

3. Which pair is ferromagnetic under ordinary conditions?
A. Glass and plastic
B. Water and air
C. Nickel and cobalt
D. Copper and aluminium

4. Why is soft iron useful for a switched electromagnet?
A. It reverses current mechanically
B. It magnetises and demagnetises readily
C. It is a permanent electrical source
D. It has no magnetic response

5. What shape is the field around a long straight wire?
A. Concentric circles
B. Straight radial electric lines
C. Only one line along the wire
D. No field outside the metal

6. What does a split-ring commutator do in the simple motor?
A. Increases the number of turns
B. Stores fuel
C. Reverses the external permanent poles each half-turn
D. Reverses coil current each half-turn

7. What input does a generator require?
A. Only a disconnected wire
B. A vanishing magnetic field everywhere
C. Mechanical work
D. No input

8. An object is attracted to a magnet. What can be concluded?
A. It must repel the other pole
B. It may be magnetised or merely magnetisable
C. It must be a permanent magnet
D. It must be non-ferrous copper

9. Current is out of the page and field rightward. Which way is force?
A. Upward
B. Downward
C. Along the current
D. Along the field

10. Reverse a straight wire’s current. What happens to its magnetic field?
A. Circles become straight radial lines
B. It becomes an electric field by definition
C. It disappears despite current
D. Circular direction reverses

11. More turns are added but current falls. What is needed for the simple turns comparison?
A. Ignore winding resistance
B. Remove the field
C. Hold current and other relevant conditions fixed
D. Assume torque must increase by any amount

12. A short empirical test gives lifting force 0.4 N at 0.2 A and 0.8 N at 0.4 A. What is the secant gradient?
A. 0.08 N/A
B. 2 N/A
C. 0.5 A/N
D. 0.4 N/A
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: N and S attract. B: Like poles repel. C: Poles are not charge signs. D: The field remains present.

2. Key D. A: That is not domain alignment. B: Matter remains. C: Ordinary dipoles have both pole aspects. D: Net cancellation decreases.

3. Key C. A: These are not the named ferromagnetic metals. B: These are not ferromagnetic examples. C: These are standard examples. D: They do not show the same strong ferromagnetism.

4. Key B. A: That is a commutator function. B: This suits on-off action. C: The coil needs input. D: Its response is the useful feature.

5. Key A. A: They surround the current axis. B: That is a different pattern. C: The magnetic field circles it. D: A compass can detect it outside.

6. Key D. A: It changes connections, not winding count. B: It is an electrical contact arrangement. C: The coil connection is reversed instead. D: This preserves the rotational torque sense.

7. Key C. A: A changing field linkage is needed. B: A useful field interaction is needed. C: This supplies its electrical output energy. D: That would create energy.

8. Key B. A: Unmagnetised iron can be attracted to either. B: Attraction alone cannot distinguish these. C: Induced attraction is an alternative. D: That is not supported.

9. Key A. A: The left-hand rule gives this direction. B: That reverses one required direction. C: Force is perpendicular in this setup. D: It is perpendicular to the field.

10. Key D. A: Shape remains circular. B: These are different fields. C: A field remains with reversed direction. D: The right-hand rule changes sense.

11. Key C. A: It can alter current. B: That removes the intended interaction. C: Otherwise two effects change together. D: Current reduction can matter.

12. Key B. A: This multiplies changes. B: Force change 0.4 N divided by current change 0.2 A. C: This is the reciprocal. D: This omits the current interval.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the interaction of like poles. [1]

(b) Name a ferromagnetic element other than iron. [1]

(c) Explain magnetisation in the dipole model. [2]

(d) Explain why the coil current reverses each half-turn in a simple DC motor. [2]

(e) Explain the expected effect of increased current at fixed coil geometry and external field. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Repulsion.

(b) Nickel.

(c) More dipoles or domains align. Their fields cancel less and give a net magnetic effect.

(d) The coil sides exchange positions. Reversing current keeps the torque in the same rotational sense.

(e) Magnetic side forces increase. Their couple produces a larger turning effect within the operating range.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for repel.
(b) One mark for nickel or cobalt.
(c) One mark for alignment; one for net effect.
(d) One mark for changed side positions; one for preserved torque sense.
(e) One mark for larger forces; one for larger moment.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for empirical lifting-force measurements for an electromagnet at fixed geometry.

| Current / A | Lifting force / N |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 0.3 |
| 0.2 | 0.5 |
| 0.3 | 0.7 |
| 0.4 | 0.9 |
| 0.5 | 1.1 |
| 0.6 | 1.3 |

(a) Draw the graph with Lifting force / N on the vertical axis and Current / A on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot lifting force vertically against coil current horizontally; fit the provided empirical range without forcing the line through zero.

Gradient: 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 N/A. The gradient is an empirical change in lifting force per current over this stated range. It is not a universal magnetic-force constant or proof of a general linear law.

Plan: 1. Wind an insulated coil on a soft-iron core and connect a current-limited low-voltage supply through an ammeter and switch. 2. Use a force gauge to measure the force needed to detach the same target at a fixed contact geometry. 3. Set a small current and record it with the corresponding detachment force. 4. Repeat at several safe currents, switching off between readings to limit warming. 5. Repeat each force reading after restoring the same target position and core state as closely as possible.
Control and accuracy: Keep turns, core, gap, target and alignment fixed; limit heating and prevent the target falling onto hands or feet.
Table: Record current / A, repeated detachment or lifting force / N and mean force / N.
Graph and conclusion: Describe the measured increase over the tested range and obtain its empirical slope; do not extrapolate the invented straight-line data into a universal magnetic law.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-25.png)
marking_guidance: Graph: axes and units (1), usable scales (1), accurate points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible wide construction (1), correctly signed calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Method: award one mark for each of the five specific operational steps (5).
Results table: quantities, necessary calculated column and units (1).
Graph: an appropriate relationship plotted with named axes (1).
Conclusion: use the observed trend or measured graph feature to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety support the method; the planning allocation totals eight marks.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to demonstrate that a current carrying conductor (a straight conductor and a solenoid) has an induced magnetic field around it
blocks.text:
A current-carrying straight wire and a solenoid produce magnetic fields. Compass deflection near them can reveal the field and its reversal when current reverses.

Compare a compass with current off and then on in a low-voltage circuit. Keep the wire fixed and reverse connections to see a direction change. A solenoid gives a stronger organised pattern along its interior. Use brief currents to avoid heating and do not short the supply.

blocks.heading: sketch the magnetic field around a current carrying solenoid and around a current- carrying wire (both shape and direction of magnetic field lines are required, the direction can be found from the right-hand grip rule)
blocks.text:
A straight wire gives circular field lines around its axis. A solenoid gives an approximately uniform internal axial field and an external bar-like return pattern.

Use the right-hand grip rule with conventional current: thumb along wire current and fingers around the field. For a coil, curl fingers in the turn-current direction and the thumb points toward the north end. The two forms of the same rule connect current geometry to magnetic direction.

blocks.heading: Draw the field of a straight current-carrying wire
blocks.text:
A straight current-carrying wire has concentric circular field lines in a perpendicular cross-section. Viewed with conventional current coming out of the page, the field is anticlockwise.

A dot indicates motion toward the viewer, like an arrow tip; a cross indicates away, like arrow feathers. Apply the right hand rather than the left-hand motor rule. Reversing current reverses circulation but not the circular shape.

blocks.heading: Draw the field of a solenoid
blocks.text:
A long solenoid has an approximately uniform field through its central interior. Its field returns outside from the north end to the south end.

Viewed from a north end, conventional current around that end is anticlockwise. For a rightward internal field, label the right end N and left end S. A compass detects the field rather than the electron drift in each wire segment. Show exterior return curves to avoid implying the field stops at an end.

blocks.heading: describe how to build an electromagnet and outline its uses
blocks.text:
An electromagnet uses insulated wire wound around a suitable core. Increasing current or suitable turn density can strengthen its field within the relevant operating range.

Wind a coil around soft iron and connect it to a rated low-voltage current-limited supply through a switch. Test attraction using the same target and contact geometry. Soft iron gives a switchable response; use insulation so adjacent turns do not short. Applications include relays, bells and lifting magnets.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment that shows the difference between the electromagnetic properties of iron and steel
blocks.text:
Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises relatively easily. Steel generally retains more magnetisation after an applied field is removed in the intended comparison.

Use equal core shapes and the same coil current and turns. Compare attraction with current on, then after switching it off. A retained attraction in the steel sample contrasts with the soft iron’s reduced effect. Initial magnetisation, target contact and remanence matter, so repeat the sequence consistently.

blocks.heading: describe and use the relative directions of the force, current and magnetic field for a wire carrying a current in the field using Fleming’s left-hand rule
blocks.text:
A current-carrying wire can experience a force in a magnetic field. Fleming’s left-hand rule relates field, conventional current and force for perpendicular directions.

First finger points along field from N to S, second finger along conventional current, and thumb along force. With field rightward and current out of the page, force is upward. Reversing either current or field reverses force; reversing both preserves it. A parallel current-field arrangement has no such perpendicular motor force in the elementary model.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to show the corresponding force on beams of charged particles
blocks.text:
A moving charged-particle beam can be deflected by a magnetic field. The force direction depends on charge sign, velocity direction and field direction.

In a teacher-operated enclosed electron-beam demonstration, compare the visible path with a magnetic field absent and present. Reversing the field reverses the deflection. An electron’s conventional-current direction is opposite its motion, so use that reversal with the left-hand rule. The apparatus can involve high voltage and is not constructed by learners.

blocks.heading: explain how a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a turning effect and that the turning effect is increased by increasing (1) the number of turns on the coil, (2) the current and (3) the strength of the magnetic field
blocks.text:
Opposite forces on the two active sides of a current-carrying coil can create a turning effect. More turns, greater current or a stronger field can increase that effect with geometry and orientation fixed.

The forces form a couple rather than simply translating the whole coil. Coil orientation also matters, so comparisons must use the same angle and dimensions. The syllabus account is qualitative; no new force or torque equation is required. Connect each proposed change to increased total side forces rather than asserting an unlimited improvement.

blocks.heading: Explain the turning effect on a current-carrying coil
blocks.text:
Opposite currents on opposite coil sides produce forces in opposite directions in a suitable field. Their separated lines of action can form a turning couple.

Use the left-hand rule separately on each side. One side can be forced up while the other is forced down, giving a common sense of rotation about the axis. In some orientations the turning effect becomes small or zero; continuous rotation needs a suitable commutation arrangement and inertia.

blocks.heading: Explain how turns affect coil torque
blocks.text:
Adding coil turns can increase the total turning effect at fixed current and field. The contribution of multiple suitably aligned turns combines.

The comparison assumes the current is actually held fixed. Adding wire to a coil can increase resistance and reduce current from a fixed-voltage source, so turns alone do not guarantee the same measured change unless the conditions are controlled.

blocks.heading: Explain how current affects coil torque
blocks.text:
Increasing coil current can increase magnetic side forces and turning effect. The comparison holds field, geometry and orientation fixed within safe operating limits.

More current also increases heating, which can change resistance or damage the coil. A stronger measured turning tendency is therefore compared over a controlled range rather than extrapolated indefinitely. A current-limited supply supports a fair classroom test.

blocks.heading: Explain how field strength affects coil torque
blocks.text:
A stronger external magnetic field can increase the force on a given current-carrying coil. At fixed orientation and geometry, this increases its turning effect.

A suitable core can concentrate the field, but comparisons must keep current and coil arrangement matched. Saturation and heating can limit a real system. The elementary qualitative relation does not mean the practical lifting-force data in this topic establish a universal force-current law.

blocks.heading: discuss how this turning effect is used to make a simple electric motor
blocks.text:
A simple DC motor uses the coil’s magnetic turning effect to convert electrical input into rotation. A split-ring commutator reverses coil current each half-turn in the basic single-coil arrangement.

Brushes connect the external DC supply to the rotating commutator halves. As the coil passes the appropriate orientation, the contacts swap the coil connections, preserving the torque’s rotational sense. Mechanical inertia helps carry the coil through a weak-torque position.

blocks.heading: suggest how to convert an electric motor into a generator
blocks.text:
A suitable motor mechanism can operate as a generator when mechanical work rotates it. The electrical supply is replaced by an output measurement or load in the intended demonstration.

Rotating conductors in the magnetic field induces an output; the mechanical input supplies the transferred energy. Merely disconnecting the supply does not produce sustained generation without driving the shaft. The output form depends on the collecting arrangement and is developed in the next topic.

blocks.heading: describe the action of a split-ring commutator in a two-pole, single-coil motor and the effect of winding the coil onto a soft-iron cylinder
blocks.text:
A split-ring commutator changes the coil’s connection to the DC supply every half-turn. A soft-iron core strengthens the magnetic response of the coil arrangement.

The ring has separate conducting halves rather than two continuous slip rings. Brushes remain stationary while contacts rotate. Distinguish the connection-changing component from the core: the core does not reverse current, and the commutator does not create a stronger permanent field by itself.

blocks.heading: Explain split-ring commutation
blocks.text:
Split-ring commutation reverses coil current at the appropriate half-turn positions. This keeps a simple DC motor’s torque in the intended rotational sense.

Without reversal, after the coil passes the relevant alignment the forces can tend to turn it back. Continuous slip rings preserve the connection to each coil end and therefore do not provide the same DC-motor commutation action. Explain using changing side positions rather than saying the supply itself becomes AC.

blocks.heading: Explain the soft-iron coil core
blocks.text:
A suitable soft-iron core strengthens the coil’s magnetic field interaction. Its easy magnetisation supports a stronger turning effect for the same basic supply conditions.

A cylindrical core also provides a practical winding support, but its magnetic role is the main explanation here. Do not confuse soft magnetic behaviour with physical softness or with a permanent magnet that remains strongly magnetised without the coil current.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: state the properties of magnets
blocks.text:
Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. They can attract suitable ferromagnetic material without that material initially being a permanent magnet.

Magnetic effects are often strongest near the poles. Cutting a bar magnet does not isolate an ordinary single pole: the pieces form smaller magnets with both poles in the school account. Attraction alone is therefore not sufficient evidence that an unknown object is a permanent magnet. Distinguish a magnetic pole from an electric charge sign.

blocks.heading: explain magnetism and induced magnetism in terms of alignment of magnetic dipoles (molecular magnets)
blocks.text:
Magnetisation can be modelled as increased alignment of microscopic magnetic dipoles. In an unmagnetised ferromagnetic sample, differently oriented regions largely cancel their effects.

An external magnetic field can align domains more strongly, producing induced magnetism. Soft iron loses much of its induced magnetisation when the field is removed, while a suitable permanent-magnet material retains more. The dipoles are not separated electric charges moving from one end to the other.

blocks.heading: state that the Earth has bar-magnet like properties and that a magnet freely suspended will align itself with the Earth’s magnetic field (convention: the north-seeking pole will be termed the “north pole” of the magnet)
blocks.text:
A freely suspended magnet tends to align with the local magnetic field, including Earth’s field. The end pointing toward magnetic north in this convention is called the north-seeking or north pole.

Keep strong nearby magnets, currents and magnetic objects away when demonstrating this alignment. Earth’s field is approximately bar-magnet-like for this school model, but magnetic and geographic directions are not identical everywhere. No current local compass correction is assumed here.

blocks.heading: distinguish between ferrous and non-ferrous materials
blocks.text:
Ferrous materials contain iron; non-ferrous materials do not have iron as their defining base. This composition classification is not identical to whether a sample is strongly magnetic.

Copper and aluminium are typical non-ferrous metals. Iron-based steels are ferrous, but alloy composition and structure influence their magnetic response. Nickel and cobalt can be ferromagnetic without being iron-based. Do not use the word ferrous as a complete synonym for every magnetic substance.

blocks.heading: state that iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys are ferromagnetic materials
blocks.text:
Iron, nickel and cobalt are important examples of ferromagnetic elements under ordinary conditions. Many suitable alloys of these elements are also ferromagnetic, though alloy behaviour depends on composition and structure.

Ferromagnetic materials can show strong magnetic response and domain alignment. Some alloys do not retain the same response as their ingredients, so the example does not imply that every mixture containing any iron must behave identically. Steel is useful in permanent-magnet comparisons, while soft iron is useful in switched electromagnets.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment to show the magnetic field around a bar magnet
blocks.text:
A plotting compass can map magnetic-field direction around a bar magnet. Iron filings can reveal pattern shape but do not by themselves mark arrow direction.

Place the magnet under paper, mark its outline and poles, and use a small compass at successive positions to trace the north-tip direction. Repeat from different starting positions. Alternatively sprinkle filings lightly and tap the sheet gently to reveal alignment. Keep the compass sufficiently far from the magnet to rotate freely rather than being pulled into contact.

blocks.heading: draw and explain the pattern of field lines around a bar magnet and a horseshoe magnet
blocks.text:
External magnetic field lines run from a magnet’s north pole toward its south pole. A horseshoe arrangement can produce an approximately uniform field in a narrow central gap.

Field lines form closed patterns including their continuation through the magnet. Denser line spacing represents stronger field qualitatively; it is not a literal collection of strings. Compare the curved external bar pattern with the more nearly parallel lines between nearby opposed pole faces.

blocks.heading: Draw a bar-magnet field
blocks.text:
A bar magnet has curved external field lines from N to S. The field continues through the magnet from S to N in a closed pattern.

Draw several smooth noncrossing loops and add outside arrowheads from N to S. Lines emerge from different regions near the north pole and enter near the south. Close spacing near the ends indicates stronger field there; do not draw lines with two directions at the same point.

blocks.heading: Draw a horseshoe-magnet field
blocks.text:
Opposed nearby horseshoe pole faces can produce an approximately uniform central-gap field. The field points from the N face to the S face.

Draw the U-shaped magnet with labelled faces and straight parallel evenly spaced lines across its central gap. Real edge regions curve, so do not extend the uniform assumption indefinitely outside the pole faces. Larger gap or irregular faces can make the simple model less accurate.

blocks.heading: describe and explain the difference between the design and use of permanent magnets and electromagnets (as used in e.g. a bell and a d.c. motor)
blocks.text:
A permanent magnet retains a substantial magnetic effect without a continuous electrical input. An electromagnet uses current in a coil and can be switched or adjusted.

A soft-iron core strengthens a coil’s field and loses much of its induced effect after current stops. A bell needs repeated switching, making an electromagnet useful. A simple motor can combine a permanent field magnet with a current-carrying rotating coil. Neither device creates energy: a motor needs an input supply.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Attraction to a magnet alone does not establish that an unknown object is a permanent magnet. An initially unmagnetised ferromagnetic object can be attracted by induced magnetism.

Test both ends of the object against a known pole while keeping other influences controlled. Repulsion supports the presence of a like pole on a magnetised object. It shows magnetisation at the time of the test; demonstrating long-term permanence also requires checking retention after other inducing influences are removed.

8. Key B. A: Unmagnetised iron can be attracted to either. B: Attraction alone cannot distinguish these. C: Induced attraction is an alternative. D: That is not supported.

9. Key A. A: The left-hand rule gives this direction. B: That reverses one required direction. C: Force is perpendicular in this setup. D: It is perpendicular to the field.

10. Key D. A: Shape remains circular. B: These are different fields. C: A field remains with reversed direction. D: The right-hand rule changes sense.

11. Key C. A: It can alter current. B: That removes the intended interaction. C: Otherwise two effects change together. D: Current reduction can matter.

12. Key B. A: This multiplies changes. B: Force change 0.4 N divided by current change 0.2 A. C: This is the reciprocal. D: This omits the current interval.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. A magnet is held stationary inside a stationary coil. What is expected after transients?
A. No sustained induced e.m.f. from the unchanged field
B. A sustained output solely because field exists
C. An increasing voltage without input
D. The coil becomes a cell

2. What does Lenz’s law oppose?
A. Every existing field by complete cancellation
B. Only the coil’s weight
C. Energy conservation
D. The change causing induction

3. What preserves connection to each rotating AC coil end?
A. A split ring used for DC commutation
B. Removing all brushes without another contact method
C. Separate continuous slip rings
D. One short circuit joining both ends

4. What supplies the changing core field in a simple transformer?
A. A stationary unchanging field alone
B. Alternating primary current
C. Steady DC indefinitely
D. No input of any kind

5. At fixed power, why raise transmission voltage?
A. To lower current and line heating
B. To increase current by definition
C. To create power
D. To remove insulation needs

6. Which is a common underground-cable advantage?
A. No excavation needed
B. Guaranteed zero repair cost
C. No need for insulation
D. Less visual impact

7. What energy input drives a generator?
A. Permanent magnet consumption as fuel
B. No input after connecting a load
C. Mechanical input
D. Charge destruction

8. Np = 200, Ns = 100 and Vp = 8 V. What is ideal Vs?
A. 0.5 V
B. 4 V
C. 16 V
D. 8 V

9. An ideal transformer supplies 12 W at 3 V. What output current flows?
A. 4 A
B. 36 A
C. 0.25 A
D. 12 A

10. Rotation rate doubles in the fixed-field two-pole model. What happens to period?
A. It doubles
B. It stays fixed
C. It becomes amplitude
D. It halves

11. The magnet’s motion through a closed coil is reversed. What changes?
A. Charge is created
B. The coil loses its turns
C. Induced polarity reverses
D. Polarity must stay fixed

12. At fixed primary conditions, secondary turns double. What is ideal output voltage?
A. Unchanged
B. Twice as large
C. Half as large
D. Four times as large
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Induction requires changing linkage. B: Field presence alone is insufficient. C: No changing linkage is specified. D: Induction is not chemical-cell action.

2. Key D. A: The rule concerns change. B: That is not the magnetic change. C: It is consistent with conservation. D: This is its directional rule.

3. Key C. A: It changes connections each half-turn. B: The output path would be absent. C: They do not interchange coil ends. D: That would short the output.

4. Key B. A: It does not induce steady secondary output. B: It creates changing linkage. C: After the transient it gives no sustained change. D: Energy transfer requires input.

5. Key A. A: The reduced current reduces resistive loss. B: P = VI gives the opposite at fixed power. C: Transformers do not create energy. D: Higher voltage requires suitable insulation.

6. Key D. A: Underground installation normally needs ground work. B: Fault access can be difficult. C: Cables require insulation. D: Large overhead structures are avoided along the cable route.

7. Key C. A: That is not the intended mechanism. B: A load does not supply free energy. C: Rotation requires work. D: Charge is conserved.

8. Key B. A: That is the turns fraction without applying voltage. B: The secondary has half the turns. C: This reverses the ratio. D: Turns differ.

9. Key A. A: Use I = P/V. B: This multiplies power and voltage. C: This reverses the ratio. D: This ignores voltage.

10. Key D. A: This reverses the frequency relation. B: The repetition rate changed. C: These are different quantities. D: Frequency doubles.

11. Key C. A: Charge flows rather than being created. B: The geometry can stay unchanged. C: The linkage change has the opposite sense. D: The change direction matters.

12. Key B. A: The turns ratio changed. B: Vs scales directly with Ns under the fixed primary conditions. C: That reverses the turns effect. D: The ideal relation is linear.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for a model transformer with fixed primary supply and idealised readings.

| Secondary turns | Secondary voltage / V |
|---:|---:|
| 20 | 1 |
| 40 | 2 |
| 60 | 3 |
| 80 | 4 |
| 100 | 5 |
| 120 | 6 |

(a) Draw the graph with Secondary voltage / V on the vertical axis and Secondary turns on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Plot secondary voltage vertically against secondary turn count horizontally at fixed primary conditions.

Gradient: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 V per turn. The slope is Vp/Np in the ideal model: voltage per secondary turn. It is not transformer efficiency, which needs input and output power.

Plan: 1. Use a purpose-built low-voltage AC transformer kit with a fixed primary winding. 2. Set and measure a safe fixed primary voltage without using exposed mains connections. 3. Fit or select a known secondary turn count and measure its open-circuit AC voltage. 4. Repeat for several secondary turn counts with the same assembled core and primary conditions. 5. Repeat readings and check primary voltage remains stable.
Control and accuracy: Use rated insulated classroom equipment, keep the core assembly consistent, avoid shorted turns and switch off before changing windings.
Table: Record secondary turns, primary voltage / V and secondary voltage / V, including repeats.
Graph and conclusion: A straight near-origin secondary-voltage versus turns line supports the ideal turns relation. Its slope gives voltage per turn; efficiency cannot be inferred from these open-circuit voltages alone.

blocks.heading: describe an experiment which shows that a changing magnetic field in a circuit or a magnetic field moves across a wire can induce an e.m.f
blocks.text:
A changing magnetic linkage can induce an e.m.f. in a coil. Current follows only when a suitable conducting path is complete.

Connect a coil to a sensitive centre-zero meter and move a magnet into it. The meter deflects during motion; holding the magnet stationary gives no sustained induction from that unchanged arrangement. Withdraw it and the deflection reverses. Moving the coil instead can give a similar relative-change effect. Use a low-energy classroom apparatus with no external supply connected to the sensing coil.

blocks.heading: state the factors affecting the magnitude of the induced e.m.f
blocks.text:
A greater rate of change of magnetic linkage gives a greater induced e.m.f. in the qualitative model. Faster motion, stronger magnetic field or more linked coil turns can increase the effect in a suitable comparison.

Hold the other factors fixed when testing one. Moving a magnet faster can increase the meter pulse, but a continuously stationary strong magnet does not provide a sustained induced output by strength alone. Coil orientation and the part of the field crossed also matter.

blocks.heading: state that the direction of induced current is such as to oppose the change causing it (Lenz’s Law)
blocks.text:
Lenz’s law gives an induced current direction that opposes the change producing it. The opposing effect is consistent with the need for energy input during generation.

If a north pole approaches a coil, the induced current can make the near face north and oppose approach. When the pole withdraws, the induced face changes so it opposes withdrawal. The current does not oppose an unchanged field by automatically cancelling all of it; it opposes the change.

blocks.heading: describe a simple form of a.c. generator (rotating coil or rotating magnet) and the use of slip rings where needed
blocks.text:
An alternating generator uses changing magnetic linkage caused by mechanical rotation. Either a coil rotates in a field or a magnet rotates relative to stationary coils.

The output polarity changes as the relative orientation changes. A rotating-coil arrangement can use continuous slip rings to connect each coil end to stationary brushes. A rotating-magnet arrangement can leave output coils stationary and avoid that particular output contact requirement. Mechanical input is the energy source for the electrical transfer.

blocks.heading: Describe a rotating-coil alternating generator
blocks.text:
A rotating-coil AC generator has a coil driven mechanically in a magnetic field. Its two ends connect to separate continuous slip rings and brushes in the simple model.

As the coil turns, its linked magnetic field changes and an e.m.f. is induced. The direction reverses each half-turn in the basic two-pole design. A complete external circuit allows current; an open circuit can have voltage without appreciable load current.

blocks.heading: Describe a rotating-magnet alternating generator
blocks.text:
A rotating-magnet generator changes the field through stationary coils. The output can be taken directly from the stationary winding connections.

A north and south pole moving past a coil change the direction and size of its magnetic linkage. Continued rotation gives periodic output. The number of poles affects cycles per mechanical turn, so the one-cycle-per-turn graph here belongs to the simple two-pole model.

blocks.heading: Explain slip-ring contact where required
blocks.text:
Each continuous slip ring maintains connection to the same rotating coil end. Unlike a split-ring commutator, this arrangement does not interchange the coil connections every half-turn.

Stationary brushes rub on the rings and pass the coil’s alternating polarity to the outside circuit. The rings are separate conductors attached to the two ends, not one shared shorted contact. Compare their connection role with the DC motor’s split-ring commutation rather than memorising only the names.

blocks.heading: sketch a graph of voltage output against time for a simple a.c. generator and the effect on the graph of increasing the frequency of rotation
blocks.text:
A simple uniformly rotating two-pole generator can produce an approximately sinusoidal voltage-time output. Faster rotation at unchanged field and coil raises peak voltage and reduces period in the ideal comparison.

A positive half-cycle is followed by a negative one. Doubling rotation frequency doubles electrical frequency in the simple two-pole model; the period halves. The faster magnetic-linkage change also raises e.m.f. amplitude. This is a voltage graph: its vertical values are not the angular speed of the coil.

blocks.heading: Sketch the alternating output voltage
blocks.text:
An AC generator’s voltage alternates positive and negative relative to a chosen terminal convention. A full cycle includes both signs and returns to the same phase.

Use an invented model with peak 2 V and period 1 s over 0–2 s. Draw two complete smooth cycles about a zero-voltage axis. A plot staying positive is not the same alternating waveform, even if its size varies. Mark both axes and the negative part of the scale.

blocks.heading: Show the effect of faster rotation on amplitude and period
blocks.text:
In the ideal fixed-field two-pole model, doubling rotation rate halves period and increases output amplitude. The comparison must keep coil geometry, turns and field unchanged.

Compare the 2 V, 1 s waveform with an illustrative 4 V, 0.5 s waveform. In the same time interval the second has twice as many complete cycles. Load and resistance can alter real terminal behaviour, so these are unloaded idealised traces for the stated comparison.

blocks.heading: discuss the generation of current using a simple generator
blocks.text:
A generator supplies current when its induced e.m.f. acts through a complete external circuit. Mechanical work supplies the energy transferred electrically.

Turning a loaded generator commonly requires greater input effort because the induced current’s magnetic effect opposes the producing change. The output does not come from consuming the permanent magnet’s material. Disconnecting a load can reduce current while the rotating generator still has an open-circuit e.m.f.

blocks.heading: describe the structure and principle of operation of a simple iron-cored transformer
blocks.text:
A transformer has primary and secondary coils linked by a magnetic core. Changing primary current produces a changing core field that induces secondary e.m.f.

An iron core provides effective linkage, and laminations reduce unwanted circulating-current heating in a real design. A steady DC input gives no sustained secondary output after the switching transient in this simple transformer. The two windings need not be electrically joined for energy transfer, because their link is the changing field.

blocks.heading: Use the ideal turns-voltage ratio Vp/Vs = Np/Ns
blocks.text:
For an ideal transformer, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. A secondary with more turns steps voltage up; fewer turns steps it down.

For primary 100 turns at 6 V and secondary 50 turns, the ideal output is 3 V. The ratios use corresponding primary and secondary positions. The practical graph of secondary voltage against secondary turns has slope Vp/Np when primary conditions are fixed.

blocks.heading: state the advantages of high voltage transmission
blocks.text:
Higher transmission voltage permits lower current for the same transferred power in the simple comparison. Lower current reduces resistive line heating for the same line resistance.

The familiar line-loss relation varies with the square of current, so reducing current can substantially reduce unwanted transfer to the wires. A step-up transformer is used near an AC generation source and step-down stages near consumers. High voltage also requires appropriate insulation and clearances; a lower loss does not make it safe for direct use.

blocks.heading: discuss the environmental and cost implications of underground power transmission compared to overhead lines
blocks.text:
Underground cables reduce visual impact and some exposure to weather compared with overhead lines. They commonly cost more to install and can make fault location, repair and heat removal more difficult.

Overhead routes need towers and clearances and affect landscape and land use. Underground routes require excavation and can disturb soil and habitats during construction. Compare the named route, terrain and maintenance requirements rather than making a universal cost statement for every project.

blocks.heading: Use VpIp = VsIs for a transformer with 100% efficiency
blocks.text:
An ideal 100%-efficient transformer has equal input and output power. For the stated model VpIp = VsIs, so voltage increase is accompanied by current decrease for the same power.

A 12 V, 0.50 A primary input is 6 W. At an ideal 3 V secondary output, current is 2 A. Real transformers have losses, so output power is smaller and the ideal equality must not be applied as an exact measured fact. Transformer voltage multiplication is not power creation.

blocks.heading: Namibia-context generation and transmission
blocks.text:
Namibia’s electricity system uses generation sources and a transmission network with voltage-changing substations. The transformer role is to match efficient high-voltage transfer with lower-voltage distribution and use.

Ruacana is a local hydroelectric example: water drives turbines coupled to generators. The Electricity Control Board’s September 2025 licensing list identifies Ruacana as hydro; this is a dated example, not a claim about today’s percentage mix. A general pathway is generator, step-up stage, transmission, step-down substations and consumers. Other supplies can enter the interconnected system without changing the basic voltage-matching purpose. Source: [ECB generation licences, September 2025](https://www.ecb.org.na/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Generation-and-other-licenses-issued_Sept-2025.pdf), consulted 31 October 2026.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. A magnet is held stationary inside a stationary coil. What is expected after transients?
A. No sustained induced e.m.f. from the unchanged field
B. A sustained output solely because field exists
C. An increasing voltage without input
D. The coil becomes a cell

2. What does Lenz’s law oppose?
A. Every existing field by complete cancellation
B. Only the coil’s weight
C. Energy conservation
D. The change causing induction

3. What preserves connection to each rotating AC coil end?
A. A split ring used for DC commutation
B. Removing all brushes without another contact method
C. Separate continuous slip rings
D. One short circuit joining both ends

4. What supplies the changing core field in a simple transformer?
A. A stationary unchanging field alone
B. Alternating primary current
C. Steady DC indefinitely
D. No input of any kind

5. At fixed power, why raise transmission voltage?
A. To lower current and line heating
B. To increase current by definition
C. To create power
D. To remove insulation needs

6. Which is a common underground-cable advantage?
A. No excavation needed
B. Guaranteed zero repair cost
C. No need for insulation
D. Less visual impact

7. What energy input drives a generator?
A. Permanent magnet consumption as fuel
B. No input after connecting a load
C. Mechanical input
D. Charge destruction

8. Np = 200, Ns = 100 and Vp = 8 V. What is ideal Vs?
A. 0.5 V
B. 4 V
C. 16 V
D. 8 V

9. An ideal transformer supplies 12 W at 3 V. What output current flows?
A. 4 A
B. 36 A
C. 0.25 A
D. 12 A

10. Rotation rate doubles in the fixed-field two-pole model. What happens to period?
A. It doubles
B. It stays fixed
C. It becomes amplitude
D. It halves

11. The magnet’s motion through a closed coil is reversed. What changes?
A. Charge is created
B. The coil loses its turns
C. Induced polarity reverses
D. Polarity must stay fixed

12. At fixed primary conditions, secondary turns double. What is ideal output voltage?
A. Unchanged
B. Twice as large
C. Half as large
D. Four times as large

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: Induction requires changing linkage. B: Field presence alone is insufficient. C: No changing linkage is specified. D: Induction is not chemical-cell action.

2. Key D. A: The rule concerns change. B: That is not the magnetic change. C: It is consistent with conservation. D: This is its directional rule.

3. Key C. A: It changes connections each half-turn. B: The output path would be absent. C: They do not interchange coil ends. D: That would short the output.

4. Key B. A: It does not induce steady secondary output. B: It creates changing linkage. C: After the transient it gives no sustained change. D: Energy transfer requires input.

5. Key A. A: The reduced current reduces resistive loss. B: P = VI gives the opposite at fixed power. C: Transformers do not create energy. D: Higher voltage requires suitable insulation.

6. Key D. A: Underground installation normally needs ground work. B: Fault access can be difficult. C: Cables require insulation. D: Large overhead structures are avoided along the cable route.

7. Key C. A: That is not the intended mechanism. B: A load does not supply free energy. C: Rotation requires work. D: Charge is conserved.

8. Key B. A: That is the turns fraction without applying voltage. B: The secondary has half the turns. C: This reverses the ratio. D: Turns differ.

9. Key A. A: Use I = P/V. B: This multiplies power and voltage. C: This reverses the ratio. D: This ignores voltage.

10. Key D. A: This reverses the frequency relation. B: The repetition rate changed. C: These are different quantities. D: Frequency doubles.

11. Key C. A: Charge flows rather than being created. B: The geometry can stay unchanged. C: The linkage change has the opposite sense. D: The change direction matters.

12. Key B. A: The turns ratio changed. B: Vs scales directly with Ns under the fixed primary conditions. C: That reverses the turns effect. D: The ideal relation is linear.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) Name the rotating contact arrangement in the simple AC coil generator. [1]

(b) State why steady DC is unsuitable for sustained output from the simple transformer. [1]

(c) Explain the loss advantage of higher transmission voltage at fixed power. [2]

(d) Calculate Vs for Vp = 10 V, Np = 200 and Ns = 80. [2]

(e) Calculate secondary current when ideal input power is 8 W and Vs = 4 V. [2]

Worked feedback

(a) Slip rings.

(b) It gives no continuing change of core field after the transient.

(c) Current is lower. Resistive heating in the same line is reduced.

(d) Vs = 10 × 80/200 = 4 V.

(e) Is = P/Vs = 2 A.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
The following are invented, idealised practice readings for a model transformer with fixed primary supply and idealised readings.

| Secondary turns | Secondary voltage / V |
|---:|---:|
| 20 | 1 |
| 40 | 2 |
| 60 | 3 |
| 80 | 4 |
| 100 | 5 |
| 120 | 6 |

(a) Draw the graph with Secondary voltage / V on the vertical axis and Secondary turns on the horizontal axis. Add a suitable fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate its gradient from a clearly shown construction and give its unit. [3]
(c) Plan an investigation in this physical context. Include the arrangement, five operational measurement steps, controls, a table and how the data would support a conclusion. [8]

Worked feedback

Graph: Plot secondary voltage vertically against secondary turn count horizontally at fixed primary conditions.

Gradient: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 V per turn. The slope is Vp/Np in the ideal model: voltage per secondary turn. It is not transformer efficiency, which needs input and output power.

Plan: 1. Use a purpose-built low-voltage AC transformer kit with a fixed primary winding. 2. Set and measure a safe fixed primary voltage without using exposed mains connections. 3. Fit or select a known secondary turn count and measure its open-circuit AC voltage. 4. Repeat for several secondary turn counts with the same assembled core and primary conditions. 5. Repeat readings and check primary voltage remains stable.
Control and accuracy: Use rated insulated classroom equipment, keep the core assembly consistent, avoid shorted turns and switch off before changing windings.
Table: Record secondary turns, primary voltage / V and secondary voltage / V, including repeats.
Graph and conclusion: A straight near-origin secondary-voltage versus turns line supports the ideal turns relation. Its slope gives voltage per turn; efficiency cannot be inferred from these open-circuit voltages alone.
