items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which particles are nucleons?
A. Protons and neutrons
B. Electrons and photons
C. Only electrons
D. Only protons in every nuclide

2. What fixes an element’s identity?
A. Neutron number alone
B. The sample’s temperature
C. The number of atoms in the sample
D. Proton number

3. Which pair can be isotopes?
A. Same neutrons, different protons
B. Different electric charge only
C. Same Z, different A
D. Different Z, same A

4. What is an alpha particle?
A. A neutron alone
B. Two protons and two neutrons
C. A single electron
D. An electromagnetic photon

5. What makes a tracer useful for locating a leak?
A. It follows the fluid and can be detected
B. It must block the pipe completely
C. Its charge must become zero instantly
D. The detector must create the leak

6. A sheet becomes thicker under a fixed suitable transmission monitor. What is expected?
A. Higher count because the source grows
B. No possible change in transmission
C. The detector becomes the isotope
D. Lower transmitted count

7. Carbon-14 dating is most directly suited to which model sample?
A. A shadow on a wall
B. An arbitrary vacuum gap
C. Once-living carbon-containing material
D. A newly cast pure metal with no relevant carbon history

8. A = 23 and Z = 11. How many neutrons?
A. 34
B. 12
C. 23
D. 11

9. Alpha decay starts with A = 210 and Z = 84. What are daughter numbers?
A. A = 206, Z = 82
B. A = 210, Z = 85
C. A = 208, Z = 80
D. A = 214, Z = 86

10. Beta-minus decay starts with A = 14 and Z = 6. What daughter results?
A. A = 10, Z = 4
B. A = 14, Z = 5
C. A = 13, Z = 6
D. A = 14, Z = 7

11. Atoms have 6 protons each and 6 or 8 neutrons. What follows?
A. Their A is equal
B. Both must be radioactive by definition
C. They are isotopes
D. They are different elements

12. A simple dating model leaves one quarter of initial activity. How many half-lives elapsed?
A. Zero
B. Two
C. One
D. Four
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: They constitute the nucleus. B: These are not nucleons. C: Electrons occupy the surrounding atom. D: Most nuclei also contain neutrons.

2. Key D. A: Isotopes can differ in it. B: Heating need not change the nucleus. C: Sample size does not set element identity. D: This is atomic number Z.

3. Key C. A: Different protons mean different elements. B: That can describe ions of the same nuclide. C: They share element identity but differ in neutrons. D: They are different elements.

4. Key B. A: An alpha has four nucleons. B: It is a helium-4 nucleus. C: That is beta-minus radiation. D: That is gamma radiation.

5. Key A. A: Its movement and signal reveal location. B: That changes the flow rather than traces it. C: That is not the detection principle. D: The detector observes radiation.

6. Key D. A: The source is unchanged. B: Thickness affects attenuation. C: Detector and source are different. D: More radiation is attenuated.

7. Key C. A: It is not a material carbon sample. B: It contains no sample. C: Its post-exchange decay supplies the clock. D: The required clock is not established.

8. Key B. A: This adds instead of subtracting. B: Subtract Z from A. C: This is total nucleons. D: This is proton count.

9. Key A. A: Subtract four and two. B: That is the beta-minus change. C: The subtractions are incorrect. D: That adds the emitted particle instead of removing it.

10. Key D. A: That is the alpha change. B: That is the wrong beta-minus charge direction. C: Nucleon count is unchanged. D: A neutron becomes a proton.

blocks.heading: define isotopes as atoms with the same proton number but different nucleon number
blocks.text:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different nucleon numbers. Their neutron numbers differ.

Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, but have six and eight neutrons respectively. Neutral atoms of these isotopes have the same electron count, which supports similar chemical behaviour. Their nuclear stability can differ, so isotope does not mean automatically radioactive: some isotopes are stable.

blocks.heading: give and explain examples of practical applications of isotopes for example in carbon-14 dating; nuclear medicine, radiology, biochemical tracers; radiotherapy, detection of leaks in pipes; determination of thickness of material; power generation; sterilisation
blocks.text:
Radioisotope applications use detectable emission, penetration, ionisation or energy release. The radiation type and half-life must suit the intended task.

A tracer should remain detectable for its measurement but need not persist far longer than required. A thickness monitor needs partial transmission that changes measurably with thickness. Sterilisation uses damage to microorganisms, while nuclear power commonly uses controlled fission of suitable fuel rather than merely detecting emissions. Name the actual mechanism for each application.

blocks.heading: Explain carbon-14 dating
blocks.text:
Carbon-14 dating uses the decrease of radioactive carbon after an organism stops exchanging carbon with its surroundings. The remaining activity or isotope ratio can be compared with an appropriate initial model.

Living material exchanges carbon; after death that exchange largely stops and the carbon-14 decays. More elapsed half-lives leave a smaller remaining fraction. Calibration and contamination matter in real dating, so the school exponential model is an approximation rather than an exact age for any arbitrary object. It does not date an unconnected metal sample merely because all objects contain atoms.

blocks.heading: Explain nuclear-medicine diagnosis and biochemical tracing
blocks.text:
A radioactive tracer labels a substance so its location or movement can be detected. Suitable penetrating emission can be measured by a detector outside the studied region.

In nuclear-medicine or biochemical examples, a selected labelled substance follows a process and its radiation provides information. Choice depends on chemical behaviour, emission and half-life. This describes the physical principle rather than selecting a patient’s tracer or dose. The tracer is the material introduced; the detector does not become the tracer.

blocks.heading: Explain radiotherapy
blocks.text:
Radiotherapy uses controlled radiation to damage targeted cells. Absorption and ionisation can affect both intended targets and healthy tissue.

Specialist planning aims to concentrate the intended effect while limiting unwanted exposure. The physics link is radiation interaction with cells, not a rule that radiation recognises disease automatically. This syllabus example supplies no individual treatment or dose advice.

blocks.heading: Explain leak tracing
blocks.text:
A detectable radioactive tracer in a fluid can help locate a pipe leak. A local change or peak in detector response can indicate where labelled fluid leaves its intended path.

Measure a suitable background and compare positions along the route. The isotope must follow the fluid and its emission must reach the detector under the stated conditions. Real use needs appropriate containment and authorised handling; the learning task interprets a supplied detector record rather than introducing material into public pipes.

blocks.heading: Explain thickness monitoring
blocks.text:
A thickness monitor measures radiation transmitted through a sheet. For a suitable radiation and range, a thicker sheet gives a smaller transmitted count under fixed source and geometry.

Beta radiation is a common school example for thin-sheet monitoring because partial absorption can respond usefully to thickness. An alpha source may be stopped too readily and a very penetrating gamma beam may change too little for that particular task. Match the radiation to the actual material rather than memorising a fixed choice for every sheet.

blocks.heading: Explain nuclear power use
blocks.text:
Suitable nuclear fuel can release energy by controlled fission. Heating can drive a turbine and generator to give electrical output.

The isotope’s nuclear properties permit the intended chain reaction; not every radioactive source is a practical power-reactor fuel. Connect released energy to the engineering stages and include cooling and radioactive-waste management as consequences. This application links to the earlier energy-source explanation rather than replacing the nuclear equations taught in this atomic topic.

blocks.heading: Explain sterilisation
blocks.text:
Radiation can sterilise suitable materials by damaging microorganisms. Penetrating radiation can reach some packaged materials without opening the package.

The absorbed radiation produces the biological effect. The suitability of packaging, exposure and material must be controlled by the intended process. Sterilisation does not mean the package itself becomes an active gamma source merely because radiation passed through it in this model.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Isotopes share proton number and differ in neutron number. Same neutron count with different proton counts does not define isotopes of one element.

Two atoms with eight protons and eight or ten neutrons are oxygen isotopes. An atom with nine protons is a different element even if its neutron count matches one of them. The proton count fixes element identity, so exchanging the roles changes the classification.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: The atomic nucleus
blocks.text:
An atomic nucleus contains protons and, for most nuclides, neutrons. Protons have positive charge and neutrons have no net electric charge.

Electrons occupy the surrounding atomic region rather than being ordinary constituent nucleons. The common hydrogen-1 nucleus is a proton without a neutron, so avoid saying every nucleus must contain both. Nearly all atomic mass is concentrated in the nucleus, while the atom’s size is much larger than the nucleus.

blocks.heading: use the term proton number (atomic number), denoted by Z
blocks.text:
Proton number Z counts the protons in a nucleus. It identifies the element.

Changing neutron number can produce another isotope of the same element, but changing proton number changes element identity. In a neutral atom, electron number equals Z; an ion can have a different electron number without changing its nucleus or element. Do not define Z by electrons without the neutrality condition.

blocks.heading: Nucleon number A
blocks.text:
Nucleon number A counts protons plus neutrons in a nucleus. Neutron number is A − Z.

A nucleus with 15 protons and 16 neutrons has A = 31. The mass number is an integer count, not a measured atomic mass in kilograms. Electrons are not included in A. A minus Z subtracts the proton count from the total, leaving the neutron count.

blocks.heading: Use nuclide notation with mass number A and atomic number Z
blocks.text:
Nuclide notation places A at the upper left and Z at the lower left of the element symbol. For phosphorus-31 the notation is ³¹₁₅P, with 15 protons and 16 neutrons.

Read the two positions independently: the upper number is the total nucleon count, while the lower is proton number. In plain text, phosphorus-31 with A = 31 and Z = 15 is an unambiguous accessible equivalent. Isotope notation does not itself specify how many electrons an ion has unless charge is also given.

blocks.heading: use the nuclide notation in equations to show alpha and beta decay
blocks.text:
Nuclear equations conserve total nucleon number and total electric charge. Alpha emission reduces daughter A by four and Z by two; beta-minus emission leaves A unchanged and increases daughter Z by one.

An alpha particle is ⁴₂He. A beta-minus electron is represented ⁰₋₁e in nuclear-number accounting. For example, ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He, while ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e gives the school beta-number balance. A beta-minus process also emits an antineutrino, omitted from that simplified number-accounting display because it changes neither A nor charge sum.

blocks.heading: Represent alpha decay using nuclear numbers
blocks.text:
Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons from the parent nucleus. The daughter has Aparent − 4 and Zparent − 2.

Using the original practice choice ²²⁶₈₈Ra, the daughter is ²²²₈₆Rn. Check both balances: 226 equals 222 + 4 and 88 equals 86 + 2. The element symbol follows the new proton number; it is not unchanged merely because the same atom started the process.

blocks.heading: Represent beta-minus decay using nuclear numbers
blocks.text:
Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton with an emitted electron and antineutrino. The nucleus’s nucleon count is unchanged while its proton number rises by one.

A phosphorus-32 nucleus can become sulfur-32: ³²₁₅P → ³²₁₆S + ⁰₋₁e in the simplified school number display. Including the antineutrino completes the particle account without changing the displayed A and charge balances. The emitted electron is produced in the decay, not an ordinary atomic-shell electron falling out.

blocks.heading: Distinguishing the ideas
blocks.text:
Nucleon number includes both protons and neutrons. Subtract proton number to obtain neutron number.

A nucleus with A = 39 and Z = 19 has 19 protons and 20 neutrons, not 39 neutrons. Treating A as neutron count adds the protons twice when reconstructing the nucleus. Reading the definitions before arithmetic keeps the particle roles clear.

blocks.heading: Practice task with worked feedback
blocks.text:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which particles are nucleons?
A. Protons and neutrons
B. Electrons and photons
C. Only electrons
D. Only protons in every nuclide

2. What fixes an element’s identity?
A. Neutron number alone
B. The sample’s temperature
C. The number of atoms in the sample
D. Proton number

3. Which pair can be isotopes?
A. Same neutrons, different protons
B. Different electric charge only
C. Same Z, different A
D. Different Z, same A

4. What is an alpha particle?
A. A neutron alone
B. Two protons and two neutrons
C. A single electron
D. An electromagnetic photon

5. What makes a tracer useful for locating a leak?
A. It follows the fluid and can be detected
B. It must block the pipe completely
C. Its charge must become zero instantly
D. The detector must create the leak

6. A sheet becomes thicker under a fixed suitable transmission monitor. What is expected?
A. Higher count because the source grows
B. No possible change in transmission
C. The detector becomes the isotope
D. Lower transmitted count

7. Carbon-14 dating is most directly suited to which model sample?
A. A shadow on a wall
B. An arbitrary vacuum gap
C. Once-living carbon-containing material
D. A newly cast pure metal with no relevant carbon history

8. A = 23 and Z = 11. How many neutrons?
A. 34
B. 12
C. 23
D. 11

9. Alpha decay starts with A = 210 and Z = 84. What are daughter numbers?
A. A = 206, Z = 82
B. A = 210, Z = 85
C. A = 208, Z = 80
D. A = 214, Z = 86

10. Beta-minus decay starts with A = 14 and Z = 6. What daughter results?
A. A = 10, Z = 4
B. A = 14, Z = 5
C. A = 13, Z = 6
D. A = 14, Z = 7

11. Atoms have 6 protons each and 6 or 8 neutrons. What follows?
A. Their A is equal
B. Both must be radioactive by definition
C. They are isotopes
D. They are different elements

12. A simple dating model leaves one quarter of initial activity. How many half-lives elapsed?
A. Zero
B. Two
C. One
D. Four

Worked feedback

1. Key A. A: They constitute the nucleus. B: These are not nucleons. C: Electrons occupy the surrounding atom. D: Most nuclei also contain neutrons.

2. Key D. A: Isotopes can differ in it. B: Heating need not change the nucleus. C: Sample size does not set element identity. D: This is atomic number Z.

3. Key C. A: Different protons mean different elements. B: That can describe ions of the same nuclide. C: They share element identity but differ in neutrons. D: They are different elements.

4. Key B. A: An alpha has four nucleons. B: It is a helium-4 nucleus. C: That is beta-minus radiation. D: That is gamma radiation.

5. Key A. A: Its movement and signal reveal location. B: That changes the flow rather than traces it. C: That is not the detection principle. D: The detector observes radiation.

6. Key D. A: The source is unchanged. B: Thickness affects attenuation. C: Detector and source are different. D: More radiation is attenuated.

7. Key C. A: It is not a material carbon sample. B: It contains no sample. C: Its post-exchange decay supplies the clock. D: The required clock is not established.

8. Key B. A: This adds instead of subtracting. B: Subtract Z from A. C: This is total nucleons. D: This is proton count.

9. Key A. A: Subtract four and two. B: That is the beta-minus change. C: The subtractions are incorrect. D: That adds the emitted particle instead of removing it.

10. Key D. A: That is the alpha change. B: That is the wrong beta-minus charge direction. C: Nucleon count is unchanged. D: A neutron becomes a proton.

11. Key C. A: Their neutron numbers differ. B: Isotope does not imply radioactivity. C: They have common Z and different A. D: Their Z is equal.

12. Key B. A: The activity has decreased. B: One half then one quarter. C: That leaves one half. D: That leaves one sixteenth.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which can contribute to background radiation?
A. Rocks and cosmic radiation
B. Only a deliberate classroom source
C. A shadow alone
D. A static ruler mark

2. What does a G-M counter record?
A. Every nucleus in the source directly
B. Only visible colour
C. The source mass with no calibration
D. Pulses triggered by radiation interactions

3. What is alpha radiation?
A. Photons
B. Neutral hydrogen atoms
C. Helium nuclei
D. Electrons

4. Which emission is neutral electromagnetic radiation?
A. A proton beam
B. Gamma
C. Alpha
D. Beta-minus

5. What is predictable for one unstable nucleus?
A. Its decay is random rather than exactly scheduled
B. Its exact decay second from its age alone
C. It must decay at one half-life
D. It cannot decay before one half-life

6. After one half-life, what expected fraction remains?
A. None
B. One quarter
C. All nuclei
D. One half

7. Which is an exposure-reduction principle?
A. Open a sealed source
B. Remove controlled storage
C. Reduce time near the source
D. Hold the source close to the body

8. Background-corrected count rate falls from 120 to 30 counts/s. How many half-lives?
A. Four
B. Two
C. One
D. Three

9. Total rate is 55 counts/s and background 5 counts/s. What source rate is used?
A. 50 counts/s
B. 60 counts/s
C. 11 counts/s
D. 55 counts/s

10. With positive plate above and negative below, which way does beta-minus deflect?
A. Downward like alpha
B. Straight solely because it is neutral
C. Only along the beam forever
D. Upward

11. Alpha emission begins at A = 230, Z = 90. What daughter numbers result?
A. A = 226, Z = 92
B. A = 234, Z = 92
C. A = 226, Z = 88
D. A = 230, Z = 91

12. Half-life is 4 h. What fraction remains after 12 h?
A. Zero
B. One eighth
C. One third
D. One quarter
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Both are natural contributors. B: Background exists without it. C: A shadow is not radioactive material. D: It is not the physical radiation source.

2. Key D. A: Only detected events are counted. B: That is not its basic signal. C: Counting is not direct weighing. D: Ionisation initiates detection.

3. Key C. A: That is gamma. B: That is not alpha. C: Two protons and two neutrons. D: That is beta-minus.

4. Key B. A: Protons are positively charged. B: It consists of photons. C: It has positive charge. D: It has negative charge.

5. Key A. A: Population statistics differ from an individual event. B: That is not predictable. C: Half-life is a population measure. D: Events can occur earlier.

6. Key D. A: Decay is not complete then. B: That follows two half-lives. C: The expected population has fallen. D: This defines the interval.

7. Key C. A: Containment should be preserved. B: Secure storage is part of control. C: Time affects accumulated exposure. D: Distance should be increased appropriately.

8. Key B. A: That leaves 7.5. B: 120 to 60 to 30. C: That leaves 60. D: That leaves 15.

9. Key A. A: Subtract background. B: This adds background. C: This divides instead. D: This leaves the background included.

10. Key D. A: Its charge sign is opposite alpha’s. B: Beta-minus is charged. C: There is a transverse force. D: The negative particle force opposes the downward field.

11. Key C. A: The Z direction is incorrect. B: This adds the emitted alpha. C: Remove four nucleons and two protons. D: That is beta-minus change.

12. Key B. A: The ideal exponential does not reach zero at that finite time. B: Three halving intervals elapsed. C: The decrease is not linear in time. D: That is two intervals.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the charge sign of beta-minus radiation. [1]

(b) State whether gamma is deflected by the simple electric-field arrangement. [1]

(c) Explain why equal short counting intervals can give different counts from the same source. [2]

(d) Calculate the half-life when corrected rate falls from 96 to 24 counts/s over 10 min. [2]

(e) Calculate corrected source count rate for 42 counts/s measured with 6 counts/s background. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Negative.

(b) It is undeflected.

(c) Individual decays occur randomly. The observed count therefore fluctuates about its expected rate.

(d) Two halvings occur, so half-life = 10/2 = 5 min.

(e) Source rate = 42 − 6 = 36 counts/s.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for negative.
(b) One mark for no deflection.
(c) One mark for random events; one for statistical fluctuation.
(d) One mark for two intervals; one for 5 min.
(e) One mark for background subtraction; one for 36 counts/s.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

blocks.heading: describe how radioactive materials are handled, used and stored in a safe way
blocks.text:
Radioactive-source work minimises exposure time, increases appropriate distance and uses suitable shielding and containment. Sources require controlled, labelled storage and authorised handling.

In a supervised school demonstration, the teacher uses the approved source holder and handling tools, keeps sources away from the body and returns them to secure designated storage. Do not touch, open or ingest source material. Shielding choice depends on radiation type and the source arrangement, so an unspecified thick object is not a complete safety plan. Learners can study supplied readings and simulations without handling sources.

blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: describe the existence and major causes of background radioactivity
blocks.text:
Background radiation is detected even without a nearby deliberate laboratory source. Contributors include cosmic radiation, radioactive rocks and soil, radon and naturally occurring isotopes in living matter.

A counter reading with the test source removed estimates background for that setup. Random variation means one short reading is not an exact fixed value. Measure over a suitable interval and convert to a rate before subtracting it from a source-plus-background rate. Compare rates in matching units.

blocks.heading: describe the detection of alpha-particles (α), beta-particles (β) and gamma-rays (γ), (cloud chamber, Geiger Mῢller (G-M) counter and photographic film)
blocks.text:
Radiation detectors reveal interactions rather than showing radioactive nuclei directly. Cloud chambers, G-M counters and photographic film provide different observable responses.

A cloud chamber makes tracks through condensation on ions, a counter records pulses associated with ionisation, and film records chemical changes after development. No one displayed count automatically identifies alpha, beta or gamma; detector design, absorption tests and controlled geometry help distinguish them.

blocks.heading: Detect radiation with a cloud chamber
blocks.text:
A cloud chamber reveals charged-particle tracks through condensation around ions. Track appearance can support interpretation but is not a direct photograph of the particle itself.

An alpha track is commonly short, thick and relatively straight in the intended comparison, while an electron track can be thinner and irregular. Gamma photons can produce secondary charged particles whose tracks are observed. Use teacher-prepared observations rather than constructing a cold or hazardous apparatus without appropriate supervision.

blocks.heading: Detect radiation with a Geiger–Müller counter
blocks.text:
A G-M tube produces electrical pulses when radiation interactions ionise its gas and trigger a discharge. A scaler counts pulses or an instrument reports a count rate.

A thin window helps some charged particles enter, while gamma detection efficiency can be lower and depends on geometry and construction. Background must be measured separately. A count rate is an instrument response, not necessarily equal to total source activity because only some emissions reach and trigger the detector.

blocks.heading: Detect radiation with photographic film
blocks.text:
Photographic film can record radiation exposure through a chemical change. After controlled development, darkening indicates interaction with the sensitive material.

A film badge can accumulate exposure information over time, while filters can help interpret the radiation reaching it. Unlike an electronic counter, it does not ordinarily give a live pulse display during exposure. Appropriate calibration is needed before converting a response into an exposure estimate.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these ideas with the neighbouring physics topics named in the topic title and with the measurement, unit and data skills taught in topics 1–3. The same quantity must keep the same physical meaning and unit when a new context is introduced.

blocks.heading: state that radioactive emissions occur randomly over space and time
blocks.text:
Radioactive decay is random for individual unstable nuclei. A large collection has statistically predictable average decay behaviour.

The exact decay time of one nucleus cannot be predicted from its age alone. Equal counting intervals can give different counts even when the expected rate is almost unchanged. Random emission direction also means a small detector intercepts only part of the total output. These fluctuations do not invalidate the repeatable half-life model for a large sample.

blocks.heading: describe radioactive emission: - their nature (e.g. its composition, relative charge, mass) - their relative ionising effects - their relative penetrating abilities
blocks.text:
Alpha, beta-minus and gamma emissions differ in nature, charge and interaction. The school comparison is alpha strongly ionising with low penetration, beta intermediate and gamma more penetrating with lower direct ionisation density.

An alpha is a helium nucleus with charge +2e and relative mass about 4. A beta-minus particle is an electron with charge −e and a mass much smaller than a nucleon. Gamma is a neutral electromagnetic photon with no rest mass. The comparison is qualitative and depends on energy and material; sufficient shielding attenuates rather than giving a magic absolute stopping thickness for every source.

blocks.heading: Describe alpha-particle nature, ionisation and penetration
blocks.text:
An alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons and has charge +2e. Its strong interactions give high ionisation density and a short range in ordinary materials.

Paper or the outer surface layer of skin can stop typical alpha particles in the school comparison, but an alpha emitter inside the body can be hazardous because it deposits energy nearby. Low external penetration therefore must not be called harmlessness.

blocks.heading: Describe beta-particle nature, ionisation and penetration
blocks.text:
Beta-minus radiation consists of fast electrons with charge −e. It generally has intermediate penetration and ionisation in the named school comparison.

Thin metal or suitable plastic can substantially attenuate beta radiation depending on energy. Electrons have much smaller mass than alpha particles and can show strong deflection in fields. The beta electron originates in nuclear decay rather than being a pre-existing electron stored inside a neutron as a tiny planetary object.

blocks.heading: Describe gamma-ray nature, ionisation and penetration
blocks.text:
Gamma radiation consists of electromagnetic photons with no net electric charge. It is typically highly penetrating and requires substantial attenuation shielding compared with alpha and beta.

Gamma can ionise indirectly when interactions create energetic charged particles. Lead or concrete can reduce the transmitted intensity, with effectiveness depending on thickness and photon energy. Neutrality means an ordinary electric or magnetic field does not bend its path in the school model; it does not mean gamma cannot transfer energy.

blocks.heading: describe their deflection in electric fields and magnetic fields
blocks.text:
Electric and magnetic fields distinguish charged radiation from neutral gamma in the basic deflection model. Alpha and beta-minus deflect oppositely when launched in the same direction through the same field arrangement.

For an electric field, force follows the positive-charge direction for alpha and the opposite direction for beta-minus. For a magnetic field, charge sign and velocity direction both matter. Gamma continues straight in the intended field-only model. Relative curvature also depends on speed and momentum, so charge alone does not set an exact radius.

blocks.heading: Describe deflection of alpha, beta and gamma in an electric field
blocks.text:
In a uniform electric field, alpha force is along the field and beta-minus force is opposite it. Gamma has no electric deflection in this model.

If a beam travels rightward between an upper positive plate and lower negative plate, the field points downward. Alpha curves downward toward the negative plate, beta-minus upward toward the positive plate, and gamma continues straight. Draw the plate signs before choosing curvature.

blocks.heading: Describe deflection of alpha, beta and gamma in a magnetic field
blocks.text:
Magnetic force on charged moving radiation is perpendicular to its motion and the field. Opposite charge signs produce opposite deflections for the same initial velocity and field.

For a rightward beam and field into the page, positive alpha curves upward. Beta-minus curves downward because its charge is negative, and gamma is undeflected. Use conventional-current direction or reverse the positive-charge result for electrons. The curved trajectory does not mean the magnetic field is doing work through a force along the velocity in this ideal account.

blocks.heading: interpret their relative ionising effects
blocks.text:
Ionisation removes or adds electrons to produce charged atoms or molecules. Different radiation types deposit energy with different spatial densities in the school comparison.

An alpha particle can create many ions along a short path, explaining its thick cloud-chamber trace and strong local biological effect when internal. Gamma can travel farther between interactions but still produce ionisation through secondary particles. Distinguish ionising effect from penetration rather than assuming the most penetrating radiation must create the densest short track.

blocks.heading: state the meaning of radioactive decay and give appropriate nuclide equations to represent changes in the composition of the nucleus when particles are emitted
blocks.text:
Radioactive decay is spontaneous change of an unstable nucleus with emission. Nuclear-number balances identify the resulting nuclide change.

Alpha reduces A by four and Z by two; beta-minus keeps A and raises Z by one; gamma emission leaves both unchanged while reducing nuclear excitation energy. As examples, ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He and ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e show the school number balances. The beta-minus antineutrino is omitted from that simplified display but contributes neither A nor charge.

blocks.heading: Define radioactive decay
blocks.text:
Radioactive decay is spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus with emission of particles or radiation. It is a nuclear process rather than ordinary electron-shell chemistry.

A nucleus can move toward a more stable configuration without an external trigger for that individual event. The event is random, while the population follows statistical patterns. Ordinary school changes of temperature or pressure do not provide a practical on-off switch for the decay.

blocks.heading: Represent nuclear changes during decay
blocks.text:
Nucleon-number and charge conservation determine daughter nuclear numbers. Alpha removes (A,Z) = (4,2), beta-minus adds one to daughter Z at unchanged A, and gamma changes neither.

Starting with A = 222 and Z = 86, alpha leaves A = 218 and Z = 84. Check the emitted particle on the same side of the equation as the daughter so both sums match the parent. Do not subtract four from Z or add two to A by confusing their notation positions.

blocks.heading: define half-life as the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei to decay
blocks.text:
Half-life is the time for half the unstable nuclei in a large sample to decay on average. The same interval halves the expected activity of a single-isotope sample under the simple model.

The next half-life removes half of the remaining nuclei rather than the same absolute number as before. After two half-lives one quarter remains, and after three one eighth. An individual nucleus does not have a scheduled appointment to decay exactly one half-life after it was formed.

blocks.heading: use the term half-life in simple calculations which might involve information in tables or decay curves
blocks.text:
Repeated half-lives give a geometric decrease of remaining nuclei or source activity. Measured count rate must be corrected for background before using a simple source-halving model.

Original curve data give background-corrected source rates of 80, 40, 20 and 10 counts/s at 0, 6, 12 and 18 min. The half-life is 6 min. If a constant background of 5 counts/s were added, the measured sequence would be 85, 45, 25 and 15 counts/s; halving those totals would be wrong. Read several halving intervals on a smooth curve and compare them.
